criticality_why:
VERDICT: critical. Kept after review, with one weak piece of evidence removed and one caveat added.

THE TEST. "Critical" needs two things at once: (1) the business stops or its licence is at risk if the system fails, and (2) it is where the firm competes.

TEST 1, BUSINESS STOPS OR LICENCE AT RISK. Met. Checked against the primary sources.
- The grain accounting system (AGRIS, Agvance, AgTrax and similar) is the system of record for scale tickets, farmer contracts, settlements, warehouse receipts and the daily grain position.
- Iowa (verified): warehouse operators must keep a daily grain position record for each grain, showing the increase, decrease and ending balance of total stocks.
- Indiana (verified in the ISDA reference guide): every licensee must keep a perpetual inventory record or daily position report (DPR), updated daily. The licence renewal package must include the DPR for the fiscal year-end, and missing documents trigger late fees.
- So if the system is down, an elevator cannot weigh grain in, pay farmers, or show the regulator that stored grain is covered.

TEST 2, WHERE THE FIRM COMPETES. Clearly met for merchants and processors, only partly met for co-ops.
- Merchants and processors: the CTRM/ERP is the position, P&L and risk book, and merchants compete on basis, logistics and risk. Evidence they treat it as differentiating: Cargill built its own AWS trading and risk platform (verified on the Solution Design Group page), and a "world-class agri-business" paid Adaptive to build a bespoke CTRM with a large, distributed team over an extended period (verified in the case study PDF).
- Co-ops and elevators: they buy packaged software and rarely build, so the core ledger is not where they compete. They do compete for farmer grain on contracts, fast settlement and farmer portals, which run on this system. That is partial support only.

WHAT I CHANGED.
- Removed the ADM material weakness as evidence. The FY2024 10-K weakness concerns how intersegment sales were classified in segment reporting, not a system failure. It does not show system criticality.
- Softened the ADM ERP point. The 10-K says ADM is upgrading its ERP systems worldwide in phases over several years. That shows scale of investment, not by itself a business-stopping risk.

CAVEAT FOR THE ICP. For the recommended first buyer (mid-market co-ops), the system is licence-critical but closer to "important" on the differentiation test. Pricing and sales should lean on the licence and compliance risk, not on competitive edge.

enterprise.evidence:
WHO: global grain merchants and large processors (ADM, Bunge-Viterra, Cargill, LDC, COFCO, Wilmar/Olam-class).

REVIEW RESULT: build verdict and spend range kept. Sources checked and supporting arguments tightened.

BUILD OR BUY: common. They usually buy an ERP base and build or own the trading and risk layer on top.
1. Cargill (verified): Solution Design Group helped Cargill build an AWS cloud-hybrid risk management and commodities trading platform that unified its applications and data. The page calls it Cargill's first production-ready cloud app.
2. Unnamed major (verified): Adaptive's case study describes a bespoke CTRM covering trade capture to invoicing for a 'world-class agri-business corporation'. A large, distributed team built it over an extended period. Its first release replaced the legacy trade-capture front end.
3. Covantis (from earlier research, not re-opened): ADM, Bunge, Cargill, COFCO, LDC and Viterra jointly own this post-trade execution platform. It shows they build shared infrastructure together, but it is not a CTRM.
4. Bought base, heavily customised: ADM's FY2024 10-K describes worldwide ERP upgrades phased over several years. A Cargill supplier document says Cargill's North American grain business went onto SAP (search snippet only, not opened).

SPEND: $2M to $50M a year per buyer.
- Floor, $2M (verified inputs): Molecule's mid-size legacy ETRM/CTRM example is a $1M licence on a 4-year contract ($250k a year), plus maintenance of about 20% of licence ($200k a year), about $450k a year in total. Molecule also says services are typically 75% of total cost. That makes the full cost about 4x the licence and maintenance, roughly $1.8M a year for a mid-size install. A multi-region enterprise sits at or above that, so $2M holds.
- Ceiling, $50M (verified input, estimated split): ADM's FY2024 10-K shows $134M of additions to capitalised software and intangibles in process. That number covers all of ADM's IT and includes capitalised internal labour. If about a third goes to ERP, commodity and trading systems, that is about $30-45M. A $50M ceiling for the very largest merchants is reasonable but not proven.
- Supporting signal (search snippet only, page returned 403): a CTRM Center post citing Moody's says Triple Point's top 10 customers made up 50% of its 2012 revenue. That fits a few enterprises each paying millions a year.

CONFIDENCE: medium on the build pattern. Low to medium on the dollars, since no merchant discloses its trading-system spend directly.

mid_market.evidence:
WHO: regional grain and farm-supply co-ops and ag retailers with about 10-100 locations, plus mid-size merchants, feed millers and crushers.

REVIEW RESULT: build verdict kept. Spend floor CUT from $100k to $50k. The per-location rate behind it was overstated by about 1.5-3x.

BUILD OR BUY: rare. They buy packaged software.
- SSI (verified): Agvance runs at 3,800+ ag-retail locations with 25,000+ users. About 50% of the CropLife Top 100 ag retailers are SSI companies.
- AGRIS says it scales from one to hundreds of locations. ION says 300+ agricultural organisations use its CTRMs (earlier research).
- AgriChain (verified): custom systems exist but are 'often expensive to maintain and difficult to update'.
- The in-house piece is usually a spreadsheet beside the core system (Eka survey from earlier research: 66% use spreadsheets for analysis), not an owned core.

SPEND: $50k to $1M a year per buyer.

Step 1, per-location rate (CORRECTED). The draft took SSI's ~163 staff (LeadIQ, verified) times an assumed $150-200k revenue per employee, giving $25-33M of revenue and $6-9k per location. Every third-party revenue estimate found is lower: ZoomInfo $20.8M, plus other directory estimates of $6M and $7.1M. LeadIQ's '$100M-$250M' does not fit 163 staff. SSI's revenue also includes EnergyForce (propane and fuel software), not only Agvance locations. Using $7-21M over 3,800+ locations gives about $2-6k per location per year. I replaced $6-9k with $2-6k.

Step 2, co-op total. 10-100 locations at $2-6k is about $20k-$600k for the core package. Grain co-ops also pay for the grain module, scale integrations, a farmer portal such as Bushel, and implementation services, which lifts the small end. $50k is a realistic floor. The draft's $100k was about 2.5x the core-package estimate at 10 locations.

Step 3, upper end. Kept at $1M. A mid-size merchant on a packaged CTRM pays about $450k a year in licence and maintenance (Molecule, verified), before services. A 100-location co-op lands around $600k plus add-ons.

Step 4, cost model (verified). Agvance's subscription bundles licences, hosting, backups, updates and support. Over 60% of Agvance users and over half of customer companies have already moved to it. No prices are published.

CONFIDENCE: low to medium. No co-op or vendor has published a real contract value, and the per-location rate rests on third-party revenue estimates.

smb.evidence:
WHO: independent country elevators with 1-3 sites, small grain dealers and small exporters. USDA counts 7,922 off-farm grain storage facilities (facilities, not firms; earlier research).

REVIEW RESULT: build verdict and range kept. The ceiling's arithmetic changed but stays within 2x.

BUILD OR BUY: rare. They buy a small package or run on spreadsheets and paper.
- Horizon Grain (verified) targets operators with one or two scales, one office and no dedicated IT or finance staff, where one person handles the scale, the buying and the admin.

SPEND: $4k to $40k a year per buyer.
- Floor, $4k (verified): Horizon Grain publishes $400 a month or $4,000 a year, with the rate held for 36 months.
- Ceiling, $40k (estimated): at the corrected $2-6k per location (see mid-market), a 2-4 location buyer on Agvance or AGRIS pays about $4-24k. An SME CTRM subscription for a small trader at about $2,500 a month is about $30k a year (search snippet, not verified). One-off costs such as about $1,900 per extra Agvance workstation licence (search snippet) sit on top. $40k is the top of the plausible band. Most SMBs will sit well below it.
- Vertical Software (Ceres) charges an annual subscription per scale licence with no per-ticket fees but publishes no price.

CONFIDENCE: medium on the floor (published price), low on the ceiling.

government.evidence:
WHO: state grain buyers and food-reserve agencies (USDA AMS commodity procurement, Food Corporation of India, Indian state procurement departments, Bulog, Philippine NFA, PASSCO). Regulators such as the Canadian Grain Commission sit on the edge of this segment.

REVIEW RESULT: build verdict and range kept. The ceiling is a contract maximum, and the floor rests on one adjacent data point.

BUILD OR BUY: common. Governments commission custom systems or run their own instance through an integrator. They do not buy AGRIS-type packages.
- USDA WBSCM (verified): a USDA system for ordering, buying, distributing and tracking commodities, built on SAP and Salesforce, sustained by CACI. The 2021 task order runs 7 years with a $376M ceiling and covers sustainment, cloud migration, S/4HANA modernisation and expanded Salesforce.
- Odisha P-PAS: a custom paddy procurement system for the state Food Supplies department (CSM Technologies case study; snippets credit the state agency OMEGA).
- FCI Depot Online System on VIT DepoSoft, with Ricoh and Mars as integrators (snippet only).
- India's e-NAM was built and run by a contracted 'strategic partner' (snippet only).

SPEND: $300k to $55M a year per buyer.
- Ceiling, $55M (verified input): $376M over 7 years is about $54M a year. This is a ceiling, so actual spend may be lower. The previous award was $199M over 5 years, about $40M a year (snippet only).
- Floor, $300k (one adjacent data point): the Canadian Grain Commission awarded a PostgreSQL database modernisation at CAD 1,450,560 over 24 months (Jan 2026 to Jan 2028), about CAD 725k or roughly US$520k a year (confirmed via search result for the CanadaBuys award notice). It is a regulator's database project, not a procurement system. The claim that small national reserves spend a few hundred thousand a year has no source.
- Middle: India's e-NAM fund of ₹200 crore over 3 years (snippet) also paid for market infrastructure, so the software share is well below the roughly $8M a year it implies.

CONFIDENCE: high on the build pattern, medium on WBSCM, low on the floor.

best_icp: Sell first to North American mid-market grain co-ops and ag retailers with 10-100 locations: they buy rather than build, spend about $50k-$1M a year on AGRIS, Agvance or AgTrax (more than half of Agvance customers have already moved to vendor-hosted subscription, so pitch better grain workflows rather than "get off on-prem"), run without big IT teams, need no government tender, and should be landed with an overlay such as daily position, settlements or contracts, because the core ledger is licence-critical and a rip-and-replace is too risky as a first sale, while SMBs pay too little ($4k-40k), enterprises build their own trading layer, and governments buy custom builds through integrators.

criticality_why:
Rating: critical. Both tests are met, though the second one only for the retailing layer.

Test 1. Does the airline stop without it? Yes. The PSS holds every booking, seat, ticket and check-in. When it goes down, sales and boarding stop within minutes. Example: a two-hour Sabre outage hit about 380 airlines. Agents wrote boarding passes by hand, websites could not book or change trips, and Virgin Australia cancelled 35 flights (IEEE Spectrum). The research file lists Amadeus (2017) and Navitaire (Spirit, Virgin Blue 2010) outages with the same effect. The Delhi High Court also called the PSS essential to Air India's continuity of operations (Travelobiz, opened).

Test 2. Is it where airlines compete? Partly. Offers, pricing, ancillaries, NDC and the move to offer-and-order retailing all run through the PSS. Evidence that buyers pay for that edge: in its 2021 quality-cum-cost tender, state-owned Air India chose Amadeus at Rs 1,957 crore over Sabre at Rs 1,039 crore, almost double the price. The court upheld the choice, saying Air India may pick the system that gives it an edge over its peers (Travelobiz, opened).

Caveat a reader should weigh: the reservation core (inventory, ticketing, DCS) is shared plumbing. More than 200 airlines run the same Altea system, so the core alone would rate 'important'. The 'critical' call rests on the retailing layer that sits on top of it.

Checker's verdict: call kept. It is justified, but it is the borderline case of 'critical'.

enterprise.evidence:
WHO: network and flag carriers with 30m to 200m+ passengers boarded (PB) a year.

BUILD VS BUY: almost all buy. Rating corrected from 'some' to 'rare'.
- Delta is the one clear owner. In May 2014 it bought back the data and IP rights to its PSS (Deltamatic) and flight-ops systems from Travelport, effective 1 July 2014. More than 175 tech staff moved to Delta, and Travelport still hosts the systems in Atlanta (Travelport IR release and Travel Weekly, confirmed by search; the pages themselves returned 403).
- ANA no longer counts. It ran its own domestic PSS (able-D, built by Unisys) from 1988, but finished moving domestic onto Amadeus Altea in May to June 2026 (ANA HD release and Amadeus H1 2026 review, via search). JAL made the same move earlier.
- Everyone else rents a hosted system. American uses SabreSonic. Southwest, Qantas and Lufthansa Group use Amadeus Altea.
Result: one owner among dozens of large carriers is 'rare', not 'some'.

SPEND: $25m to $200m a year (unchanged). How it was built:
Step 1. Price per passenger, from vendor results.
- Amadeus Air IT Solutions: EUR 2,345.9m revenue on 2,248.6m PB in FY2025 = EUR 1.04 per PB, about $1.15 to $1.20 (Amadeus FY2025 release, opened; both figures confirmed). This average includes add-on modules.
- Sabre IT Solutions: about $570m to $580m in 2024 (Q4 alone was $145m) on about 680m PB = about $0.85 per PB (Sabre 2024 release, via search).
Step 2. Multiply by volume. $0.8 to $1.2 per PB x 30m to 200m PB = about $25m to $240m.
Step 3. Cap the top at $200m, because the biggest carriers win volume discounts.
Step 4. Cross-check with a real contract. Air India's 7-year Amadeus award (Rs 1,957 crore) = about Rs 280 crore a year = about $37m at 2021 rates (Rs 74/USD). That sits at the low end, as expected for a carrier of Air India's 2021 size.

CONFIDENCE: medium. Built from vendor averages and one tender, not from disclosed per-airline prices.

mid_market.evidence:
WHO: LCCs, hybrid carriers and mid-size flag carriers with about 2m to 30m PB a year.

BUILD VS BUY: they buy. Common systems are Navitaire New Skies (70+ airlines), Hitit Crane (73 airlines in 51 countries, Hitit release, opened), Radixx, Altea and SabreSonic. No mid-size airline building its own PSS turned up. Rating 'rare' confirmed.

SPEND: $1m to $25m a year (unchanged). Three anchors:
Anchor 1. Biman Bangladesh, a real contract at the bottom edge of this segment (Daily Star report of an auditor-general audit, opened). 10-year Sabre deal from a public tender.
- PSS usage fee: $50,000 a month covers the first 100,000 PB, then $0.88 per extra passenger.
- At 1.83m PB a year that is about $1.17m a year, or about $0.64 per PB.
- Note: 1.83m PB is just under this segment's 2m floor, so treat Biman as the boundary case.
- The audit puts the whole 10-year deal at Tk 1,019 to 1,059 crore, about $10m a year. That total covers PSS, DCS, e-commerce, loyalty, BI and the GDS Sabre has supplied since 2003, so it is wider than the PSS alone.
Anchor 2. Hitit, a vendor selling into this segment. Revenue was $34.2m in 2024 and $31.2m in the first nine months of 2025 (Hitit release, opened). Across 73 airlines that averages $0.5m to $0.6m each, pulled down by many small customers.
Anchor 3. Per-passenger math. $0.6 to $1.2 per PB x 2m to 30m PB = about $1.2m to $36m. The top is trimmed to $25m because at 30m PB a carrier negotiates toward $0.8 per PB, and Air India, a larger carrier, pays about $37m.

CONFIDENCE: medium.

smb.evidence:
CORRECTION: the low figure was entered as $15,000,000, which is above the $1m high. The evidence supports $15,000. Fixed.

WHO: small regional, charter, island and new-start airlines with under about 2m PB a year (EU Category B licences, US Part 135 operators, small Category A carriers).

BUILD VS BUY: they buy light hosted systems such as Videcom VRS, GO7/AeroCRS, Radixx or entry-level Hitit. In-house builds are essentially absent. Rating 'rare' confirmed.

SPEND: $15k to $1m a year. How it was built:
Step 1. A published price. AeroCRS charges $0.70 per booked segment, where a segment is one passenger on one flight. API requests are free up to 400,000 a month, then $0.001 each. The page says these rates apply to all integration types (AeroCRS pricing docs, opened). Listing sites quote platform plans of $99 to $713 a month; Capterra says 'contact vendor'.
Step 2. Per-passenger math. $0.5 to $0.9 per segment x 20k to 1.5m segments = about $10k to $1.35m a year, rounded to $15k to $1m.
Step 3. Cross-checks. Hitit's average of about $0.5m per customer falls inside the range. Biman, at 1.83m PB, pays about $1.17m for PSS usage, which matches the top end.

CAVEAT: the AeroCRS segment fee is for bookings made through integrations and may not be the full PSS bill. Small airlines also pay separately for GDS, DCS and payments.

CONFIDENCE: low to medium.

government.evidence:
WHO: the only government buyers are state-owned airlines, for example Air India before its 2022 privatisation, Biman Bangladesh, Vietnam Airlines, Garuda and PIA. Ministries and agencies do not buy a PSS.

BUILD VS BUY: these airlines buy through public tenders. No in-house builds found. Rating 'rare' confirmed.

SPEND: $1m to $40m a year (unchanged). Two public tenders set the range:
Tender 1. Air India, 2021 (Travelobiz report of the Delhi High Court ruling, opened). 7-year PSS covering scheduling, reservations, e-commerce, loyalty and DCS, replacing SITA before its contract ended in June 2022. Amadeus won at Rs 1,957 crore (about $37m a year). Sabre bid Rs 1,039 crore (about $20m a year). Amadeus won on a quality-cum-cost score, not price.
Tender 2. Biman Bangladesh, 2020 (Daily Star audit report, opened). Sabre won. PSS usage fee about $1.17m a year. Whole 10-year deal, including GDS and other services, about Tk 1,019 to 1,059 crore.
The range runs from Biman at the bottom to Air India at the top, set by airline size.

CAVEAT: very large state-owned carriers (for example Emirates or Saudia) would land in the enterprise math and could exceed $40m a year. Chinese state carriers use TravelSky, a state-owned shared system, so they are not an open market. Treat those as enterprise accounts, not as this segment.

WHAT A SELLER SHOULD EXPECT: formal tenders, often scored on quality as well as cost. Losing bidders sue (Sabre sued Air India and lost) and auditors review the deals (Bangladesh's auditor-general on Biman). Expect long sales cycles and 7- to 10-year contracts.

CONFIDENCE: medium.

best_icp: Start with small mid-market and new-start airlines carrying about 0.5m to 10m passengers a year (LCCs, regionals and greenfield carriers), because they always buy rather than build, spend about $0.5m to $10m a year on per-passenger SaaS terms, sign roughly 5-year deals (for example Air Montenegro's move to Hitit), and can cut over in months, while enterprise carriers need multi-year migrations (Southwest used 1,500+ people), sit in 3- to 10-year hosted contracts, and in Delta's case own the system outright.

criticality_why:
VERDICT: critical. The call holds, with one caveat about small brokers.

TEST 1. Does failure stop the business or put the licence at risk? Yes.
- A broker-dealer that cannot clear, settle and keep its books cannot trade.
- The system carries the firm's legal duties for customer custody (SEC Rule 15c3-3) and books and records (SEC Rule 17a-3). SEBI and OJK impose the same duties in India and Indonesia.
- Regulators gate every cutover. Checked: SEBI wrote to MCX on 28 Sep 2023 telling it to hold the planned 3 Oct 2023 go-live of its new TCS platform. SEBI lifted the hold only after its Technical Advisory Committee cleared it. In Australia, the RBA and ASIC oversee the CHESS replacement.

TEST 2. Is it where the firm competes? Yes, for the firms that own these systems.
- Robinhood built its own clearing over about two years and launched it in Oct 2018. Checked in InvestmentNews: the goals were to cut the fees it paid Apex, and to run statements, tax documents and customer service itself. CORRECTION: the earlier draft said 'roughly 70 staff'. The cited source gives no headcount, so I removed it.
- Pinetree Securities (Vietnam) has run its own core since 2019. A May 2026 FireAnt review credits that core with a smoother switch to the new KRX system at HOSE than rivals on vendor platforms had.
- Zerodha built its Kite trading platform and Console back office in-house. This is widely reported, but no source in the list covers it.
- For exchanges and clearing houses (MCX, ASX, HOSE), the trading and clearing stack is the product they sell.

CAVEAT. Small introducing brokers outsource clearing to a carrying firm and treat it as a utility. For them it is closer to 'important'. They are customers of the firms that own these systems, not owners.

enterprise.evidence:
SUMMARY: about $5M to $60M a year per firm in vendor processing fees. Building in-house is common. CORRECTION: low end cut from $10M to $5M. The old figure had no support, and the Broadridge data below points nearer $4-5M for a tier-2 client.

1. WHO BUYS
Large self-clearing broker-dealers, primary dealers, wirehouses and the largest retail brokers. FINRA counted 155 large member firms (500+ registered reps) at end-2025. Checked: FINRA 2026 Industry Snapshot, which gives 155 large, 197 mid-size and 2,832 small firms, 3,184 in all.

2. BUILD OR BUY: building is common
(a) Broadridge's 2010 investor deck (slide 19): of 191 US firms that process equities, 87 (45%) did it in-house, 53 (28%) used Broadridge and 51 (27%) used other vendors. Checked.
(b) Broadridge FY2026 10-K: its capital markets solutions 'compete with in-house operations'. The 10-K also warns that larger merged clients could take services in-house. Checked.
(c) Many of the biggest firms still buy. Broadridge says it serves the 15 largest US wealth providers and 22 of the 26 US primary dealers. Checked in the FY2026 10-K.

3. SPEND, STEP BY STEP
Broadridge does not publish what each client pays. The figures below come from its disclosed share of revenue from its 15 largest clients.
Step 1, FY2022 (best data). GTO segment revenue was $1,474.4M. The 15 largest GTO clients produced about 46% of it. Both figures checked in the FY2022 10-K. 46% x $1,474.4M = about $678M, or about $45M per top-15 client.
Step 2, FY2026 scale-up. GTO revenue grew to $1,916.0M ($1,184.2M Capital Markets plus $731.8M Wealth). Checked in the Q4 FY2026 earnings release. The FY2026 10-K does not restate the top-15 share. If it is still about 46%, the average top-15 client pays about $59M. That gives the $60M high end.
Step 3, FY2010 cross-check. Securities Processing revenue was $535.9M, and the top 15 clients produced about 70% of it. Checked in the FY2010 10-K. That is $375M, or $25M per top-15 client. The other 30% (about $161M) was spread over the remaining clients, at roughly $4M or less each. That is why the low end is $5M, not $10M.

4. CAVEATS
- These are averages for one vendor. Its top-15 clients are the very largest banks and wealth firms.
- GTO includes wealth-management tools and order management (Itiviti), not only clearing and back office. That makes the figures slightly too high for clearing alone.
- Firms that build in-house spend mainly on their own staff, which this range leaves out.

mid_market.evidence:
SUMMARY: about $0.3M to $6M a year. Most firms buy and a few build. CORRECTION: high end raised from $5M to $6M. The Siebert filing has a $3.99M data-processing line that the earlier draft left out. The change is small; the range was not off by 2x.

1. WHO BUYS
Regional and specialist self-clearing broker-dealers, and mid-size Asian securities companies. Counts: 197 FINRA mid-size firms (151-499 reps, end-2025, checked). Also about 40 Vietnamese firms on FSS FLEX (checked: FSS says 'nearly 40 securities companies'). Not re-checked: 119 Indonesian securities companies (OJK) and 36 SET member firms in Thailand.

2. BUILD OR BUY: mostly buy, some build
- Most firms license packaged cores: FSS FLEX in Vietnam (checked); ShilpiSoft in India (checked: '200+ live brokers'); MPC S21 in Indonesia (the vendor says it serves more than half of IDX members; not verified); and KGiSL Dolphin.
- A few build their own. Pinetree in Vietnam has run its own core since 2019 (checked, FireAnt).

3. SPEND, STEP BY STEP
Step 1, a US anchor from Siebert Financial's FY2025 10-K (all checked). Siebert had $94.2M net revenue and 166 staff. It self-clears in part and also clears through Fidelity's NFS. It reported:
- clearing fees, including execution costs: $2.149M
- data processing: $3.989M
- technology and communications: $5.255M
Clearing plus data processing is about $6.1M. Adding part of the technology line puts the whole stack at about $6-8M. The $6M high end uses the narrower figure.
Step 2, contract minimums (checked, new evidence).
- Siebert's 2023 Broadridge back-office agreement carries a total minimum of about $1.2M over five years, about $240K a year.
- Siebert's NFS clearing amendment sets a $40,000 monthly minimum for clearing and execution, about $480K a year.
These minimums support the $0.3M low end.
Step 3, Asia. Mid-size Asian brokers likely sit at about $0.3-1M. This is an inference only. FSS, MPC and KGiSL do not publish prices.

4. WHY THIS MATTERS FOR SALES
Contracts are long and costly to leave. The Broadridge deal runs five years, to June 2028. The NFS amendment sets early-termination fees from $8.0M in year 1 down to $3.25M in year 4. A new vendor has to time its approach to renewal windows.

5. CAVEATS
No public price list exists for this segment. The US anchor is a single firm.

smb.evidence:
SUMMARY: about $2,000 to $150,000 a year. Building is rare. CORRECTION: the source for the high end changed. The earlier draft cited a '$10,000 monthly minimum' from a sample clearing agreement. I opened that agreement (Legent / Network 1, SEC exhibit 99.1). It mentions a 'stated monthly minimum' but gives no dollar amount, so that figure is withdrawn. The $150K high end now rests on the reasoning in Step 2 and is marked as an estimate.

1. WHO BUYS
Small introducing brokers and sub-brokers. FINRA counted 2,832 small firms (1-150 reps) at end-2025 (checked). Many are investment-banking or M&A boutiques that never clear retail trades. Not re-checked: about 4,993 SEBI-registered equity brokers in India.

2. BUILD OR BUY: building is rare
- US: most small firms clear 'fully disclosed' through a carrying firm (Pershing, NFS, Apex and others) under FINRA Rule 4311. The carrying firm handles their back office.
- Thailand: SET picked KGiSL Dolphin in Aug 2021 as a shared back office that SET hosts for its brokers (checked).
- Indonesia: IDX's IT subsidiary (IDXSTI) sells BOFIS, a managed front- and back-office service for exchange members, on an opex basis (checked). Correction: the earlier draft said 'pay-as-you-go'. The page says 'OPEX scheme' and gives no prices.
- India: at least a third of NSE's 800+ members relied only on NSE's free NOW terminal until NSE shut it in 2020 (checked, Moneylife).

3. SPEND, STEP BY STEP
Step 1, low end. Microsign's iLedger cloud back office for Indian stockbrokers is listed at Rs 2,00,000 a year, about $2,300-2,400. Seen in search results; the IndiaMART page itself was rate-limited.
Step 2, high end (estimate). Siebert, a mid-size firm with 166 staff, has a $40K monthly NFS minimum, about $480K a year (checked). A small introducing firm should pay well below that, so up to about $150K a year.
Step 3, a market-value check. ODIN, the dominant Indian broker terminal (the vendor claims a 70-80% share), sold to Synapsewave for about Rs 98 cr (about $11.8M). The deal was agreed Aug 2024 and closed 20 Jan 2025 (checked, MarketScreener). A business that cheap implies small licence fees per broker.

4. CAVEATS
US clearing fees pay for a service (capital, custody, operations), not only software. The high end is an inference, not a disclosed price.

government.evidence:
SUMMARY: about $1M to $10M a year to run, plus one-off replacements of about $35M to $300M. No change to the range. All key figures checked.

1. WHO BUYS
State-owned exchanges, depositories and central-bank securities systems. Examples are HOSE in Vietnam and central banks such as Kosovo's, which runs a Montran depository. Regulators (SEBI, RBA/ASIC, OJK) do not buy these systems, but they approve cutovers and set deadlines. There are about one or two buyers per country.

2. BUILD OR BUY: some build
- Older utilities built their own: ASX built CHESS in 1994, and NSE built NOW around 2008.
- Current replacements go to vendors through tenders: Korea Exchange for HOSE, TCS for MCX, and Montran for the Central Bank of Kosovo.

3. SPEND, STEP BY STEP
Step 1, HOSE (state-owned). Korea Exchange won the KRX package in 2012 for VND900bn ($36.6M) (checked, The Investor). It went live on 5 May 2025 (checked, FireAnt). Spread over about 13 years, that is about $3M a year.
Step 2, MCX (a listed exchange, used as a cost analogue). Checked in Moneylife and ICICI Direct.
- In FY22 MCX paid 63 moons Rs 15 cr a quarter, about $7M a year.
- While the switch to TCS was delayed, the extension fees rose to Rs 60 cr, then 81 cr, then 125 cr a quarter: Rs 222 cr over three quarters.
- The TCS contract runs six years. Annual maintenance of Rs 8-10 cr (about $1.0-1.2M) starts in year two.
- MCX's own capex on the new platform was Rs 300-350 cr (about $36-42M).
Step 3, ASX (a listed company, used as an analogue). Checked in the ASX release of 26 Nov 2024.
- CHESS Release 1 (clearing, due 2026) is expected at the upper end of A$105-125M.
- Release 2 (settlement and subregister, targeted for 2029) is estimated at A$270-320M.
In US dollars that is about $80M plus $175-210M of one-off project cost.

4. CAVEATS
MCX and ASX are not government-owned. They show what a national market utility spends, not a government budget. Large utilities in the middle of a replacement can spend well above $10M a year.

best_icp: Sell first to mid-market self-clearing brokers and mid-size Asian securities companies that spend about $0.3-6M a year on aging packaged cores (FSS FLEX, MPC S21, KGiSL, ShilpiSoft); they cannot build their own and switch on 3-5 year contract cycles, so the pitch should be timed to renewals, whereas enterprise firms build in-house or are tied to Broadridge, national utilities are regulator-gated single-buyer tenders, and small introducing brokers outsource to their clearing firm on tiny budgets.

criticality_why: VERDICT: critical, kept after review, with one scope limit. WHY THE BUSINESS STOPS WITHOUT IT. For a card issuer, the processing platform is the card product. It authorizes every purchase, posts transactions, calculates interest and fees, produces statements and connects to Visa and Mastercard. If it goes down, cardholders cannot spend and the issuer earns no interchange or interest. It also carries scheme certification, PCI and consumer-credit duties, so a failure brings regulatory and scheme penalties. WHY IT IS WHERE ISSUERS COMPETE. Rewards, credit-line logic and how fast a new card product can launch all live in this system. American Express re-platformed its own payments network starting in 2018 and says no transactions were interrupted in either migration (americanexpress.io). WHAT THE CONTRACTS SHOW. Global Payments' 10-K says most Issuer Solutions contracts carry annual minimums, early-termination penalties and service-level penalties. Bank of America signed a minimum six-year TSYS term in 2012 with a conversion of about 24 months. Buyers do not accept terms like these for a convenience system. SCOPE LIMIT. The rating applies to firms that issue and run their own card portfolio. A small bank that offers a branded card through an agent issuer (Elan, Fiserv) does not run the system and would rate it 'important' at most. REVIEW NOTE. The earlier draft quoted Amex as reporting "zero customer-impacting downtime". That wording does not appear on the page. Replaced with what the page says. The draft also said Amex built its network 'for this reason', which the source does not state. Removed.

enterprise.evidence: SUMMARY. Spend runs from about $5M a year (large regional issuer, about 2M accounts) to about $250M (top-5 issuer). In-house ownership is common among the top five or so issuers and rare below them, so 'some' fits the whole band better than 'common'. CORRECTIONS MADE. (1) Low end cut from $20M to $5M: the per-account math below puts a 2M-account issuer at about $5-6M, so $20M was off by more than 2x for the bottom of the band. (2) build_in_house changed from 'common' to 'some'. The draft's own evidence said ownership becomes outsourcing as you move down the band. STEP 1. WHO OWNS IT (verified examples). In-house: American Express runs and re-platformed its own network (americanexpress.io). JPMorgan Chase: TSYS's 2004 release gave Chase the option to move in-house under a perpetual TS2 license with a six-year payment term. Citi reportedly runs a licensed VisionPLUS copy (carried from earlier research, not re-verified here). Outsourced: Bank of America signed a minimum six-year TSYS term in 2012. It was moving back from its own in-house system and kept an option to go in-house again later under a TS2 license. So BofA has used both models. Capital One has used TSYS for North American and UK portfolios since 2005-2007, extended in 2017-2018. STEP 2. PRICE PER ACCOUNT. TSYS's 2018 annual report shows Issuer Solutions net revenue of $1,718.2M and 614.0M traditional accounts on file (739.3M total). That is about $2.30-$2.80 per account per year, all services included. TSYS bills per account on file, per transaction and authorization, per statement and per card embossed, plus licence and professional services (GPN 10-K). STEP 3. AVERAGE PER CLIENT. Global Payments' 2024 Issuer Solutions revenue was $2,483.7M GAAP and $2,113.2M adjusted net (Q4 2024 earnings release, verified). FIS says the unit serves 'over 150 financial institutions and corporate clients'. $2.1B / 150 = about $14M per client. A few large clients pull this mean up, so the median is lower. STEP 4. LARGEST CLIENTS (sets the ceiling). In 2010, Bank of America was 12.9% of TSYS total revenue of $1,717.6M, about $220M (2010 10-K; total revenue from TSYS's 2011 annual report). A newer bound: in 2018 the Issuer segment had two 'major customers' but TSYS had none on a consolidated basis. If 'major' means 10% of segment revenue, each paid at least about $170M and less than about $400M (10% of TSYS's roughly $4.0B 2018 revenue). That threshold is my inference, not stated in the filing. STEP 5. RESULT. Regional issuer with 2M accounts x $2.30-$2.80 = about $5-6M. Top-5 issuer = about $170-400M by the 2018 bound, so $250M is a fair midpoint. For in-house operators, spend shifts to licence fees, mainframe hosting and vendor services, which are not disclosed. CONFIDENCE. Medium. Ceiling rests on one 2010 disclosure plus an inferred 2018 bound.

mid_market.evidence: SUMMARY. About $0.4M-$5M a year for an issuer running roughly 100K-1.5M card accounts. Kept as drafted; three methods agree within 2x. WHO OWNS IT. Mid-sized issuers buy. They outsource to a processor (TSYS, Fiserv, FIS, Velera) or license a packaged card system (VisionPLUS, Way4, PowerCARD) and run it themselves. I found no mid-sized bank that wrote its own processor. METHOD 1. PER-ACCOUNT PRICE. TSYS's 2018 figures give about $2.30-$2.80 per account per year (see enterprise). 100K-1.5M accounts gives about $0.25M-$4M, plus minimums and project fees. METHOD 2. A PUBLIC TENDER (verified in the RFP text). Union Bank of India, RFP UBI/CCD & MAB/2023-24/019 (GeM/2023/B/3524883), issued 10 June 2023. Scope: end-to-end credit and prepaid card management, bought under a CAPEX model. The bank's current system was also bought under CAPEX. Term: five years, extendable by five more. The bank has about 6 lakh (600K) credit cards today and projects 15 lakh in year 1 rising to 55 lakh (5.5M) in year 5. Bid security is Rs 2.80 crore. India's GFR Rule 170 sets bid security at 2-5% of estimated value, so the estimate is Rs 56-140 crore over five years. At about 83 INR/USD that is $6.7M-$16.9M, or $1.3M-$3.4M a year. Two cautions. Union Bank of India is a large bank, so it is mid-market only by card portfolio size. Indian pricing works out to about $0.40-$1.00 per card per year, well below US rates, so a US issuer of the same size would pay more. The RFP also covers debit-card 3-D Secure (ACS) volumes, not only credit. METHOD 3. CREDIT-UNION AVERAGE. Velera reports $1.6B revenue across 4,000 institutions (velera.com, verified). That is about $400K per institution for its full bundle (credit, debit, ATM, fraud, contact centre). Larger credit unions, which are mid-market, sit above that average. RESULT. $0.4M-$5M. CONFIDENCE. Medium. Inferred from a bid-security rule, a per-account average and a revenue average, not from disclosed contract prices.

smb.evidence: SUMMARY. About $10K-$400K a year. Kept as drafted. The top of the range applies only to a small credit union that issues its own credit and debit cards through a full processor bundle. WHO OWNS IT. Small institutions do not build this. For credit cards, many do not run a portfolio at all. They use an agent issuer that holds the receivables and does processing and servicing, while the bank keeps its brand and a revenue share. Elan (U.S. Bank) says it has 1,300 bank and credit union partners on this model (verified). Fiserv's case study on FNB Community Bank, a $550M-asset bank in the Oklahoma City area, describes the same set-up (verified). Fiserv handles risk and call-centre work, and the bank shares in branded card revenue with no receivables to fund. On that model the bank's direct spend is near zero, or it earns net revenue. Institutions that keep their own credit portfolio, and almost all that issue debit cards, outsource to a processor or credit union service organization (CUSO): Velera, Fiserv, Jack Henry, FIS. HOW THE SPEND WAS DERIVED. Low end: an agent-issued credit card plus a small debit processing bill. At about $2.30-$2.80 per account (TSYS 2018), 5,000 debit cards cost roughly $12-14K. High end: Velera's average of about $400K per institution for a full card, ATM and contact-centre bundle. Larger credit unions pull that average up, so a typical small institution sits well below it. A small issuer with 20-50K accounts would pay roughly $50K-$150K. The Kansas City Fed paper notes that small issuers pay more per transaction than large ones but gives no dollar figure I could use. CONFIDENCE. Low to medium. No public per-account price list for small issuers.

government.evidence: SUMMARY. About $1M-$6M a year per state for benefit-card (EBT) processing. Kept as drafted. The federal Direct Express program is a separate, much larger case. Facts corrected below. WHAT GOVERNMENTS BUY. Governments do not issue credit cards. They buy card issuing and processing for benefit payments: SNAP/TANF EBT cards at state level and the federal Direct Express prepaid card. All of it is outsourced (FIS, Conduent, Fiserv, Comerica and others). I found no government that builds its own processor. STATE EVIDENCE (both verified in the source documents). (1) Tennessee: FIS EBT contract (Edison contract 79236, request RFS# 34530-00322). Maximum liability is $10,005,435.60 for 1 March 2024 to 22 September 2029, about 67 months. That is about $1.8M a year, with $2.96M in calendar 2024, which includes added Summer EBT scope. The draft listed 34530-00322 as the Edison number; it is the request number. (2) Maryland: EBT bids were priced per case-month on a five-year base term with two two-year renewal options. Best-and-final grand totals were $19.98M (Conduent) and $30.72M (FIS). FIS's first offer was $31.04M. That is $2.2M-$6.1M a year, depending on whether the total covers five or nine years. The draft's $31.8M figure was wrong and is replaced. The press figure of $11.1M over five years could not be checked (the page blocks access) and is dropped. Larger states such as California, New York and Texas are probably above $6M, but I found no contract value. FEDERAL OUTLIER, DIRECT EXPRESS. About 4.5M cardholders. A search summary of Comerica's filings puts Direct Express card fee income at $137M in 2023 against $138M of outside processing expense. I could not confirm this in the 10-K text, and the draft's $121M for 2024 is unverified. Much of the program is funded by cardholder fees and interchange, not appropriations. CORRECTION. The draft said Treasury picked Galileo (SoFi) as processor in 2025. Treasury did name BNY as financial agent from January 2025, with Galileo among its providers. But in September 2025 Treasury dropped BNY over 'readiness challenges' and named Fifth Third, with Money Network Financial (a Fiserv company) as program manager (Banking Dive). CONFIDENCE. Medium for states (two signed or bid documents), low for the federal figures.

best_icp: Mid-market issuers are the best first customer: regional banks, larger credit unions and fintech card programs running about 100K to 1.5M accounts. They spend about $0.4M to $5M a year, buy rather than build, and some buy through open tenders that admit start-ups (Union Bank of India's 2023 RFP waived the deposit and relaxed turnover rules for them). The other segments are harder. The top five issuers often own or license their platforms and need multi-year conversions. Small banks mostly hand credit cards to agent issuers for a revenue share. State EBT is a $1M to $6M-a-year niche held by FIS and Conduent, with heavy procurement.

criticality_why: VERDICT: 'important' holds. The check found no reason to change it. TEST USED: 'critical' needs two things together. (a) The business stops or loses its licence if the system fails. (b) The system is where the firm competes. Construction project accounting passes (a) in practice but fails (b). WHY IT PASSES (a), THE BUSINESS STOPS: three jobs fail together. (1) Payroll, including certified, prevailing-wage (Davis-Bacon) and union fringe payroll. (2) Owner billing: AIA-style pay applications, retainage and change orders. These drive cash flow. (3) WIP schedules and job-cost reports. Sureties and auditors use them to set bonding capacity, and without a bond a contractor cannot bid public work. No regulator pulls a licence the way one would over a failed bank core. Even so, the business halts within a pay cycle. WHY IT FAILS (b), NOT WHERE FIRMS COMPETE: contractors win on estimating, execution, safety and relationships, not on their ledger. They buy the system off the shelf. VERIFIED in the JBKnowledge 2020 ConTech Report, 'Top Accounting/ERP Software' chart: Sage 21%, Viewpoint 17%, Jonas 8%, CMiC 7%, QuickBooks 7%, Plexxis 6%, Dexter + Chaney 5%, Foundation 4%, Oracle JD Edwards 4%, ComputerEase 3%, SAP 2%, COINS 2%, Other 19%. Custom in-house software is only 4%. WHY IT STILL MATTERS: job-cost history feeds estimating, so replacing the system is slow and risky. VERIFIED (Construction News, 2019): Kier's Oracle ERP was budgeted at GBP 30m in 2014, cost GBP 90m by go-live in September 2018 (planned for November 2016), and was followed by a GBP 7.3m writedown in 2019 for functionality that would not be used.

enterprise.evidence: CHECK RESULT: range kept. All sourced facts checked out, with two wording fixes noted below. Both endpoints are derived estimates, not quoted prices. WHO: ENR 400-scale US contractors and UK tier-one contractors. Roughly $500M+ revenue, with hundreds to thousands of users. BUILD VS BUY = 'some'. (1) Few write the ledger from scratch. VERIFIED: custom in-house accounting/ERP is 4% of all JBKnowledge 2020 respondents. (2) The largest firms do own and heavily customise tier-one ERPs, which works like an in-house build on a bought platform. VERIFIED: Oracle JD Edwards 4% and SAP 2% in the same chart. Kier ran a group Oracle ERP programme (Construction News). (3) The next tier buys construction suites. VERIFIED: Viewpoint served '46 percent of the ENR 400' (Trimble 8-K exhibit, April 2018). CMiC says 25% of the ENR 400 and 33% of the top 100 run CMiC. That is a vendor claim seen in search results, not an independent figure. SPEND, LOW END = $250k a year. This is a large contractor on CMiC or Vista. VERIFIED on ERP Research's CMiC page: software is '$50,000 to $150,000+/yr', implementation is $100k to $500k, deployment takes 6 to 18 months, and CMiC publishes no price list. Add implementation spread over about 5 years ($20k to $100k a year), plus hosting, support and ongoing partner services, and a large CMiC or Vista estate reaches about $250k a year. That is a derivation, but it is within 2x of the verified parts. SPEND, HIGH END = $5M a year. This is a tier-one contractor on Oracle or SAP, at steady state. Context, VERIFIED in Construction News (2019): the UK's nine largest contractors added GBP 451m of capitalised software intangibles over the decade to 2019. Kier added GBP 172m (about GBP 17m a year) and Balfour Beatty GBP 145m (about GBP 14.5m a year). Kier's ERP alone cost GBP 90m over 2014 to 2018, about GBP 20m a year during the build. FIXES: the earlier draft said 'top 10'. The article covers nine firms, because Morgan Sindall does not split out IT spend. The figures are capitalised software additions, not total IT or finance-only spend. HOW $5M WAS SET: those totals cover all software and include build years, so they overstate the finance run-rate. $5M is a judgment for steady-state finance ERP run cost (licence or support, hosting, managed services). Build peaks can run 3 to 4 times higher. No source gives a finance-only run-rate, so this endpoint is the least certain number in the record.

mid_market.evidence: CHECK RESULT: range kept. One unsourced statistic removed. WHO: contractors with about $10M to $500M revenue: general contractors, specialty trades and civil firms. Most of the legacy installed base sits here: Sage 300 CRE (formerly Timberline), Viewpoint Vista and Spectrum, Foundation, Jonas, ComputerEase. REMOVED: the earlier claim that AppsRunTheWorld puts 58.6% of Vista users at 101 to 1,000 employees. No AppsRunTheWorld page was opened or listed in the sources. BUILD VS BUY = 'rare'. VERIFIED in JBKnowledge 2020: custom in-house accounting is 4% of respondents. 65% of respondent firms have 1 to 5 IT employees. The CFO (31%) or CEO (26%) most often leads IT. These firms have no capacity to build an ERP. SPEND, three cross-checks. (1) Vendor filing, which sets the low end. VERIFIED in the Trimble 8-K exhibit (April 2018): Viewpoint expected 'approximately $200 million of non-GAAP revenue in 2019' from 'approximately 8,000 customers'. That averages about $25k per customer per year. The average includes some enterprise accounts, so a typical mid-market customer may sit a little lower. Still, $25k is a fair floor for a firm on a construction ERP. (2) Third-party pricing, from search snippets only (vendors publish no prices). Vista subscriptions run $30k to $60k a year for mid-market firms, with mid-market implementations of $80k to $200k (SelectHub and ERP Research via search; ERP Research's own Vista page confirms only that Trimble does not publish pricing). Sage Intacct Construction licences by size (ERP Research via search): $18k to $32k a year for a $10M to $30M firm with 10 to 25 users. $32k to $65k for a $30M to $150M firm with 25 to 60 users. $60k to $100k for a $150M+ multi-entity firm with 60 to 150 users. (3) On top of licence, add hosting (Sage 300 CRE is often run on hosted remote-desktop servers), add-on modules and partner services for upgrades, report writing and payroll tax updates. With these, larger multi-entity firms reach about $150k a year. RANGE: $25k to $150k a year, excluding internal staff. Every check above falls inside it.

smb.evidence: CHECK RESULT: range kept. One survey citation replaced with the verified figure. WHO: contractors under about $10M revenue. By count, they are most construction firms: about 950k US construction establishments (BLS, carried over from an earlier research file and not re-opened). BUILD VS BUY = 'rare'. Small firms do not build software. Most run QuickBooks, often with spreadsheets or a construction add-on. FIX: the earlier draft cited QuickBooks at 9.7% in a 2019 survey seen only through search. The verified 2020 JBKnowledge figure is 7%. That survey under-samples small firms: its most common respondent firm has 201 to 500 employees, and firms under $5M revenue are a small share of respondents. Expect real QuickBooks use among SMBs to be far higher than 7%. SPEND, LOW END = about $2k a year. This is QuickBooks plus a light add-on. Current QuickBooks Online plans run roughly $1k to $3k a year. This is general knowledge of list prices; no source page was opened. SPEND, HIGH END = about $20k a year. This is a construction-specific system. VERIFIED on Foundation Software's own pricing guide: cloud systems cost 'between a couple hundred and several thousand dollars per month', and on-premise systems cost $2,000 to well over $50,000 up front. Search snippets, not opened: Foundation runs about $500 to $1,500 a month ($6k to $18k a year), plus $3k to $8k one-time implementation (SaaSworthy, ITQlick). Adaptive starts at $575 a month (about $6.9k a year) for firms up to $5M revenue, with no implementation or per-seat fees (Software Finder and Adaptive's pricing page via search). Sage Intacct Construction starts around $18k a year even for a $10M to $30M firm, which sets the ceiling where SMB meets mid-market. RANGE: $2k to $20k a year. The ceiling is low, and switching to cheaper tools is easy.

government.evidence: SCOPE WARNING, read first: agencies do not buy contractor-side project accounting (payroll, AIA billing, WIP for bonding). Agencies are project owners. They buy the owner-side counterpart: systems that track capital-project budgets, change orders and progress payments to contractors. Every figure below is for that adjacent product. If the study counts only contractor accounting, set this segment to null. CHECK RESULT: range kept. One price citation corrected. BUILD VS BUY = 'some'. State DOTs jointly fund and govern AASHTOWare Project through AASHTO's member cooperative. This is shared ownership, between build and buy. Cities, counties and housing authorities more often buy SaaS such as Trimble e-Builder or Oracle Unifier. SPEND, all from public documents opened and read. (a) AASHTOWare FY2027 catalog: the Construction & Materials module (construction and materials management, including change orders, stockpiles and contractor payments) costs $350,000 a year. Two hosted bundles include that module: Option 2 at $836,000 a year and Option 3 at $1,062,000 a year. FIX: the earlier draft also cited Option 1 ($611,000). Option 1 does not include Construction & Materials. It covers bidding, preconstruction, civil rights and labor, estimation and analytics, so it was dropped as evidence for this product. (b) Trimble e-Builder contracts. Portland, OR: $314,620.59 a year from August 31, 2022, covering two bureaus (Environmental Services and Transportation), rising 5% a year. The not-to-exceed total is $3,823,129.37 for a contract running December 2014 to August 2026 (Ordinance 190817). Chicago Housing Authority: the 2026 renewal is $225,530.01 a year ($217,440.81 for the enterprise bundle sized to up to $300M of annual capital spend, plus $8,089.20 automation maintenance). Note that e-Builder prices on the owner's annual capital spend, not on users. Arlington, TX: $161,700 for annual support and maintenance in FY2017 (staff report dated December 2016, so the figure is dated). RANGE: about $150k to $1M a year per agency. Every verified data point falls between $161,700 and $1,062,000. UNVERIFIED: LA County's PMCS contract reportedly allows up to $8.2M of subscription fees over its term. This came from a search snippet only, so treat it as a sign that large counties can exceed the range, not as a data point.

best_icp: Sell first to US mid-market contractors with about $10M to $250M revenue, especially specialty trades and regional GCs still on Sage 300 CRE, Vista/Spectrum or Foundation. They spend about $25k to $150k a year, rarely build (4% custom in-house, and 65% have 1 to 5 IT staff), and their pain is labour-heavy AP, billing and WIP work that an AI layer can absorb. Adaptive (750+ customers, $5M to $1B revenue, $57M raised) shows the way in: it sits on top of QuickBooks, Sage and Acumatica rather than replacing them, and replacing the ledger later is an inference, not something Adaptive has shown. Enterprise means 6 to 18 month projects with Kier-style overrun risk (GBP 30m to 90m), and SMB tops out near $20k a year.
