criticality_why: Verdict: important, not critical. The rating stands after review. Test 1, does the business stop without it? Yes. The core banking system is the ledger for every deposit and loan. If it fails, a credit union, BPR, rural bank or PACS cannot open accounts, disburse loans or file regulatory returns. Regulators also require it. Indonesia's POJK 34/2025 (effective 18 Dec 2025, verified on ojk.go.id) sets IT governance, IT-vendor, cyber and disaster-recovery rules for BPRs and BPRS. RBI earlier pushed state and district co-op banks onto core banking (general knowledge, not re-opened). Test 2, is it where the firm competes? No. Peers run the same shared core. Atruvia serves every German Volksbank and Raiffeisenbank (verified). About 715 US credit unions run Jack Henry Symitar (verified in the FY2025 10-K). India is putting about 63,000 PACS on one NABARD-run national software (verified in the scheme guidelines). Fiserv and Symitar together held about 83% of US credit unions over $1B in assets in 2018 (creditunions.com). Co-ops compete on member relationships, local credit knowledge and pricing, not on the ledger. It passes test 1 and fails test 2, so 'important' is correct.

enterprise.evidence: WHO BUYS: the largest co-operative lenders (1M+ members) and the IT utilities that co-op groups own. HOW THEY SOURCE IT: at group level they mostly own the core through a captive utility. Large standalone US credit unions are the exception: most of them buy. Verified facts: (1) Atruvia, owned by the German co-operative group, reported EUR 1.9bn revenue in FY2025 from more than 900 clients, including all German Volksbanken and Raiffeisenbanken, and runs 97M accounts. For the group this is in-house IT, even though each member bank pays it like a vendor. (2) Allitude, Cassa Centrale's IT subsidiary, reported EUR 190M net revenue in 2022, 83% of it from its own group. Same captive model. (3) Correction: Navy Federal (13M+ members) is moving from a legacy mainframe to a cloud-native real-time core (Zafin release, April 2024). Zafin supplies only a product and pricing layer on top of that core. The release does not say whether the new core is built in-house or bought, so it is no longer cited as proof of in-house build. (4) Counterweight: in 2018 Fiserv and Symitar together held 83.3% of US credit unions over $1B in assets (creditunions.com). Large US credit unions mostly buy. Net rating: 'common' holds for co-op groups with captive utilities and is weaker for US credit unions. HOW THE SPEND RANGE WAS DERIVED (estimate): CUCollaborate's February 2018 data for credit unions over $1B in assets gives median core cost per member of $3.11 (FIS Miser), $4.58 (Symitar) and $5.74 (Fiserv DNA). Verified. At 1M members that is about $3M to $6M a year. At 13M members linear scaling would give $40M to $75M, but cost per member falls with scale, so $50M is a reasonable ceiling. Atruvia's revenue per client, about EUR 2.1M (about $2.3M), is per member bank, not per group. CHECK RESULT: range kept. Every cited number matched its source. CONFIDENCE: low to medium. No single enterprise co-op core contract value was found.

mid_market.evidence: WHO BUYS: US credit unions and community banks with about $500M to $10B in assets, plus mid-sized European co-op banks inside group utilities. HOW THEY SOURCE IT: they almost always buy. Verified in Jack Henry's FY2025 10-K: SilverLake has 520 banks, CIF 20/20 has 260, Core Director has 170+, and Symitar has about 715 credit unions with $20M to $33B in assets. Hosted core clients typically sign six-year contracts with per-account fees and minimum guaranteed payments. On-premise clients typically sign one-year contracts. HOW THE SPEND RANGE WAS DERIVED: (1) Jack Henry's FY2025 Core segment revenue was $739.3M GAAP ($724.5M excluding deconversion fees), verified in the earnings release. Across about 1,665 core clients that averages about $435K to $444K per client a year. This is core only, with payments and digital excluded. (2) CUCollaborate (2018) median cost per member for credit unions with $500M to $1B in assets: Corelation KeyStone $6.53, Fiserv DataSafe $5.03, Fiserv Spectrum $11.13. Verified. At 40K to 250K members that is about $200K to $2.8M a year. (3) In Europe, revenue per member bank is about EUR 2.1M (about $2.3M) at Atruvia and about EUR 2.4M (about $2.6M) at Allitude. The Allitude figure is EUR 158M of group revenue (83% of EUR 190M, verified) divided by roughly 65 group banks; the bank count is general knowledge, not from an opened source. Both figures cover full IT outsourcing, not only the core, so they cap the range at about $3M. CHECK RESULT: range kept, all numbers verified. CONFIDENCE: medium. This tier has the best evidence.

smb.evidence: WHO BUYS: credit unions under about $500M in assets, Indonesian BPR and BPRS (about 1,500, falling with consolidation), Philippine rural banks, Indian urban co-op banks, and microfinance institutions. HOW THEY SOURCE IT: they buy from local vendors or run on spreadsheets and paper. Correction: build-in-house changed from 'some' to 'rare'. The only source opened on this point (TechCrunch, 2015, on Oradian's market) says MFIs rely on 'expensive legacy software, Excel spreadsheets or plain old pen and paper'. That describes manual work, not home-built cores. The earlier claim about in-house PowerBuilder or Delphi cores had no source. Small lenders seldom have the IT staff to build a core. HOW THE SPEND RANGE WAS DERIVED, cheapest first: (1) Indonesian BPR, verified. Starfield lists a perpetual BPR core licence at Rp 75M (about $4.6K) including core modules, accounting, OJK reporting, multi-branch, one-year warranty and support. Annual maintenance afterwards is 'competitive' but not priced. Over five years with maintenance, that is about $2K to $10K a year. USSI's IBS Core claim (300+ BPRs, since 1994) could not be verified because the page did not load. (2) Indian UCB, unverified. The AP Mahesh Co-operative Urban Bank figure of about Rs 4 crore (about $460K) for a whole-bank CBS, or about $65K to $90K a year, comes from a Business Standard page that returned 403. It is kept only as an indication. (3) Small US credit union with 5K to 40K members: about $25K to $400K at roughly $5 to $10 per member. Correction: CUCollaborate publishes per-member figures only for tiers over $500M. Applying them to small credit unions is an extrapolation, not a sourced figure. The top is capped at $300K because most credit unions in this tier have fewer than 30K members. (4) MFIs. Correction: the earlier claims that Mambu sells six-figure contracts most MFIs cannot afford, and that Oradian charges per end client, are not in the cited sources. PeerSpot reviewers call Mambu cheap for a core, with no dollar figures. TechCrunch gives no Oradian pricing. CHECK RESULT: range kept; derivation relabelled where unsourced. CONFIDENCE: low to medium. No emerging-market SaaS price list was found.

government.evidence: WHO BUYS: governments, central banks and development banks that buy core systems for a whole sector of small lenders. HOW THEY SOURCE IT: a mix of government-owned platforms and bought services. Correction: build-in-house changed from 'common' to 'some'. Of the three cases below, only India's PACS programme results in a government-owned platform, and even that is built by a contracted vendor. NABARD's earlier co-op bank CBS and the BSP programme both buy from vendors. (1) India PACS, verified in the Ministry of Cooperation scheme guidelines. Outlay is Rs 2,516 crore for about 63,000 PACS over five years (2022-23 to 2026-27), later revised to Rs 2,925 crore (the revision is from secondary reporting). NABARD contracts a National Level PACS Software Vendor for common software and runs a national data repository. Cost per PACS is Rs 3,91,369: hardware with 5-year AMC Rs 1,22,158; software with cyber security and storage Rs 72,103; training Rs 10,198; implementation and handholding Rs 1,86,910. Excluding hardware that is about Rs 54K (about $620) per PACS per year. The whole programme runs about Rs 500 to 585 crore a year, about $58M to $67M at Rs 87 per USD. This sets the top of the range. Note it includes hardware and is a one-time project ending in 2027. The guidelines say NABARD will set a pay-per-use arrangement with state co-op banks after year five. (2) NABARD earlier moved about 200 state and district co-op banks (6,939 branches) to cloud CBS run by two vendors (103 and 98 banks) on an opex model with a minimum monthly subscription fee (CIO.com, 2014). No cost figures were published. (3) Philippines, verified. BSP Memorandum M-2026-042 (issued August 2026) funds implementation help and a free three-year SaaS core subscription. It is open only to rural banks on a Rural Bank Strengthening Program track (merger, acquisition, licence upgrade or capital build-up) that applied between Sept 2022 and Sept 2025 and have no existing SaaS core. Budget and bank count were not disclosed. The earlier '6 months of implementation' detail was not confirmed in the sources that loaded. (4) Tamil Nadu urban co-op bank CBS tender (Rs 2 lakh EMD). The tender page returned 403, so this is unverified. Correction: Indian EMDs usually run 2% to 5% of contract value, so Rs 2 lakh implies roughly Rs 40 lakh to Rs 1 crore ($46K to $115K), not a firm Rs 1 crore. The bottom of the range is lowered from $100K to $50K. CONFIDENCE: medium for India, low elsewhere.

best_icp: Start with Philippine rural banks that qualify under BSP M-2026-042, where the central bank pays for three years of SaaS core so price is not the barrier. The catch is that only banks on a consolidation, upgrade or capital-build track without an existing SaaS core qualify, so getting onto the eligible vendor list comes first. Pair them with Indonesian BPRs that must meet POJK 34/2025 IT and disaster-recovery rules, priced around the local level of a few thousand dollars a year. Move up to US credit unions with $500M to $3B in assets ($250K to $2.5M a year) only as their six-year Jack Henry and Fiserv contracts come up for renewal.

criticality_why:
VERDICT: critical. Review result: confirmed. Core banking passes both tests in the definition. A documented case proves the failure test. The differentiation test holds fully for large banks and only partly for small ones.

TEST 1. Does the business stop if it fails? Yes.
- What the core does. It is the system of record for every deposit, loan and general-ledger entry. Jack Henry's FY2026 10-K defines core as the 'integrated applications required to process deposit, loan, and general ledger transactions' (checked in the filing).
- What happens when it fails. TSB's 2018 move to Sabadell's Proteo4UK platform is the standard case. The FCA Final Notice (2022, checked) says TSB did not return to business as usual until 10 December 2018. It received 225,492 complaints (about 4.3% of customers), paid GBP 32.7M in redress and was fined GBP 29.75M by the FCA. The PRA fined it separately. So a core failure is a regulatory event, not only an IT outage.
- The public sector depends on it the same way. North Carolina's State Treasurer runs a system it calls 'Core Banking'. In FY2012-13 it processed more than 5.5M state warrants (about $20B) and about 21,600 wires worth $153.6B (NC State Auditor, checked).

TEST 2. Is it where the firm competes? Yes for large banks. Partly for small ones.
- Products live in the core. Rates, fees, account types and how fast a bank can launch a new product are all set up there.
- Large banks treat the core as strategy. Sabadell built Proteo in 2000 with its acquisition strategy in mind. It expected IT savings of about GBP 160M a year (pre-tax) from moving TSB onto Proteo (FCA Final Notice, checked). Lloyds, JPMorgan Chase and Intesa Sanpaolo license Thought Machine to rebuild their product layer (tech.eu, checked).

CAVEAT. Small US community banks and credit unions mostly buy the core as a near-commodity bundle from Fiserv, FIS or Jack Henry. A consultant quoted in ABA Banking Journal (2015) said the top three vendors hold about 85% of the market and that a bank has only about a 4% chance of switching at a renewal. Correction: the original draft gave these figures as ABA's own. They are one consultant's estimates from 2015. For these banks the core is critical to survival but is usually not how they win customers. That gap is the opening for a new entrant.

enterprise.evidence:
WHO: banks above about $50B in assets. Temenos calls these tier 1-2 and uses the same $50B line (2025 annual report, checked).

BUILD OR BUY: Common. Review result: confirmed.
- Kansas City Fed (checked): 'Larger DIs with ample resources are more likely to use in-house core system processing', while most smaller ones outsource.
- Many large banks run a package licensed decades ago (Hogan, Systematics) that they have customised so heavily it is now effectively their own. Others wrote their own. Example: Sabadell built Proteo in 2000 (FCA TSB Final Notice, checked).
- Temenos's 2025 annual report (checked) counts about +$2B of 'in-house spend' moving to vendors as future market growth. That only makes sense if a large share of big-bank core spend is still internal.

ANNUAL SPEND: $10M to $50M per bank on vendor licences, maintenance, hosting and services, with staff excluded. Modernisation years run far higher.

WHAT THE REVIEW CHANGED: the high end drops from $100M to $50M. None of the four inputs supports $100M as a typical figure. The inputs point to about $10-30M for a typical tier 1-2 bank. A handful of global megabanks may exceed $50M once mainframe hosting is counted, but no source here shows it.

HOW THE RANGE IS BUILT (no filing gives this number, so it comes from four indirect signals):
1. Market size, the main anchor. Temenos (checked) puts third-party banking software spend by tier 1-2 banks at about $9B in 2025, out of about $25B for all banks. Spread over roughly 300-450 banks above $50B, that is about $20-30M per bank for all banking software, not just the core. The core is the largest single piece, so core alone is probably $8-15M on average. The bank count is an estimate and was not verified.
2. Per-account benchmark. Cornerstone Advisors (via Monetizely, a secondary source, checked) puts core cost at $5-10 per account per year for banks above $10B. A $50B bank with about 1.5-2.5M accounts would pay about $7.5-25M. This sets the low end at about $10M.
3. A modern-core vendor. Thought Machine passed $100M of revenue in 2025 (tech.eu, checked). The article names four clients (Lloyds, JPMorgan Chase, Intesa Sanpaolo, Lunar) but gives no client count. Correction: the original draft inferred 'high single-digit to low double-digit $M per client'. That cannot be derived, because the client count is unknown and revenue includes services. Treat this only as proof that large banks pay modern-core vendors millions a year.
4. Ceilings and one-offs. Sabadell's GBP 160M a year saving covered TSB's whole IT platform, not just the core, so it is a ceiling and not a core figure. CBA spent five years and more than A$1B replacing its core (iTnews, checked). That is a one-off programme, not running cost.

CONFIDENCE: medium-low. Every input is indirect. The Temenos market figure is the strongest.

mid_market.evidence:
WHO: banks and credit unions with about $1B to $50B in assets. In the US these are regional and larger community banks. Elsewhere they are part of Temenos's tier 3-5 (banks under $50B).

BUILD OR BUY: Rare. Review result: confirmed. They buy from Fiserv, FIS or Jack Henry in the US, or from Temenos, Finastra, Oracle FLEXCUBE or Finacle elsewhere. They choose either an on-premise licence or hosted processing.
- Jack Henry FY2026 10-K (checked): hosted core contracts typically run six years, priced with per-account fees and guaranteed minimum payments. On-premise clients pay a licence plus annual maintenance.
- A consultant quoted in ABA Banking Journal (2015) estimates the top three vendors hold about 85% of the US market.

ANNUAL SPEND: $0.4M to $15M per institution. Spend scales with account count, so a $1B bank sits near the bottom and a $50B bank near the top.

WHAT THE REVIEW CHANGED: the high end rises from $5M to $15M. The original top end came from the per-account benchmark applied to a $10B bank. But this band runs to $50B, and the same benchmark gives a $50B bank $7.5-25M. The original $5M was off by about 3x at the top of the band. $15M also lines up with the enterprise floor of $10M.

HOW THE RANGE IS BUILT:
1. Low end, from an SEC filing (the strongest number in this report). Jack Henry's Core segment earned $768.5M in FY2026 (checked). It has more than 900 bank and more than 700 credit-union core clients, about 1,600 in total. That averages about $480K per client per year. The average bank client holds about $1.4B in assets and the average credit union about $1.3B (same 10-K). This is core only. Payments and digital banking are reported in other segments.
2. A real contract. HomeTrust Bank ($2.6B in assets) renegotiated its core contract with a consultant. It saved $1.2M immediately and $5-8M over the contract's life (ABA Banking Journal 2015, checked). A contract that yields savings of that size was likely worth a few million dollars a year.
3. Per-account benchmark, middle of the band. Cornerstone via Monetizely (secondary, undated) puts core cost at $10-15 per account per year for $1-10B institutions. A $5B bank with 150,000-250,000 accounts would pay about $1.5-3.75M.
4. Per-account benchmark, top of the band. The same source gives $5-10 per account above $10B. A $10B bank with about 400,000-500,000 accounts pays about $2-5M. A $50B bank with about 1.5-2.5M accounts pays about $7.5-25M. $15M is the midpoint for the largest banks in the band.

CONFIDENCE: medium. The low end rests on an SEC filing. The top end rests on a secondary benchmark and estimated account counts.

smb.evidence:
WHO: banks and credit unions under about $1B in assets. Examples: US community banks and smaller credit unions, Indonesia's rural banks (BPRs, about 1,300-1,400), India's urban co-operative banks and Philippine rural banks.

BUILD OR BUY: Rare. Review result: confirmed. ABA Banking Journal (December 2025, checked): community banks 'typically operate with limited in-house technical resources and are particularly dependent on their core processors'. The norm is hosted processing in the US, or a cheap perpetual licence in emerging markets.

ANNUAL SPEND: about $25K to $400K per institution in the US. Emerging-market small banks can spend far less.

WHAT THE REVIEW CHANGED: the numbers stand. One step in the reasoning was corrected (point 2 below).

HOW THE RANGE IS BUILT:
1. Low end, from a published price list. CU*Answers, a credit-union cooperative, publishes its 2026 core prices (checked). The fee is $0.56 per member per month on a 7-year contract, $0.58 on 5 years, $0.60 on 3 years and $0.80 on a 1-year renewal. The minimum is $2,000 a month. That works out to $24K a year at the minimum, about $67K for 10,000 members and about $235K for 35,000 members. These are core fees only. Online banking and other add-ons are billed separately.
2. High end, from the filing. Jack Henry averages about $480K per core client, and its average client holds about $1.3-1.4B in assets (FY2026 10-K). Its smaller systems, Core Director (about 200 banks, up to $2B) and CIF 20/20 (more than 200 banks, from de novo to above $1B), serve the bottom of that base. So a bank under $1B paying up to about $400K fits. Correction: the original draft applied the Cornerstone benchmark ($15-25 per account for $500M-$1B banks) to 10,000-16,000 accounts. A bank of that size more likely has 15,000-50,000 accounts, which would imply $225K-$1.25M. That conflicts with the filing. The filing is the stronger source, so the $400K top is kept, but some banks near $1B will pay more.
3. Emerging-market low end. Indonesian vendor Starfield sells BPR core software for Rp 75M (about $4,600) as a one-time perpetual licence, with one year of warranty and support (checked). Later maintenance is optional and its price is not published.

CONFIDENCE: medium. One published US price list and one filing, plus a secondary benchmark that points higher.

government.evidence:
WHO: public bodies that run a banking ledger themselves. This means central banks, state treasuries, postal savings banks and state development banks. Large state-owned commercial banks behave like enterprise buyers and are counted there.

BUILD OR BUY: Some. Review result: confirmed. Most buy a package and pay a systems integrator to install it. A few commission custom builds.
- Central Bank of Kenya runs Temenos T24 R09 across its banking, finance, markets and currency departments. Its tender (checked) seeks a partner for an upgrade and re-implementation expected to take about two years.
- North Carolina's State Treasurer runs Oracle FLEXCUBE as its 'Core Banking' system. In January 2014 it hired Mythics Consulting, with Oracle as vendor, for an upgrade estimated at about $5M (NC State Auditor, checked).
- The Reserve Bank of India's e-Kuber was implemented by Polaris. That is a vendor build, not a pure in-house build (not re-checked).

ANNUAL SPEND: $0.5M to $20M per buyer, scaling with the number of accounts and branches served.

WHAT THE REVIEW CHANGED: the low end rises from $0.3M to $0.5M. The original low end was built partly on North Carolina's separate cash-management system ($1.1M to implement plus about $200K for three years of support). That is not the core. The core upgrade alone ($5M) works out to about $0.7-1.0M a year over a 5-7 year cycle. $0.5M allows for smaller central banks while staying within 2x of the only hard data point.

HOW THE RANGE IS BUILT:
1. Low end. NC Treasurer core upgrade: about $5M, or about $0.7-1.0M a year over 5-7 years.
2. High end. In August 2012 India Post awarded Infosys an INR 700 crore (about $126M) contract (Moneylife, checked; Forrester, via search summary). The scope was Finacle core banking plus McCamish insurance software, 1,000 ATMs, hardware, document management and managed services. The rollout covered about 25,000 departmental offices over 24 months, within a network of about 150,000 post offices serving more than 200M customers. Correction: the 7-year term was marked unverified in the draft. A search summary of the Forrester note confirms the contract is valid for seven years. That gives about $18M a year all-in. Core banking is only part of that scope, so $20M is the ceiling, reached only by the very largest postal banks.
3. No price in the Kenya tender. Its KES 80M figure (about $720K) is the minimum professional-indemnity cover bidders must hold (checked). It is not the contract value.

CONFIDENCE: low-medium. There are few public award values. Each end rests on one contract.

best_icp: Start with mid-market banks and credit unions at the small end of that band (about $1B-$10B in assets): they almost never build their own core, they spend about $0.4M-$4M a year on it, about a sixth of their typical six-year contracts come up for renewal each year, and the SMB segment pays too little per institution while enterprise banks often run their own core and take about five years to replace it; the main risk is a low switching rate (one consultant's 2015 estimate is about 4% per renewal), so target banks at a renewal, a merger or a failed vendor upgrade rather than at random.

criticality_why:
Verdict: critical. The call holds after checking the sources. Two corrections to the supporting evidence are listed at the end.

WHAT THE SYSTEM IS. The court case management system (CMS) is the court's legal system of record. It holds dockets, filings, judgments, warrants, fines and the release dates that jails act on.

HOW IT MEETS THE TWO TESTS.
Test 1, the operation stops if it fails: met. Evidence (sources opened in this check):
- Galveston TX: staff wrote that if the $61,343 annual Tyler Incode maintenance was not paid, Technology Services "will not be able to guarantee the programs will remain functional".
- Austin TX renewed Journal Technologies sole-source in May 2026. The council memo says stopping the software "may result in data loss" and break critical integrations with justice partners, and that a replacement would take "multiple years".
- Dallas County (2023 to 2024): after the criminal courts moved to Tyler Odyssey, defence lawyers said tasks that took hours took days. Release delays and wrongful-detention payouts followed. Causation is disputed: the County Clerk said Odyssey was not the cause, and the jail's own system never connected to Odyssey.
Test 2, it is where the organisation differentiates: met in the way that fits a public body. Courts do not compete in a market. Their whole mission is deciding cases, and the CMS runs that core function, not the back office. That makes it the court equivalent of a bank's core ledger, not of its payroll.

WHAT A FAILURE EXPOSES. People held past their release date, lost or wrong statutory records, and damaged official statistics.

CORRECTIONS MADE IN THIS CHECK.
(1) Dallas was described as a "failed" switch backed only by a search snippet. It is now cited to Texas Standard and Dallas Morning News reporting, and the disputed cause is stated.
(2) The UK point was overstated. The statistics regulator (OSR) found staff typed Common Platform results as free text instead of result codes, which lowered the quality of criminal court statistics. It was fixed in August 2024. "Corrupted" was too strong, and that source was not reopened in this check.

enterprise.evidence: Spend is null because private companies do not buy this system. Every buyer of court case management is a public body: a national or state judiciary, a county clerk or a city court. Journal Technologies' FY2025 10-K says almost all of its customers are government agencies. The earlier research found no private-company court CMS customer. Nearby private buyers use different software that belongs to other categories. Law firms buy docketing and practice management. Arbitration providers run their own case systems, which this run did not research. How to read the size labels for this category: a statewide or national judiciary is the 'enterprise' buyer, a large county or city court is the 'mid-market' buyer, and a small county or town court is the 'SMB' buyer. All three are priced under the government segment.

mid_market.evidence: Spend is null because private mid-sized companies do not run courts. The public buyer of comparable size is a large county or city court. Verified examples: Cook County IL (about $4.6m a year), Bexar County TX (about $3.8m a year) and Austin Municipal Court ($535k to $850k a year). That tier spends about $0.5m to $5m a year and is priced under the government segment.

smb.evidence: Spend is null because small private businesses do not run courts. The public buyer of comparable size is a small county, justice court or town court. Verified examples: Altamont KS ($365 a year ongoing), Galveston TX municipal court ($61k a year) and Storey County NV (about $417k a year, including implementation). That tier spends about $400 to $400k a year and is priced under the government segment. The low end was corrected from $5k: Altamont's $5,090 was a one-time switching year, and its ongoing cost is $365.

government.evidence:
SUMMARY
Government is the only buyer. Annual vendor spend runs from about $400 for a tiny town court to about $10m for a large US state. National programmes abroad cost more but are paid in irregular multi-year budgets. In-house builds still exist at state and national level and are almost absent at county and city level.

CORRECTIONS MADE IN THIS CHECK
- Low end changed from $5,000 to $400. Altamont KS pays $365 a year ongoing. Its $5,090 was the first-year switching cost.
- Dallas County's roughly $10m Odyssey agreements were signed in 2020, not 2023. Its total Tyler contracts since 2020 are at least $17.5m (from search results, articles not opened).
- Kentucky's '3,300 court staff' appears in neither source, so it was removed.
- Storey County's contract covers the Storey district and justice courts. The Carson City share is only a planned interlocal agreement.
- Journal Technologies' '500+ courts and agencies' comes from a secondary source with no date. The 10-K says only 'about 37 states'.
The high end ($10m) and all other figures matched their sources.

PART 1: BUILD OR BUY, BY TIER
(a) Statewide and national judiciaries: some still build or own. The trend in the US is toward buying.
- Washington AOC still runs the 37-year-old in-house DISCIS/JIS on two IBM z/OS mainframes in its Olympia data centre. It is replacing it with Tyler Enterprise Justice, which it hosts itself, in 143 limited-jurisdiction courts. 11 courts were live by November 2025, and the rest are due by the end of 2027.
- Kentucky replaced its two-decade-old in-house system with Tyler SaaS on AWS, funded by $38m of ARPA money (2022). The courts said they chose a vendor because it was hard to attract and keep technical staff.
- Other in-house builds (from the earlier research): Hawaii (Adabas/Natural/COBOL), US federal CM/ECF, UK HMCTS Common Platform, India's NIC CIS, Indonesia's SIPP and Germany's GeFa.
- Tyler reports 22 statewide Enterprise Justice implementations, 17 of them for trial courts. Outside the US, systems built by government IT agencies remain the norm.
(b) Large counties: a few run their own systems. In Washington, the King and Pierce County superior court clerks use local systems instead of the state's Enterprise Justice.
(c) Small counties and cities: they almost always buy.

PART 2: ANNUAL SPEND, BY TIER
Includes vendor licence, subscription, maintenance, hosting and services. Staff are excluded unless noted.

Tier 1. Statewide judiciary: about $1m to $10m a year in the US.
- North Carolina: about $85m over 10 years for Odyssey Case Manager, File & Serve and Attorney Manager as SaaS. That is about $8.5m a year, including implementation.
- Indiana: the Supreme Court's 2020 budget letter says it pays $1m a year to its Odyssey vendor and $5m a year to its e-filing vendor. Data storage and servers cost nearly $1m more. Total: about $7m a year. Separately, FY2020 equipment plus in-house and contracted developers cost over $12m. Odyssey is free to Indiana counties.
- Washington: the CLJ-CMS budget for 2025-27 is $28,676,000 with 34.5 FTE, about $14m a year. This figure includes staff, so it overstates vendor spend.
- Kentucky: $38m one-time ARPA funding.
- Maryland: about $45m in 2011 for licences, services and multi-year maintenance (search result only).
- Illinois Supreme Court statewide integration: cost grew from $8.4m (2016) to $89m.
- Outside the US: Victoria (Australia) allocated A$89.2m (about US$58m) for a new Magistrates' and Children's Courts system with Journal Technologies. That is a programme budget, not the vendor contract. The UK HMCTS reform programme has £1.3bn and covers far more than case management.

Tier 2. Large county or city court: about $0.5m to $5m a year.
- Cook County IL Clerk: $36.5m Odyssey contract signed in April 2017. It has grown to $48m authorised through 2027, about $4.6m a year.
- Bexar County TX: $7,650,861 for May 2026 to April 2028, covering court, jail, DA and juvenile modules. That is about $3.8m a year, with up to a 5% annual increase allowed.
- Austin Municipal Court: Journal Technologies, sole-source. $535,400 in year 1, rising to $850,000 in year 5, for $3.55m over 5 years.
- Dallas County: about $10m of Odyssey, jury and civil-process agreements (2020), and at least $17.5m of Tyler contracts since 2020 (search results).

Tier 3. Small county, justice court or town court: about $400 to $400k a year.
- Storey County NV: Journal eCourt, up to $1.25m over 3 years, about $417k a year including implementation.
- Galveston TX municipal court: $61,343 a year in Tyler Incode maintenance. Incode has been in use since 2004 and renewed sole-source every year since 2005.
- Altamont KS municipal court: $5,090 in year 1, then $365 a year (CIC). A competing quote from Jayhawk Software was $15,630.

PART 3: CROSS-CHECK FROM A VENDOR FILING
- Journal Technologies' FY2025 revenue was $69.9m: $31.7m licensing and maintenance, $22.7m consulting and $15.5m public-service fees. Filers pay most of the public-service fees, not courts.
- A secondary source says Journal serves over 500 courts and agencies.
- Revenue divided by agencies gives about $110k to $140k per agency per year. That sits inside tier 3 and the bottom of tier 2, which fits a customer base made mostly of counties and cities. Treat this as rough: the revenue is from 2025, and the agency count has no date.

CAVEATS
- Contract totals often include one-time implementation, so the yearly figures overstate steady running cost.
- Washington's budget line includes staff.
- Maryland and the Dallas contract amounts come from search results only. Those articles were not opened.

best_icp: The best first buyer is a mid-sized US county or municipal court of limited jurisdiction, roughly 50k to 1m residents, in a state where each court picks its own system (for example Texas, Ohio or Michigan). Four reasons: these courts buy rather than build; the clerk and county board decide contracts of about $50k to $850k a year locally (Galveston $61k, Austin $535k to $850k); many sit on old Incode, FullCourt or CourtView installs renewed sole-source every year; and statewide deals ($38m to $85m, 10-year terms, decade-long rollouts) are closed to a newcomer until it has reference sites. The safest way in is an AI layer on top of the existing system (intake, docketing, reminders), timed to a renewal date, expanding later into full replacement.

criticality_why:
Verdict: critical. Both tests pass, but the second one only partly.

Test 1. Does the business stop if it fails? Yes, clearly.
- The hospital EHR is the system of record for care and for billing. Registration, orders, medication administration, results, documentation and the claim all run through one database.
- When it fails, the hospital drops to paper downtime procedures. Labs, prescriptions, referrals and registrations go manual. Selayang Hospital in Malaysia did exactly this after its 2021 Cerner outage (from prior research, not re-checked here).
- Billing stops too, because revenue-cycle modules sit on the same database. LA County's June 2026 board memo says its minimum requirement since 2011 has been one integrated database, a "single source for truth" for patient information (verified in the memo).

Test 2. Is it where the hospital competes? Partly, and more so every year.
- The EHR shapes clinician productivity, patient access (portals such as MyChart), interoperability and revenue capture.
- LA County's memo (verified) says the EHR's importance in care delivery has "dramatically changed" since 2011. It justifies a sole-source move to Epic on clinical, workforce, operational and cost grounds. (Correction: the memo does not use the words "central to care delivery", as the earlier draft said.)
- Ardent Health's 2024 IPO prospectus (verified) sells its single Epic instance to investors as a competitive advantage. It cites its Epic Gold Stars 9 rating (top 22% of Epic users) and says Epic makes it a better partner for new technology.
- Switching costs are very high. Large systems spend $1B+ in total programme cost to switch. VA has been replacing its EHR since 2018, and its Oracle contract ceiling rose from about $10B to nearly $27B (FedScoop, verified).

Caveat: most hospitals run fairly standard Epic, Oracle or MEDITECH builds. They differentiate through how they configure and use the system, not through owning unique code. A strict reader could call this "important" instead. "Critical" is still the better fit, because failure halts operations and buyers explicitly cite the EHR as a basis for competing.

enterprise.evidence:
WHO: multi-hospital systems with 10+ hospitals, and academic medical centres.

BUILD VS BUY: rare.
- The famous homegrown EHRs (Vanderbilt, Partners/Beth Israel, Intermountain HELP) have all been replaced by commercial systems, mostly Epic.
- KLAS 2026 (via healthsystemcio, verified): only two 10+ hospital systems made enterprise-wide EHR decisions in 2025, and both chose Epic. Epic now has 43.7% of US acute hospitals and 56.9% of beds.
- These systems own heavy configuration and large in-house analyst teams, but they license the core.

SPEND (vendor licence, maintenance, hosting and services only; not staff). Three independent checks:
1. Epic average (top-down). Epic revenue was $6.7B in 2025 (Wikipedia, verified), across 3,700+ hospitals (Epic figure, via search). That is about $1.8M per hospital a year. This overstates the hospital share, because the revenue also covers clinics and ambulatory-only customers. For a 10-30 hospital system, that implies $18M-$54M a year.
2. NYC Health + Hospitals (verified press release). 11 hospitals plus long-term care sites, 6 diagnostic centres and 70+ clinics. A 15-year Epic contract capped at $302.8M covered licences, professional services, testing, training, maintenance and upgrades. That is about $20M a year (2013 dollars, before hosting). A separate revenue-cycle project came on top (from search, not verified).
3. LA County DHS (4 large hospitals plus clinics; verified board letters). Its Cerner ORCHID contract sum is $784.8M from Dec 2012 to 2027, about $52M a year. That figure includes hosting and application management. Adding only Oracle's revenue-cycle module was projected at over $200M of 10-year total cost of ownership, which is more than $20M a year. (LA County is a public buyer, so it is counted under government. It is shown here as a size check.)

RANGE: $15M-$60M a year. Kaiser and HCA-scale systems sit above it.

NOT IN THIS FIGURE: published all-in programme totals (Kaiser $4B, Mayo $1.5B, Northwell $1.2B; from search, not verified). These include internal staff, hardware and backfill, so they are not comparable to the annual vendor spend above.

mid_market.evidence:
WHO: single hospitals and 2-9 hospital systems, roughly 150-1,000 beds. NHS acute trusts are this size too, but they are counted under government.

BUILD VS BUY: rare. KLAS 2026 (verified via healthsystemcio) says systems with 2-10 hospitals made most 2025 EHR decisions. All of them bought from a vendor (Epic, Oracle Health, MEDITECH, Altera). No vendor other than Epic won a decision covering more than three hospitals.

SPEND:
1. Low end, from MEDITECH's 2019 10-K (verified). A typical 150-bed hospital pays a $3M product fee, a $1M implementation fee and a $30K monthly service fee (about 1% of product fees). Spreading the $4M upfront over 10 years gives $0.4M a year. Adding $0.36M a year in service fees gives about $0.76M a year. These are 2019 list economics, before hosting.
2. High end, from a comparable NHS contract. Lewisham and Greenwich NHS Trust (two acute hospitals plus community services) signed a 10-year, GBP 52M Epic deal (HTN, verified). That is about GBP 5.2M, or roughly $6.8M, a year at $1.30 per pound. It joins a larger Epic instance through a Connect model, which is cheaper than a standalone install.
3. Supporting data, not verified (search snippets only): Norfolk and Waveney's 3-trust MEDITECH deal at GBP 88M, and Somerset/Dorset's 4-trust Epic deal at GBP 222M.

RANGE: $0.7M-$8M a year. Spend scales with beds and with whether revenue cycle and hosting are bundled.

CAVEAT: the top of this range is the weakest number. A standalone 7-9 hospital Epic system could reach $10M-$15M a year, given Epic's ~$1.8M per-hospital average. That is within 2x of $8M, so the figure was not changed.

smb.evidence:
WHO: US critical-access, rural and community hospitals under about 100 beds, plus small private hospitals abroad. TruBridge's 2024 10-K (verified) counts about 2,900 US community hospitals under 100 beds and about 3,800 under 200 beds.

BUILD VS BUY: rare.
- These hospitals buy a packaged EHR (TruBridge, MEDITECH Expanse, Oracle CommunityWorks), or they rent a larger system's Epic instance through Community Connect.
- A Black Book survey (July 2025, 202 rural hospitals in 41 states; verified via newswire) found 83% lack enough internal IT resources.

SPEND:
1. MEDITECH average (10-K, verified). 2019 revenue was $493.8M across about 2,200 active sites, or about $225K per site a year. Sites include non-hospital facilities, and HCA (200+ hospitals) alone was 7% of revenue.
2. TruBridge (10-K, verified). The Patient Care (EHR) segment earned $125.0M in 2024. About 98% of its acute clients have under 100 beds. KLAS gives TruBridge 7.6% of US acute hospitals, which is roughly 400-450 hospitals (my estimate). That implies about $250K-$300K per hospital a year. (Correction: the earlier draft cited 1,200 hospitals, which includes revenue-cycle-only clients and understates spend per EHR hospital.)
3. Epic Community Connect. Veterans Memorial Hospital, a 25-bed critical-access hospital in Iowa, went live for $3.88M (Becker's, via search). Spread over 10 years, that is about $0.39M a year before the host system's ongoing fees.
4. Pricing model. MEDITECH sells its cloud EHR to these hospitals as a monthly subscription with go-live in about 6 months (Healthcare Dive). It publishes no price.

RANGE: $0.1M-$0.6M a year.

BUYING PRESSURE (Black Book, verified): 85% of surveyed rural hospitals call their total cost of ownership unsustainable, and 55% plan to reassess or replace their EHR by the end of 2026.

government.evidence:
WHO: public hospital systems, NHS trusts, military health and national health ministries.

BUILD VS BUY: some. Government is the one segment that still builds, but rich countries are moving to buy.
- Built: the US VA built and runs VistA. GAO-19-125 (verified via GAO summary) found VistA-related costs of $913.7M, $664.3M and $711.1M in FY2015-17, including government labour. VistA is now being replaced by Oracle.
- Built: the Philippine Department of Health's iHOMIS is installed and supported free for government hospitals (search snippet, not verified).
- Built: India's NIC e-Hospital runs on the national cloud in 650-1,000+ public facilities (search snippet, not verified).
- Built: Indonesia's ministry offers SIMGOS (prior research).
- Buying: VA and DoD now buy Oracle, Singapore's public clusters buy Epic, and LA County is moving from Oracle to Epic.

TYPICAL SPEND for a developed-market public hospital system or trust: $1M-$55M a year.
- Lewisham and Greenwich NHS Trust pays about $6.8M a year to Epic (verified).
- NYC Health + Hospitals pays about $20M a year to Epic (2013 contract, verified).
- LA County DHS pays about $52M a year to Cerner (ORCHID contract sum of $784.8M over Dec 2012-2027, including hosting and managed services; verified in a May 2026 board letter). Adding Oracle revenue cycle would have added more than $20M a year (June 2026 memo, verified).
- Correction: the earlier draft capped this range at $40M. LA County's verified contract shows a large county system above that, so the cap is raised to $55M.

The two extreme tails sit outside the typical range and are shown separately.

TOP TAIL, US federal programmes:
- VA's Oracle contract ceiling is nearly $27B, now running to May 2031 (FedScoop, verified). That is about $2.1B a year over 13 years, for roughly 170 medical centres. It is a ceiling, not actual spend.
- DoD's MHS GENESIS sustainment extension with Leidos is $1.13B over 3 years, about $377M a year, plus a $263M transition option. It covers 3,600+ locations and 194,000 clinical users (Nextgov, verified).

BOTTOM TAIL, emerging-market public hospitals:
- RSPAD Gatot Soebroto, an Indonesian army hospital, awarded its 2025 SIMRS maintenance contract at Rp 360M, about $22K a year at Rp 16,300 per dollar (LPSE, verified).
- RSUD Abdul Moeloek put SIMRS development out to tender in 2024 with a Rp 2B ceiling (about $123K). The selection failed, so no contract was awarded (verified; the earlier draft omitted this).
- Hospitals on free ministry-built systems pay close to zero in vendor fees.

best_icp: Start with SMB: the ~2,900 US rural, critical-access and community hospitals under 100 beds, sold a subscription cloud EHR with revenue cycle built in. They buy rather than build, spend $0.1M-$0.6M a year, 85% call their costs unsustainable, 55% plan to reassess by end-2026, and their incumbents are in flux (IKS agreed in April 2026 to buy TruBridge, and Oracle has been the largest net loser of hospitals for three straight years). The main threat is Epic Community Connect, which large systems are extending to these hospitals. Move up to 2-9 hospital systems next, where most 2025 decisions were made. Avoid enterprise and government at first: they are consolidating on Epic or face multi-year public procurements.
