criticality_why: VERDICT: critical. Both tests pass, and the check found no reason to downgrade. TEST 1, THE BUSINESS STOPS WITHOUT IT: for a wholesale distributor the ERP is the transaction engine. Counter and phone order entry, quoting, customer and contract pricing, rebates, multi-branch stock, purchasing, picking and shipping all run through it. If it is down, branches cannot quote, take orders, check stock or ship. Margins are thin: ERP Research's wholesale guide uses a $50M distributor at 2% net margin and says a 1-point gross-margin gain from better pricing and inventory control is worth about $500K a year. TEST 2, IT IS WHERE THE FIRM COMPETES: distributors win on availability, fill rate, price accuracy and speed of service. Those live in the ERP's pricing matrices, replenishment logic and branch-transfer rules. That is why vertical systems persist (Eclipse for electrical, plumbing and HVAC; BisTrack for lumber; P21 for industrial and MRO) and why add-on vendors sell into the ERP's order and margin logic. Conexiom, which automates order capture, says 16 of the top 20 distributors and manufacturers use it. SWITCHING IS SLOW AND RISKY: ERP Research gives 4 to 9 months to implement P21 at a mid-size distributor and 12 to 18 months for larger multi-branch rollouts. MSC Industrial took a phased, multi-year path off its homegrown AS/400 core, and its CIO called the first upgrade alone about a year of painful work. Wesco has a $500M multi-year technology program ($270M spent by Feb 2025) that includes streamlining backend systems. CORRECTIONS FROM THE CHECK: (1) Conexiom's claim is '16 of the top 20 distributors and manufacturers', not '16 of the top 20 industrial distributors'. (2) The earlier '12 to 18 months for mid-market migrations' was wrong. That range is ERP Research's figure for larger multi-branch rollouts. Mid-size is 4 to 9 months. (3) The Proton.ai mention was dropped because no source for it was opened.

enterprise.evidence: WHO: distributors with roughly $1B+ revenue, 150+ ERP users and several distribution centres (Grainger, Fastenal, MSC, Wesco, Sysco tier). BUILD VS BUY: some build (verified). Fastenal's FY2025 10-K says its systems are 'custom in-house developed, purchased, and subscription licensed software' and that each selling location runs a locally installed point-of-sale system. IT is 34% to 39% of its 2,220 support staff, about 755 to 865 people. MSC Industrial ran a homegrown IBM AS/400 ERP (with JD Edwards for finance and PeopleSoft for HR) and decided in 2016 to move to SAP. It went first to S/4HANA Finance, then to S/4HANA private cloud on Google Cloud (TechTarget). The usual pattern is a tier-1 package (SAP, Oracle, Infor) with heavy customisation, while a minority still run homegrown cores. SPEND, STEP BY STEP. Step 1, software: ERP Research's wholesale guide puts enterprise distributors (150+ users, multiple DCs) at $350K to $3M+ a year in subscription. Its SAP S/4HANA Private Cloud page gives a total cost of $500K to $5M+ and cites third-party estimates of $140 to $220 per FUE per month. At 1,000 FUEs that is about $1.7M to $2.6M a year. Step 2, implementation: the wholesale guide gives $500K to $5M+ for enterprise (the SAP page goes up to $10M). That is typically 1x to 3x annual software cost. Spread over 5 years, it adds about $100K to $1M+ a year. Step 3, add the pieces. LOW END: about $350K subscription, $100K amortised implementation and some hosting or partner support comes to about $0.5M a year, for a 150 to 300 user single instance. TYPICAL TOP OF ONE INSTANCE: about $3M subscription, about $1M amortised implementation and about $1M of systems-integrator run support comes to about $5M a year. MULTI-ERP ESTATES: the largest distributors pay for old and new systems in parallel during consolidation, which can double that to about $10M a year. RESULT: $0.5M to $10M a year. CORRECTIONS FROM THE CHECK: (1) The low end fell from $1M to $0.5M. The $1M figure assumed 1,000 users, but the segment starts at 150 users, and the source's own low end is $350K subscription. (2) The high end fell from $15M to $10M. No source supported $15M, and the sourced pieces add up to about $5M per instance. Wesco's $500M program covers ecommerce, supply chain and AI as well as backend systems, so it cannot be used to support an ERP-only number. (3) The claim that the SAP page gives '$1.5M to $2M for 1,000 users after discounts' is not on the page and has been replaced with the per-FUE arithmetic above. (4) The '18 ERPs at Wesco' claim was dropped. Wesco's FY2025 10-K and the Digital Commerce 360 article do not give an ERP count. CAVEAT: SAP and Infor publish no list prices, so every figure here is a third-party benchmark.

mid_market.evidence: WHO: branch-based distributors with about $20M to $1B revenue and 30 to 150 ERP users. This is the core base of Epicor P21 (ERP Research cites 5,000+ distributor customers but notes Epicor does not publish counts), Epicor Eclipse, Infor CloudSuite Distribution / SX.e (Infor said almost 1,000 SX.e customers in 2011; A+ had about 1,200 customers when Infor's predecessor bought it in 2004; Infor now says 'over 4,000 distribution companies run on Infor'), DDI Inform and Dynamics GP. BUILD VS BUY: rarely build. These firms buy a packaged vertical ERP and customise it through resellers. Their real constraint is the vendor's roadmap, and every deadline below was verified. P21's last on-prem release is 2028.1 (about May 2028), with active support to 30 June 2029. Dynamics GP product support ends 31 December 2029, with security patches to 30 April 2031. Infor no longer sells SX.e on-prem (new buyers must take CloudSuite Distribution) and no longer sells new FACTS licences. SPEND, STEP BY STEP. Step 1, published benchmark: ERP Research's wholesale guide gives $75K to $400K a year in subscription for 30 to 150 users, plus $100K to $600K to implement. Spread over 5 years, implementation adds $20K to $120K a year, for a total of about $95K to $520K a year. Step 2, bottom-up for P21: ERP Research lists a platform fee of about $1,000 a month plus $100 to $175 per user per month. That is about $48K to $75K a year at 30 users, $72K to $117K at 50 users and $132K to $222K at 100 users. Implementation for a mid-size distributor is $50K to $250K, and support is about 20% of licence. Step 3, bottom-up for Infor CloudSuite Distribution: third-party pricing summaries give $150 to $275 per user per month (the source page returned 403, so this is a search-summary figure). That is about $90K to $400K a year at 50 to 120 users. RESULT: about $75K a year (a 30 to 50 user P21 or Acumatica site with services) to about $500K a year (a 150-user, multi-branch CloudSuite or P21 site with services). CORRECTIONS FROM THE CHECK: (1) The P21 per-user arithmetic was wrong because it left out most of the platform fee. It is now $72K to $117K at 50 users (was $61K to $105K) and $132K to $222K at 100 users (was $121K to $211K). (2) ERP Research's '$60K to $300K' for P21 is a total project cost (software plus implementation), not a yearly cost as first stated. (3) The A+ customer count dates from 2004, not 2011. None of these changes moves the range.

smb.evidence: WHO: wholesalers under about $20M revenue with 5 to 30 users. This is most of the buyer universe. The earlier research counted about 628K US wholesale establishments, 1.58M EU27 wholesale enterprises and about 101K UK wholesale enterprises. Those counts were not re-checked here, and a search summary of the 2022 Economic Census gives about 697K US establishments, so treat the counts as roughly right. BUILD VS BUY: rarely build. These firms buy packaged SMB ERP (Business Central, NetSuite, Acumatica, SAP Business One, Sage, Pronto) or stay on accounting software and spreadsheets. SPEND, STEP BY STEP. Step 1, cheapest credible ERP: Microsoft lists Business Central Essentials at $80 and Premium at $110 per user per month, paid yearly (verified). For 10 users that is about $9.6K to $13.2K a year before partner fees. Step 2, NetSuite: ERP Research gives $999 a month base plus $99 to $199 per user per month, and says about 10 users usually pay about $12K to $60K a year in subscription only (verified). Step 3, published distribution benchmark: ERP Research's wholesale guide gives $20K to $90K a year in subscription for 5 to 30 users, plus $20K to $80K to implement. Spread over 5 years, implementation adds about $4K to $16K a year. Acumatica distribution pricing is resource-based, with search summaries giving about $1,800 to $2,500 a month, or about $22K to $30K a year. RESULT: about $10K a year (a 10-user Business Central site) to about $100K a year (a 30-user distribution package with amortised implementation and partner fees). CORRECTION FROM THE CHECK: the high end rose from $90K to $100K. The $90K was subscription only, and this field also counts vendor and partner services. CAVEAT: the smallest wholesalers (under about 5 users) often spend under $5K a year on accounting software and are not realistic ERP buyers.

government.evidence: WHO: a niche, not a mainstream segment. The real public buyers of distribution-style ERP are the alcohol monopolies in the roughly 17 US control jurisdictions (they run wholesale DCs and often retail stores), plus central stores, central medical stores and defence logistics agencies. Ordinary government agencies do not buy wholesale-distribution ERP. BUILD VS BUY: some build. Virginia ABC's 2023 report to the Senate Finance committee says its licensing system was 'custom built to reflect unique ABC licensing requirements' ($8.3M capitalised). It is also replacing inventory and order management under a policy that prefers SaaS. The Pennsylvania Liquor Control Board (PLCB) calls IBMS 'the Agency's main computer system that runs the day-to-day operations' (board minutes, 20 March 2024) and is moving its core to Oracle. SPEND, STEP BY STEP. Step 1, top end (PLCB, verified): Oracle contract purchase agreement No. 63017408 was approved 17 Jan 2018 and runs to 26 Feb 2030. Its cap was raised from $136M to $162M to pay for Release 3 (merchandise planning, project management), Release 4 (retail point of sale) and legacy-system maintenance. $162M over about 12 years is about $13.5M a year. That is a cap, not actual spend, and it includes about 600 stores' retail and POS, so it overstates the distribution-ERP share. Step 2, mid point (Virginia ABC, new datum): its financial management system replacement was capitalised at $5.8M and amortised at about $0.83M a year. Its POS system cost $17.3M. Step 3, low end: a smaller control-state agency running a mid-market or enterprise package with services lands at about $0.5M a year. That is consistent with Virginia ABC's finance system at $0.83M a year in a large state. RESULT: $0.5M to $13.5M a year. CORRECTIONS FROM THE CHECK: (1) The 'highly customized' quote in the PLCB minutes refers to the PLCB+ online licensing system. That system comes from a vendor, Computronix, under a sole-source extension of about $1.74M, so it is not evidence of in-house build. The build evidence now rests on Virginia ABC's custom licensing system and PLCB's legacy IBMS core. (2) The low end is now anchored to the Virginia ABC data rather than inference alone. CAVEAT: low confidence and a small segment. It should not drive go-to-market.

best_icp: Sell first to mid-market branch-based distributors (about $20M to $500M revenue, 30 to 150 users) on Epicor P21, Eclipse, Infor SX.e or A+, DDI Inform or Dynamics GP, for four reasons: they almost never build in-house, they spend a meaningful $75K to $500K a year, verified vendor deadlines (P21 on-prem active support ends June 2029, GP support ends December 2029, Infor no longer sells SX.e on-prem) force a re-platforming decision anyway, and their projects run 4 to 9 months against 6 to 18 months for enterprise S/4HANA estates, which partly build their own cores; SMB budgets of $10K to $100K are thin and government is a niche.

criticality_why: VERDICT: important (checked and kept). Under this study's rules, 'critical' needs two things. The business must stop or lose its licence when the system fails, AND the system must be where the firm competes. Manufacturing ERP passes the first test and fails the second. TEST 1, does the business stop when it fails? Yes. Manufacturing ERP runs MRP, purchasing, inventory, work orders, shipping and invoicing. Two Clorox events show the damage. (a) The August 2023 cyberattack disrupted its systems and forced reduced-rate operations with workarounds. Q1 FY24 net sales fell 20%, from $1.74B to about $1.39B, roughly $350M, which Clorox attributed mainly to lower volume from the attack (Clorox 8-K press release, Nov 2023). (b) The 2025 cutover to its new cloud ERP cut quarterly net sales 19% (organic -17%) for the quarter ended 30 Sep 2025, and the CEO said the ramp-up cost it more market share than expected (CIO Dive). Few back-office systems can do that much harm. TEST 2, is it where the firm competes? No. Manufacturers compete on product, process engineering, quality and cost. The ERP is a standard package (SAP, Epicor, QAD, Infor, Plex) that their competitors also run. Tesla, which built its own ERP called Warp (The Register), is the notable exception. No regulator licenses a plant based on its ERP. Traceability rules in automotive, aerospace and life sciences raise the stakes, but those records usually sit in quality or MES modules. RESULT: important, not critical. WHAT IT MEANS FOR AN ENTRANT: buyers switch only when the cutover is low-risk. Being better is not enough. Clorox shows what a bad cutover costs, so overlays, modernisation of the existing system, and phased cutovers will sell more easily than a big-bang replacement. CHECKER NOTES: the Clorox cyberattack numbers were attributed to Cybersecurity Dive, which does not carry them. They are now sourced to Clorox's own 8-K. The earlier claim that Tesla built Warp 'around 2012' is not in the cited source and has been removed.

enterprise.evidence: VERDICT: range kept at $1.5M-$25M a year. All four checks below land inside it. WHO: manufacturers with more than $1B revenue, typically on SAP ECC or S/4HANA, Oracle or Infor LN, often across many plants. BUILD VS BUY: rare. Nearly all large manufacturers buy a packaged ERP and then customise it heavily. Custom ABAP code is one reason ECC-to-S/4 migrations are slow. Tesla's Warp is the notable exception (The Register). SPEND, four independent checks. (1) RISE subscription benchmark. ERP Research puts SAP S/4HANA Private Cloud (licence plus hosting) at $500K to $5M+ a year, citing third-party benchmarks of $140-$220 per FUE per month. SAP publishes no list price. At 2,000-10,000 FUE that is about $3.4M-$26M a year. (2) Per-user benchmark for manufacturers. ERP Research's manufacturing page gives $3,500-$10,000+ per user a year. 500 users at the low rate is $1.75M. 2,500 users at the high rate is $25M. (3) On-prem maintenance. SAP Enterprise Support is typically 22% of net licence fees a year (UpperEdge). A $7M-$50M licence estate implies $1.5M-$11M a year in maintenance alone, before hosting and outsourced application management (AMS). The licence-estate sizes are an assumption, not sourced. (4) Programme scale (a one-off peak, not run-rate). Clorox budgeted $500M over five years for its ERP-led digital transformation and later raised it to $580M. About three-quarters is incremental operating cost, mostly tied to the ERP (CIO Dive). RESULT: about $1.5M a year for a $1B single-region manufacturer, rising to $25M+ for a global multi-plant SAP estate. This covers licence or subscription, support, hosting and outsourced AMS, not internal staff. The bottom of the range overlaps with large customers of Epicor, QAD and Infor, who can spend under $1M. CONFIDENCE: medium. SAP does not publish prices, so every figure rests on third-party benchmarks.

mid_market.evidence: VERDICT: range kept at $50K-$400K a year. The vendor averages, rechecked against filings, sit between $43K and $215K per customer. WHO: discrete and process manufacturers with roughly $20M-$1B revenue. This is the core installed base of the legacy systems in scope: Epicor Vantage, Vista and Kinetic, QAD (MFG/PRO lineage), Infor LN, IBM i RPG systems (Infor XA and LX, JD Edwards World) and Plex. BUILD VS BUY: rare. These firms lack the IT staff to build an ERP. Their in-house work is mostly keeping old RPG or Progress code alive, which is the retiring-developer problem from the earlier research. SPEND, vendor revenue divided by customers (all rechecked). (1) Epicor. More than $1B ARR and more than 23,000 customers, announced 9 April 2024 (ERP Global Insights). That is about $43K of recurring revenue per customer. The average is pulled down by small distribution and retail customers. ERP Research gives Kinetic cloud at $100-$200 per user a month plus a $1,500 monthly platform fee. A 25-user manufacturer pays $5K-$8K a month, and mid-market manufacturers typically pay $4K-$20K a month all-in. That is $48K-$240K a year. (2) QAD, fiscal year ended 31 Jan 2021 (Q4 FY21 financial statements, checked line by line). Total revenue $307.9M: subscription $131.1M, maintenance $107.1M, licence $11.2M, professional services $58.5M. The 10-K says over 2,000 manufacturing companies at about 4,000 sites. That is about $154K per customer in total, or about $119K recurring. QAD's base includes some large global firms, which lifts the average. (3) Plex. More than $150M of sales in 2020 (BizTimes) and more than 700 customers (Rockwell press release). That is about $215K per customer. (4) Infor LN. 1,500+ discrete manufacturers, no pricing published. RESULT: $50K-$400K a year, centred on $100K-$200K. The top end is multi-site manufacturers on QAD, Plex or Infor LN. CONFIDENCE: medium-high. The figures come from filings and vendor disclosures. The averages include some services revenue and some non-manufacturing customers.

smb.evidence: VERDICT: range kept at $3K-$40K a year. All three price lists were reopened and match, with one fix to the Odoo prices. WHO: manufacturers with fewer than about 100 staff and under about $20M revenue. In the US there are about 180,000 manufacturing firms with fewer than 20 employees and 44,917 with 20-99 (Census SUSB 2022, from the earlier research). BUILD VS BUY: rare to build a real system. The usual substitute is spreadsheets or accounting software, not a homegrown ERP. A small-sample Qlector survey found 50% of manufacturers still rely on Excel or paper for planning. Many SMBs buy nothing, so the main competitor is the spreadsheet. SPEND, from published price lists. (1) Katana. Core plan from $299 a month. Add-ons: Manufacturing Management $199, Warehouse Management $149 and Traceability $249 a month. Optional onboarding is $2,000. Extra locations and sales orders are billed by usage. Core alone is about $3.6K a year. Core plus all three add-ons is about $10.8K a year, rising toward $15K with usage, and the custom-priced Advantage plan sits above that. (2) MRPeasy. $49, $69, $99 and $149 per user a month across four tiers, with users beyond 10 at $79 per extra block of 10. Example: 12 Enterprise users cost $1,069 a month, about $12.8K a year. (3) Odoo. List prices are $38.90 (Standard) and $76.20 (Custom) per user a month, discounted to $31.10 and $61.00 in the first year. Manufacturing (MRP) is included. 20 Custom users at list price is about $18.3K a year before partner implementation. RESULT: $3K-$40K a year, including light partner services. CONFIDENCE: high on list prices, medium on what customers actually pay. Few SMBs run decades-old ERP, so demand to replace legacy systems is thin here.

government.evidence: VERDICT: range kept at $1M-$150M a year. The ceiling is supported by two separate sources. The floor is still an estimate. WHO: a niche segment. Most of government does not buy manufacturing ERP. The buyers are government-owned production and maintenance sites: defence depots, arsenals and ammunition plants, naval shipyards, mints, and state-owned manufacturers (for example Indian defence PSUs; no source found to size these). BUILD VS BUY: some. Today the pattern is a COTS core plus a large, integrator-built, government-owned configuration. The systems they replaced were often written in-house. The US Army Logistics Modernization Program (LMP) is the reference case. It is an SAP-based COTS ERP running the Army Materiel Command's Organic Industrial Base at more than 50 depots, arsenals and plants, with about 30,000 users. It includes electronic work instructions and capacity planning and scheduling (army.mil). The integrator was CSC, under a contract signed in December 1999 (GovExec, FCW). The army.mil article does not name CSC, so that claim is now sourced separately. SPEND. (1) Ceiling. GAO puts LMP life-cycle cost at over $4B for FY2000-2026, about $150M a year averaged over 27 years, with Increment 2 alone at $730M. This includes build-out as well as run cost. A second check: after a contract dispute, CSC received a five-year LMP extension worth about $1B, roughly $200M a year (HKA case study). So $150M is the top of the segment, a whole service's industrial base, not a typical buyer. (2) Context, not used for the range. The Navy's SAP software and maintenance BPA has a ceiling of $975.9M over up to 10 years, about $98M a year, but it covers all Navy SAP use, not only manufacturing (Washington Technology). (3) Floor. $1M is an estimate for a single government-owned plant on a packaged ERP, set near the enterprise floor. No contract was found to confirm it. The Sellafield SAP award cited earlier is a GBP 33M HR SaaS contract, not manufacturing ERP, and was removed as evidence. RESULT: about $1M a year for one plant, up to about $150M for a service-wide industrial-base ERP. CONFIDENCE: low at the floor, medium at the ceiling. This is a poor first market because of FedRAMP and IL accreditation, long procurement cycles and incumbent integrators.

best_icp: Start with mid-market discrete manufacturers ($20M-$500M revenue, one to ten plants) still running ageing IBM i/RPG, Progress or Epicor Vantage-era ERP. They spend about $50K-$400K a year on it (vendor filings imply $43K-$215K per customer), almost never build in-house, face a retiring-developer problem, and can be reached without SAP-scale integrators. Enterprises are locked into SAP programmes costing millions a year, and SMBs pay only $3K-$40K in a market already crowded by Katana, MRPeasy and Odoo.

criticality_why:
Verdict: important. Checked and kept.

What the system does. EAM/CMMS holds work orders, preventive-maintenance schedules, spare parts and asset histories. Plants, fleets and networks rely on it to stay running. In regulated sectors (nuclear, aviation, rail, water) its records are part of the compliance evidence. Example: the Toronto Transit Commission (TTC) board paper calls Maximo a centralized platform for managing its critical asset data (source opened and confirmed).

Why it is not 'critical'. The 'critical' label needs two things at once: (1) the business stops or loses its licence when the system fails, and (2) the system is where the firm competes. EAM fails both tests.
Test 1, failure impact. A failure degrades operations slowly. Plants can fall back to paper or spreadsheets for a while. UpKeep (a vendor, 2018 data, source opened) reports 55% of facilities use spreadsheets and 44% use paper, while only 53% use a CMMS. A bank core or billing outage stops the business the same day. An EAM outage does not.
Test 2, differentiation. Maintenance practice is broadly the same across firms, so buyers take packages off the shelf. In a 2000 survey of 87 maintenance practitioners (plant-maintenance.com, opened), only 1 (1.1%) ran a CMMS built in-house.

Why it is not 'supporting'. Regulated operators cannot run for long without the maintenance record, and asset-heavy firms lose uptime without PM scheduling. That is more than back-office convenience.

Result: the business depends on it, but it is not where the firm competes. 'Important' is justified.

enterprise.evidence:
Verdict: range kept at $250k-5M a year. Build-in-house kept at 'rare'. All primary figures checked against their sources. Wording on the IBM floor tightened.

BUILD VS BUY
Large enterprises buy (Maximo, SAP PM, Infor/HxGN EAM, IFS) and then customize heavily. 'Owning' here means heavily scripted on-prem Maximo or SAP PM, not software written from scratch.
- 2000 survey: 1 of 87 respondents (1.1%) used an in-house CMMS (opened, confirmed).
- Datastream's 2005 10-K: 'over 6,500 customers, including more than 60 percent of the Fortune 500' (opened, confirmed; a 2005 vendor claim).
- SAP shops run PM as a module of the ERP they already own. There is no separate PM bill to isolate, so they fall outside the spend range below.

SPEND RANGE (licence or subscription plus support, no staff)
Step 1, the IBM list floor. The AWS Marketplace listing prices client-managed MAS at $1,416 per AppPoint for 12 months, with a 500-AppPoint minimum (confirmed). 500 x $1,416 = $708k a year. Caveat: IBM's own pricing page puts Essentials SaaS at under $40k for 150 AppPoints (about $270 per AppPoint) and Standard SaaS starting at 300 AppPoints with no published price. So $708k is the floor for client-managed software only. A single-division Standard SaaS estate can come in well below it.
Step 2, real contracts.
- TTC (large transit operator, an enterprise-scale proxy): CAD 22.78M including HST over 10 years from Jan 2025. Of that, CAD 1.56M is one-off capital for extra licences. Operating spend is CAD 1.75M in 2025, rising to CAD 2.07M in 2029, including a 10% contingency. At about 0.72 USD per CAD that is USD 1.25-1.5M a year (confirmed from Table 1 of the board paper).
- US Department of Veterans Affairs: $4,394,686 for Maximo subscription and support, 1 Jan to 31 Dec 2025, via NASA SEWP (confirmed).
Step 3, a vendor cross-check. Facilio, a competitor (treat with caution), says large-enterprise Maximo exceeds $500k in year one. That figure includes $80-100k of implementation. The same article puts SAP EAM at $200k+ a year.

HOW THE ENDS WERE SET
- Low, $250k: a single-division Maximo Standard SaaS or HxGN EAM estate. This sits between Facilio's $200k+ SAP EAM figure and its $500k+ first-year Maximo figure, so it is within 2x of the evidence.
- High, about $5M: agency-wide or global multi-site estates. Anchored on the VA's $4.39M.
- Upgrade years can add integrator services on top of that. Base support for Maximo 7.6.1 ended 30 Sep 2025, and paid Extended Support ended 30 Sep 2026, which forces MAS migrations now.

mid_market.evidence:
Verdict: range kept at $15k-150k a year. Build-in-house kept at 'rare'. Arithmetic rechecked. Two sources downgraded to secondary.

BUILD VS BUY
Mid-market plants buy. They run older packaged products (Datastream MP2, Infor/HxGN EAM, IFS/Ultimo, SAP PM inside a mid-size ERP) or have moved to cloud CMMS (Fiix, Limble, MaintainX, eMaint). No source showed a mid-market firm writing its own system.

SPEND RANGE, FIVE INDEPENDENT ANCHORS
1. Per-seat list prices for 20-50 technicians, annual billing:
   - Fiix $45-75 per user per month (Fiix pricing page, confirmed).
   - MaintainX $20-65 (MaintainX pricing page, confirmed).
   - Limble $28-69. Limble's own page now shows only a calculator, so this figure comes from third-party listings.
   Math: 20 x $20 x 12 = $4.8k up to 50 x $75 x 12 = $45k. Most teams land at about $10k-45k a year.
2. IBM Maximo Essentials SaaS: under $40k a year for up to 25 users and 150 AppPoints (IBM pricing page, confirmed). That is the incumbent's own mid-market floor.
3. HxGN EAM: ReliaMag (secondary) gives $100-300 per user per month. At $100 and 50-100 users that is $60k-120k a year. At higher rates it can pass $150k.
4. Historical average: Datastream had $101.62M revenue in 2005 across about 6,500 customers, about $15.6k per customer a year (10-K, confirmed). 71.6% of that was services and support. The base mixed mid-market MP2 sites with enterprise 7i sites.
5. Facilio (a competitor, treat with caution): a mid-sized Maximo deployment costs $150k-350k in year one, all-in, including $80-100k of implementation. Without implementation, the recurring part is roughly $70k-250k.

RESULT
Recurring spend is about $15k-150k a year. Single-site cloud CMMS users sit at the bottom. Multi-site firms on a full EAM sit at the top, and some go above it.

smb.evidence:
Verdict: range kept at $0-10k a year. 'Common' kept, with the definition made explicit. The cross-check is flagged as weak.

BUILD VS BUY: WHY 'COMMON'
SMBs do not write software. 'Common' here means they often run maintenance on tools they own instead of buying a CMMS: paper, spreadsheets and whiteboards. UpKeep (a vendor, 2018 data, opened) reports that across facilities of all sizes, 55% use spreadsheets, 44% use paper and only 53% use a CMMS. The data is not broken out by company size. Small sites are the likeliest non-adopters, so the share for SMBs is probably higher. This do-it-yourself setup is the main competitor in this segment.

SPEND RANGE
Buyers pay published per-seat prices on annual billing:
- MaintainX: free Basic tier, Essential $20, Premium $65 per user per month (confirmed).
- Fiix: free tier, Basic $45, Professional $75 (confirmed).
- Limble: $28-69 (third-party listings).
Math: 1-10 technicians pay $0 (free tier) up to 10 x $75 x 12 = $9k a year. Range: $0-10k.

CROSS-CHECK (weak)
MaintainX expects more than $135M ARR for calendar 2026 (Autodesk 8-K for the roughly $3.6B acquisition, confirmed). The filing gives no customer count. A secondary directory lists 'over 13,000' customers, an older figure. $135M / 13,000 is about $10.4k per customer. The two figures come from different dates, and large accounts pull the average up, so this is only a rough ceiling. It is consistent with a typical SMB paying a few thousand dollars a year.

government.evidence:
Verdict: range kept at $25k-5M a year. 'Some' kept. Two data points corrected: the Rancho Palos Verdes implementation figure was wrong, and the Western Australia Department of Transport figures were removed because the source does not support them.

BUILD VS BUY: WHY 'SOME'
Civilian agencies, transit operators, water utilities and cities mostly buy: Maximo, Cityworks, Lucity or HxGN EAM. Defence is the exception. The US Air Force runs its own Base Maintenance (BMx) family of systems: IMDS (the Integrated Maintenance Data System), the Maintenance Scheduling Module, the Enhanced Maintenance Operations Center and others. Citizant sustains them under a $20.7M, five-year task order, about $4.1M a year in vendor services alone (confirmed). The article does not use the words 'government-owned'. But these are Air Force systems sustained by a services contractor, not licensed products. So some large agencies do own and run custom systems.

SPEND LADDER BY BUYER SIZE (all recurring unless noted)
- Small city: Rancho Palos Verdes, CA (about 42k people) licenses Cityworks Workgroup edition for $27,000 a year. One-time implementation by Miller Spatial is $48,825, or up to $53,707.50 with contingency. Year one totals $80,707.50, licence included. CORRECTED: the earlier draft said 'plus $80.7k for implementation'. In fact $80.7k is the year-one total.
- Mid-size city: Ventura, CA approved a $61,222.73 amendment for one year (June 2022 to June 2023) of Lucity licensing, service and support, and consulting (confirmed). The contract total rose from $109,278 to $170,500.73.
- State authority: NY Environmental Facilities Corporation approved an estimated $695k over five years for Maximo SaaS, about $139k a year (confirmed). The scope is phase two of a wastewater asset-management pilot, so a full rollout would cost more.
- Transit operator: TTC pays about USD 1.25-1.5M a year for Maximo licences and support (confirmed from the board paper).
- Federal department: the VA paid $4.39M for calendar 2025 Maximo subscription and support (confirmed).
- REMOVED: Western Australia Department of Transport. The earlier draft cited A$822k for a licence renewal and A$218.6k for application support. The linked govmarket page shows only a A$98.6k Maximo upgrade contract awarded to BPD Zenith in August 2022 (from 7.6.0.9 to 7.6.1.2 or version 8). The other two figures could not be found, so they were dropped.

RESULT
About $25k a year for a small city up to about $5M for a federal department.

best_icp: Sell first to mid-market asset-heavy operators with about 50-1,000 employees (multi-site manufacturers, food and beverage plants, mid-size water and power utilities and municipalities). They buy rather than build and spend about $15k-150k a year, so the deal size is large enough to matter. Many still run aging MP2, Infor or Maximo 7.6.1 installs or spreadsheets, and with Maximo 7.6.1 base support ended in Sept 2025 and Extended Support ended in Sept 2026, Maximo users now face a forced, costly MAS migration. That is a natural trigger to switch. (The earlier '1-3 month sales cycle' had no source and was removed.) SMB is crowded by MaintainX, Limble and UpKeep at a few thousand dollars per account, and enterprise and federal deals bring long procurements and heavy customization lock-in.

criticality_why: VERDICT: 'important' is correct. Kept. WHY THE BUSINESS DEPENDS ON IT: The general ledger is the audited system of record. If it fails at quarter-end, the company cannot close its books, cannot file statutory or SEC reports on time, and fails SOX/ICFR testing. Lenders, auditors and regulators all rely on it. That dependence is why replacements are slow (Hawaii's COBOL ledger FAMIS has run since 1970 and its replacement is scheduled over 5 to 6 years; the 1.5 to 6 year industry range from ASUG 2024 was not re-checked in this pass). WHY IT IS NOT 'CRITICAL': This study's 'critical' needs two things: the business stops if it fails, AND it is where the firm competes. The GL passes the first test and fails the second. Two competitors can run the same SAP, Oracle or NetSuite ledger and neither gains an edge. EXCEPTION: In banks and insurers the accounting hub sits closer to the product, but even there the core GL is bought (Finantrix: buy unless you are a Tier 1 bank with a $500M+ tech budget) and only sub-ledgers and hubs are custom.

enterprise.evidence: VERDICT: Range $0.3M to $5M a year kept. Build = rare, kept. Two small wording fixes below. BUILD (checked): Enterprises buy the GL (SAP ECC/S4, Oracle EBS/Fusion, PeopleSoft) and customize it. Finantrix's buyer guide says to buy unless you are a Tier 1 global bank with a $500M+ tech budget. It puts an in-house build at $15-50M over 3-4 years plus 15-20 FTE a year to maintain, and notes regional banks that tried building ran $20-50M over budget. FIX: the original said '$2-8M to buy'. The source's $2-8M is implementation cost for mid-market banks, not the buy price. Its annual buy figures are $0.5-2M (community banks) and $5-20M+ (Tier 1 banks). SPEND, three checked anchors: (1) Rimini Street 10-K: $421.5M 2025 revenue, over 1,560 unique clients, so about $270K per client. It charges about 50% of the vendor's annual support fee for full replacement support (25% for supplemental), implying roughly $540K a year of vendor maintenance per client. This covers the whole Oracle/SAP estate, not just finance. (2) BlackLine: $702M ARR, 4,394 customers (10-K), so about $160K average. 600 customers pay over $250K ARR and 85 pay over $1M (Q4 2025 slides). (3) Oracle support runs about 22% of net licence (vendorbenchmark, a third-party estimate), so a $3-15M financials licence carries $0.66-3.3M a year. HOW THE RANGE IS BUILT: GL share of ERP maintenance ($150K-$1.5M) + close tool ($100K-$1M) + consolidation such as HFM or OneStream ($100K-$1M) + hosting and partner support. Low end: one-ERP Fortune 2000 firm, about $0.3M. High end: Fortune 100 firm with several ERPs, $5M+. Tier 1 banks can exceed this (Finantrix: $5-20M+). Excludes one-off S/4 or Fusion migrations.

mid_market.evidence: VERDICT: Range $25K to $250K a year kept. Build = rare, kept. One count corrected. BUILD: Mid-market firms buy packaged GLs (NetSuite, Sage Intacct, Dynamics GP/Business Central, JD Edwards, SunSystems, Acumatica) and fill gaps in Excel. No source suggests they write their own. SPEND, checked: (1) NetSuite on Vendr: median $74,816 a year, range $7,160 to $299,115, based on 1,512 purchases. (2) BlackLine on Vendr: median $40,125, range $13,154 to $101,000. FIX: Vendr shows 59 deals, not 74. (3) Sage Intacct at $25-35K average, $25-75K for most mid-market and $100K+ multi-entity (Cargas). NOT RE-CHECKED: the Cargas page blocked access (403), but these figures sit inside the Vendr-backed range. HOW THE RANGE IS BUILT: Low end is a single-entity Intacct or GP customer, about $25K. High end is a multi-entity NetSuite or JDE customer with a close tool and partner support, about $250K, which matches Vendr's NetSuite top deal of $299K. TIMING: Microsoft ends Dynamics GP product support on 31 Dec 2029 (extended from 2028) and security patches on 30 Apr 2031. Every GP customer has to move within about 3 years.

smb.evidence: VERDICT: Range $300 to $5,000 a year kept. Build = rare, kept. Two unsupported details removed. BUILD: SMBs use off-the-shelf bookkeeping software. When they do not, the fallback is spreadsheets, not custom code. SPEND, checked: QuickBooks Online lists $38 (Simple Start), $85 (Essentials), $140 (Plus) and $340 (Advanced) a month, which is $456, $1,020, $1,680 and $4,080 a year (FitSmallBusiness, Sept 2026). Xero US lists $25, $55 and $90 a month, which is $300 to $1,080 a year. Costbench's median Xero contract is $564 a year across 147 purchases. TallyPrime in India: ₹22,500 Silver or ₹67,500 Gold one-time plus 18% GST (about $270 or $810), or rental at ₹750-₹2,250 a month. FIXES: the original said the QBO prices followed an 'Aug 2026 increase' and that Xero rises to $27-$97 on 1 Oct 2026. Neither cited source supports this, and costbench still shows $25-$90 in October 2026. The '2.5M+ Tally businesses' figure is not on the cited page. HOW THE RANGE IS BUILT: about $300 a year (Xero entry plan or Tally rental) up to about $5K (QBO Advanced plus apps). Most SMB close work is done by an outside bookkeeper or accountant, which this study counts as services or staff and excludes.

government.evidence: VERDICT: Low end CORRECTED from $100K to $20K. High end $10M kept. Build = some, kept. WHY THE LOW END CHANGED: small-city council reports show financial systems costing $20-55K a year, so $100K overstated the floor by more than 2x. Brainerd, MN chose BS&A at $20,415 a year (Tyler Incode bid $35,204). Corte Madera, CA pays $40,896 a year for hosted Tyler Incode 10. These are whole municipal suites, so the GL alone costs less. BUILD: Governments build more often than companies. Hawaii's FAMIS has run as a custom COBOL system since 1970, with 242 satellite systems (53 to be kept). India's central PFMS was built by the Controller General of Accounts with NIC. New projects mostly buy: Hawaii picked Workday with Guidehouse as integrator in April 2026, and USDA runs SAP (FMMI). SPEND, checked: (1) Menifee, CA (about 110K residents), Tyler Munis, 2023: $657,843 one-time plus $290,024 first-year subscription, capped at $408,093 by year 10. This is a full ERP; financials are the core. (2) Cook County, IL: Oracle E-Business Suite and Hyperion, not to exceed $12.15M for 2015-2020, about $2.4M a year including licences. FIX: Amendment 3 raised the total to $13.81M, not $18.4M. (3) Hawaii: $63.7M Guidehouse contract, core in 2-3 years and the rest in 5-6 years, roughly $9-10M a year before Workday fees. FIX: the source does not give the Oct 2026 to Sep 2033 dates. (4) Coast Guard: part of a $510M modernization program (GAO-23-105194). FIX: GAO does not name the software, so 'chose Oracle Federal Financials' is unsupported here. HOW THE RANGE IS BUILT: small cities and towns $20-60K a year; mid-size cities $100-400K; large counties and states $2-10M, plus one-off integration contracts of $50-500M. Sales cycles run 1-3 years through RFPs.

best_icp: Sell first to mid-market multi-entity firms (roughly $20M to $1B revenue) on Dynamics GP, Sage, older NetSuite or JD Edwards plus Excel: they buy rather than build, spend $25K to $250K a year, decide in months, and GP's end of support on 31 Dec 2029 forces every GP customer to re-platform within about 3 years; approach enterprises later with a close and consolidation layer on their existing ERP rather than a ledger swap (the original claim that Rillet and Campfire are already proving the GP-migration route was unsourced and has been removed).

criticality_why:
VERDICT: critical. The original call holds after review.

WHY, IN THREE STEPS
1. The system is the agency. A benefits agency exists to decide who is entitled under statute and to pay them. This system does both. The rules from decades of legislation exist as code only here. If it fails, payments stop or go out wrong, and the agency breaks its legal duty. That meets the first test (the business stops).
2. It is the mission, not back office. Governments do not compete for customers, so 'where the firm differentiates' has no exact public-sector match. The closest match is the agency's core mission, and this system delivers that mission. That meets the second test. Payroll or HR at the same agency would only be 'important'.
3. Failures become political events. NAO (2021): DWP underpaid State Pension to about 134,000 pensioners, about GBP 1.05bn in arrears. Part of the cause was manual prompts on PSCS, a system launched in 1988 that still runs the live caseload. KFF Health News: Deloitte-run Medicaid eligibility systems in 25 states produced errors that cost millions and took years to fix.

SCALE (checked against sources)
- DWP: about 70% of its benefit and pension caseload, about GBP 200bn paid each year, still runs on legacy systems (Capgemini legacy-discovery deal, Oct 2025, GBP 24m plus a GBP 6m option). Correction: the earlier draft said 70% 'of GBP 200bn'. The source says the 70% legacy share IS the GBP 200bn.
- Services Australia: a March 2026 procurement analysis says Model 204 and related systems 'remain central to payment processing'.
- SSA: over 60 million lines of COBOL run core retirement and disability processing (SSA OIG, as of June 2010).

enterprise.evidence:
NOT A BUYER SEGMENT. Spend is null on purpose.

Only public bodies run social security, unemployment insurance (UI), Medicaid/SNAP eligibility and pension-entitlement cores. The earlier buyer-universe research found no private enterprise that buys or builds one.

Nearest private buyers: Medicaid managed-care plans and health systems. They buy add-on tools that sit next to the state core, such as member engagement and verification (for example the Unite Us and Fortuna Health partnership). They do not buy the core. Those tools belong in a different category.

How to read 'rare': the schema needs a value. Here 'rare' means 'not applicable'. It does not mean these firms buy instead of build.

mid_market.evidence:
NOT A BUYER SEGMENT. Spend is null on purpose.

No mid-market company runs or buys a government benefits core. Private firms touch only the edge. Example: employers file social-insurance contributions through tools such as VNPT-BHXH in Vietnam. That is payroll and compliance software, not this category.

'rare' means 'not applicable' here, as in the enterprise row.

smb.evidence:
NOT A BUYER SEGMENT. Spend is null on purpose.

Small businesses meet this system only as employers filing contributions or as claimants. They never buy or run it.

'rare' means 'not applicable' here, as in the enterprise row.

government.evidence:
BOTTOM LINE
Government is the entire market. A small US state pays about $2M a year to run a benefits core. California pays about $422M. National agencies spend more, but their IT budgets also cover systems outside benefits. Most cores are built and owned by the government, or built by an integrator and then owned by the state.

1. WHO OWNS THE SYSTEM (build vs buy = common)
- National agencies built their cores and still own them. SSA: 60M+ lines of in-house COBOL (SSA OIG). DWP: PSCS, launched 1988, still runs the State Pension caseload (NAO 2021). Services Australia: ISIS was built in-house on licensed Model 204 database software.
- US states mostly hire an integrator (Deloitte, Accenture, Optum, FAST) to build or configure a system, then run it under long contracts. Federal funding rules push states to own or hold rights to what they pay for, so these count as 'owned'.
- Packaged products exist (FAST UI, Merative Curam) but are the minority. They are more common in UI than in Medicaid eligibility.
- Result: building or owning in-house is common.

2. ANNUAL SPEND PER BUYER, SMALLEST TO LARGEST
(Vendor and licence costs only. Agency staff excluded.)

a) Small state UI, the LOW END (about $2M a year at steady state)
Vermont is replacing a 1970 mainframe with FAST Enterprises. Go-live is planned for spring or summer 2026.
- Winning bid: $28.1M for implementation, hosting, licences and 5 years of support. Total life-cycle cost: $46.2M (VDOL memo to the legislature, Sept 2025).
- Build years: about $30M of technical spend over a 25-month build, about $14-15M a year. Correction: the earlier draft said $6-9M a year. That is about half the sourced figure.
- Run years: software maintenance is $1.0M to $1.17M a year. Add vendor hosting (about $0.43M) and application support ($0.3M to $1.0M). Vendor-side running cost is about $1.9M to $2.6M a year (Vermont Joint Fiscal Office independent review, Jan 2024).
- Correction: the earlier low end of $1M counted the maintenance fee alone. The low end is now $2M, the full vendor-side running cost.

b) Mid-size state Medicaid eligibility (about $10-35M a year)
- Kentucky / Deloitte: over $157M for 5 years, about $31M a year.
- Iowa / Accenture: over $60M (term not given).
- Vermont / Optum: $125.6M (term not given).
- Tennessee / Deloitte: $823M in total. The cap on out-of-scope change orders rose from $103.6M to $417M in a 2023 amendment (KFF Health News).
- Texas / Deloitte: $295M. Across 25 states, Deloitte eligibility contracts total at least $6B.

c) Largest state, the HIGH END (about $422M a year)
CalSAWS, the shared eligibility system for all 58 California counties. SFY 2025/26 budget: $422.5M. Of that, $371.3M is maintenance and operations and $45.8M is on-premise changes (CalSAWS quarterly financial report, Feb 2026). The high end is set to $425M. The earlier $450M was within 2x but rounded up more than the source supports.

d) National agencies, ABOVE THE RANGE (their budgets cover more than benefits)
- SSA: FY2025 IT request of nearly $2.5B. About $1.6B is operations and maintenance. Over $850M is new development.
- DWP: GBP 1.9bn through its Digital and Transformation Group in FY26, up from GBP 1bn the year before.
- Services Australia: A$98.5M on Model 204 licences from 2003 to 2014, then A$35.1M for 2014-2017 (about A$11.7M, or about US$8M, a year). A later Rocket Software licence and support contract is A$118.6M (published May 2025). It is part of A$178M in Rocket contracts that expire in June 2026.

e) Counties, BELOW THE RANGE (they buy add-ons, not the core)
Aitkin County, Minnesota bought CaseWorks, a case and document layer on top of the state systems. One-time cost is about $378k in two phases ($201.7k + $176.6k). Correction: the earlier draft said about $200k, which is phase 1 only. Annual support is $71k to $82k. That is below the core range and is excluded.

3. WHO PAYS
For Medicaid eligibility systems, the federal government pays 90% of development and 75% of ongoing maintenance and operations (KFF). A state's own cost is therefore a fraction of the contract value. For UI, federal grants such as ARPA modernisation funds and state appropriations do the same job. Vermont used a $30M state IT modernisation appropriation.

best_icp: Start with small and mid-size US state agencies, and sell them a bounded module or a new program, not a full national core: for example paid family leave builds (Nava's Maryland FAMLI prime contract is $15.6M over two years), Medicaid and SNAP work-requirement and income verification before the 1 January 2027 deadline (CMS vendor pledges cluster near $2M per state one-time, Missouri has already signed SteadyIQ, and Gainwell adds $50 per member per year to run it), or a small state's UI replacement (Vermont: about $28M build, about $2M a year to run); federal 90/10 and 75/25 Medicaid matching cuts the state's own share, and national agencies (SSA, DWP, Services Australia) and large-state systems such as CalSAWS sit inside long, politically exposed integrator relationships, so leave them for later.

criticality_why:
VERDICT: important. Changed from "critical".

WHY THE CHANGE
The rubric needs two things for "critical": (a) the business stops or loses its licence if the system fails, and (b) the system is where the buyer competes. For the buyer that actually signs the contract, the city or county, neither holds.
- Who the buyer is: the city, not one department. Berkeley's Accela contract was submitted by the IT Director, approved by council, and paid from the General Fund, Sewer Fund and Permit Service Fund. One system serves Planning, Public Works and Finance (business licences).
- Test (a), the business stops: only partly. If the system fails, permit issuance, inspection scheduling and permit fee collection stop. That is serious, and the department may depend on those fees. But the city keeps running: police, utilities, payroll and tax all continue. Nothing is revoked, and staff can fall back to paper or counter processing for a time.
- Test (b), where it competes: weak. Permit speed does matter. San Francisco's Executive Directive 25-01 (Feb 13, 2025) made permit technology one of three reform priorities, with a one-year deadline. But a city does not win or lose customers on this system the way a bank does on its core ledger.

WHAT STAYS TRUE
- It is the system of record for a statutory function, and the buyer itself calls it critical (Berkeley's staff report calls Accela "a critical enterprise software platform").
- It runs at large scale. LADBS issued 167,000+ permits and ran 1M+ inspections in 2023. The Clariti contract consolidates all LADBS development services onto one platform.
- For a single-purpose licensing body, such as a state professional board, the system is the whole operation. In that narrow case it comes close to "critical".

BOTTOM LINE: the city depends on it, but it is not where the city competes. That is "important".

criticality_why:
VERDICT: critical. The call is kept, with one caveat stated openly.

TEST 1. Does the organisation stop if the system fails? Yes. This test is met cleanly.
- The core tax system registers taxpayers, processes returns, posts payments, issues refunds and runs collections. When it fails, revenue stops.
- Virginia Tax's legacy IRMS handles 36 tax types and about 12 million returns a year. It brings in close to $30bn, which is 95% of the state's General Fund revenue. [verified, Virginia RD719, Nov 2025]
- HMRC's SAP ETMP platform handles over GBP 800bn of tax and payments a year. [verified, The Register, Jan 2026]
- Local example: Cook County's Tyler upgrade left about 83,000 owners waiting on $186m of property tax refunds from May 2025. It also held up revenue owed to municipalities. [verified, ABC7 Chicago]

TEST 2. Is it where the organisation differentiates? Yes, but only by analogy. This is the caveat.
- Governments do not compete for customers, so the literal test does not apply. The closest equivalent is the organisation's core mission and how its performance is judged.
- On that reading the test is met. For a revenue agency the tax system is the core product. It sets processing time, refund speed, compliance and the cost of each policy change.
- India's CPC 2.0 was justified by a target of cutting return processing from 63 days to 1. That is a target, not a measured result. [verified, Millennium Post]
- Finland's COTS replacement reports EUR 15-20m a year in IT savings and faster, cheaper tax policy changes. [verified, OECD FTA 2019]
- Failures are public and political. Examples: IRS CADE 1 was abandoned, Indonesia's Coretax launch drew complaints in 2025, and the Cook County refunds above.

WHY NOT 'IMPORTANT': 'Important' fits systems a business relies on but that are not its purpose, like payroll at a retailer. For a tax agency, and for a county treasurer's tax office, collecting tax is the purpose itself. So 'critical' is the better fit.

What enterprises do buy is tax compliance software for their own filings, such as Vertex, Avalara, ONESOURCE or SAP tax engines. That is a different category and is left out here.

'Rare' only fills the required field. Build-versus-buy does not apply.

government.evidence:
SUMMARY
- Government is the only segment that buys this system.
- Typical annual spend runs from about $5k for a small town to about $150m for a large national agency. The IRS is left out as an outlier.
- Spend depends mostly on the level of government, so the range is built up from four tiers below.

HOW TO READ THIS
- Annual figure = contract value divided by its term. Where a figure includes implementation, that is stated.
- Staff costs are excluded where the source separates them.
- Tags: [verified] means the source was opened and the figure matched. [search only] means the figure came from a search summary because the page returned 403. [corrected] means this review changed the number.
- FX assumptions: GBP 1 = about $1.30, EUR 1 = about $1.10, INR 70 = $1 (2019 rate), IDR 14,500 = $1 (2020 rate).

CHANGES MADE IN THIS REVIEW
1. Low end of the range cut from $10k to $5k. The original tier 1 cited $1k-10k figures but set the floor at $10k, which did not match. The new floor is still within 2x of the old one.
2. Newcastle-under-Lyme raised from GBP 71k to GBP 235k a year. The current NEC contract (from May 2023, hosted) is GBP 235k a year, GBP 2.27m over up to 7 years. The old GBP 71k could not be traced and is more than 3x too low for today's spend.
3. Tandridge raised from GBP 70k to about GBP 95k a year: GBP 70k licence plus GBP 25k support.
4. India's 8.5-year term is now confirmed (Cabinet approval, Jan 2019). The outlay includes GST, rent, postage and project management, so it overstates spend on software alone.
5. Indiana's '$17.5m for 10 years of maintenance' was removed. The source gives only the $77.7m total.
6. Durham's GBP 8m over 10 years was dropped from the evidence. No source could confirm it.
7. Cook County's 10+ year spread is now sourced: ABC7 reports that the county has paid Tyler more than $30m since the contract began over 10 years ago.

TIER 1. SMALL LOCAL GOVERNMENTS (US towns, townships, small districts): about $3k-50k a year
- Edmunds GovTech perpetual licences start at $5k. [verified, SoftwareConnect]
- SoftwareConnect puts entry-level municipal software at $3k-10k a year and mid-tier at $10k-50k. [verified]
- Caveat: those bands cover municipal suites in general (finance, ERP), not tax collection alone. Tax collection is usually one module within them, so these are upper bounds for the tax piece.

TIER 2. COUNTIES AND UK COUNCILS: about $50k-3m a year
UK councils buy revenues and benefits systems from Civica, NEC (formerly Northgate) or Capita. These systems cover council tax and business rates, and also housing benefit.
- North Norfolk (Civica): GBP 40k a year. [search only]
- Rutland (Civica): GBP 45k maintenance, 2017-2022. [search only] It is unclear whether this is per year or the total for the period.
- Tandridge (Capita): about GBP 95k a year. [search only, corrected]
- Westmorland and Furness (Civica, 2025-2032): 1.92m over 7 years, about GBP 275k or $360k a year. [verified] Govmarket labels the currency AUD, which is almost certainly a listing error for a UK council.
- Newcastle-under-Lyme (NEC, hosted, from 2023): GBP 235k a year, about $305k. [search only, corrected]
- Taken together, UK councils spend about $50k-420k a year.

US counties buy integrated assessment and tax systems.
- Bucks County, PA (Tyler iasWorld, 2008): over $2.4m including licences, services and maintenance. [verified] The term is not stated.
- Dakota County, MN (Tyler iasWorld, 2009): $3.5m. [search only, Tyler press release]
- Cook County, IL (Tyler, 2015): $30m for an integrated property tax system. It covers 5 offices and 1.8m parcels and replaced 1970s mainframe applications. [verified] More than $30m has been paid over 10+ years [verified, ABC7], so about $3m a year. This is the top of the tier.

TIER 3. US STATE REVENUE DEPARTMENTS: about $3m-30m a year
- Oregon (FAST GenTax), steady state: $6.5m General Fund plus $0.56m Other Funds per two-year budget, for maintenance, support and vendor staff. That is about $3.5m a year. [verified, Oregon Legislative Fiscal Office] Implementation cost $69.7m, of which $27.5m went to FAST. [verified]
- Indiana (FAST): $77.7m paid over 10 years, including a 4-year implementation. About $7.8m a year. [verified, StateScoop]
- Tennessee (FAST, sole source, to provide and maintain GenTax): $30.6m over 3 years, about $10m a year. About 40% higher than the previous contract. [verified]
- Virginia (FAST GenTax, replacing IRMS from 1999-2005): $131m appropriated for the full build, with $30.5m budgeted for year one. About $30m a year during the 4-rollout build. [verified, RD719] This is build-phase spend. Run costs will be lower.

TIER 4. NATIONAL TAX ADMINISTRATIONS: about $15m-150m+ a year
- Finland (FAST GenTax): EUR 226m over 15 years, covering implementation, licences, application management and development. About EUR 15m or $16-17m a year. [verified, OECD FTA 2019]
- Indonesia (Coretax): Rp1.2tn to the LG CNS-Qualysoft consortium plus Rp110bn to Deloitte, about $90m in total. [verified, Liputan6] Spread over 2020-2025, that is about $15-18m a year.
- India (CPC 2.0, Infosys): Rs4,242 crore, about $600m, over 8.5 years. About $70m a year. [contract value verified, Millennium Post; term search only]
- UK (HMRC): SAP S/4HANA ETMP at GBP 275m to 2035, about $37-40m a year. Plus Capgemini at up to GBP 574m to run legacy tax systems from July 2024 to 2029, about $150m a year. [both verified, The Register]
- US (IRS), outlier: $5.7bn of IRA funding spent on technology from Aug 2022 to Mar 2025, about $2.2bn a year, on top of base operations and maintenance. [verified, TIGTA 2025] Left out of the headline range.

BUILD VS BUY: 'some'. The answer differs by tier.
- National: building or owning is common. The IRS still runs its 1960s IBM-built Individual Master File. India and Indonesia commission custom builds from integrators. HMRC runs a heavily customised SAP platform. Finland is the counter-example: a COTS buyer.
- State: buying is the norm. FAST GenTax is in use at 34 state revenue agencies besides Virginia. [verified, RD719] Oregon chose a 'no customisation' approach. [verified]
- Local: buying is the norm. Counties and councils buy COTS from Tyler, Civica, NEC or Capita.

GAPS
- No source gives the share of tax administrations running COTS versus in-house systems. The OECD COTS report describes Finland's case only.
- Four UK council figures rely on search summaries because the council PDFs returned 403.

Why: there are about 3,100 US counties plus thousands of townships, they buy rather than build, and deals run about $50k-3m a year. The alternatives are harder: FAST GenTax holds 35 state agencies, often on sole-source renewals, and national systems are $15m-150m+ a year programmes that take years to procure. Watch-outs: Tyler dominates US county property tax, and the 296 English billing authorities buy from Civica, NEC and Capita through CCS framework RM6259.

criticality_why:
Verdict: critical for insurers. Important (not critical) for self-insured buyers. The original call holds.

What the system does. A claims system takes the first notice of loss, sets reserves, manages the adjuster's work and issues payments. For an insurer, paying claims is the product.

Test 1. Does the business stop if it fails? Yes. Without the claims system a carrier cannot log new claims, reserve for them or pay them. Ohio BWC's Sapiens claims system supports 2,500 daily users, and the vendor stressed that the upgrade went live with no interruption to them. That emphasis shows how little downtime the buyer can tolerate.

Test 2. Is the licence at risk? Yes. US states adopt versions of the NAIC Unfair Claims Settlement Practices model law. These rules require prompt, documented claim handling, and regulators audit claim files in market-conduct exams. A carrier that cannot show this record faces fines and action against its licence.

Test 3. Is it where firms compete? Yes. Claims and loss-adjustment cost are most of what an insurer spends, and claims service is the moment customers judge the product. ClaimCenter is one of the three core applications in Guidewire's InsuranceSuite, alongside policy and billing.

One exception. Self-insured counties, risk pools and corporates run claims systems, usually called an RMIS (risk management information system), to administer their own losses. They do not sell insurance and do not compete on claims. For them the system is important, not critical.

Corrections made in this review:
- Removed the Five Sigma figures of about 30% shorter handle time and $3.6M savings per customer. They do not appear on the cited Five Sigma page, and a search found no source for them. That page claims only "up to" gains for single tasks, for example a 50% cut in document handling time. These are the vendor's own figures.
- Reworded the Guidewire point. The 10-K supports that claims is one of three core applications. It does not use the wording "modernise to compete".

enterprise.evidence:
WHO: large carriers with about $1B or more in direct written premium (DWP).

BUILD VS BUY: common.
- McKinsey: roughly half of the leading US P&C carriers build their own core systems and half buy and configure. The share that build is shrinking. (Search snippet. The page timed out twice when opened.)
- Guidewire FY2025 10-K (verified): the first competitor it names is 'customers' internally developed proprietary solutions'. It also says large customers can 'develop such systems internally'.
- Insurance Journal, Sept 2026 (verified): carriers describe feeling 'held hostage' by SaaS fees. Some, such as Universal Shield, are building on open-source cores with AI tools. This supports the view that building is getting easier.

SPEND: about $1M to $10M a year on claims. Steps:
(1) Guidewire average (verified): $1,041M ARR across about 500 customers, so about $2.1M per customer per year. This covers policy, billing and claims together. The ten largest customers hold 20% of ARR, about $21M each. Pricing is set by the DWP managed on the platform.
(2) Benchmark for a $5B-premium carrier (vendorbenchmark.com, secondary source, verified on page): full Guidewire Cloud suite $3.2M to $8.4M a year. Duck Creek $2.4M to $6.4M. Implementation services for the suite run $14M to $42M over 24 to 36 months, so about $5M to $14M a year during the rollout.
(3) Claims share: claims is one of three core apps, so it gets about one third of the cost. Subscription is about $1M to $3M a year. During a rollout, claims' share of services adds about $1.5M to $5M a year.
(4) Guidewire's own services revenue was $219.2M in FY2025, 18% of revenue (verified). Outside integrators bill more on top.

RESULT: steady state is about $1M to $3M a year. During a multi-year rollout, or at a top-10 carrier, it reaches $5M to $10M.

CORRECTION: the low end moved from $2M to $1M. Pricing scales with DWP. A carrier near $1B DWP pays well under the $5B-carrier benchmark, so claims alone at steady state is closer to $0.5M to $1.5M. The $2M floor was more than 2x too high for the bottom of this tier.

(3) Five Sigma (verified): it prices with a scoped launch package, an annual platform fee and usage fees. Its Starter tier is aimed at teams modernizing for the first time. No dollar amounts are published.
(4) Small regulated carriers sit at the top of the range. They need full reserving, payments and regulatory reporting, not just claim tracking.

RESULT: about $25K to $250K a year. No change from the original.

government.evidence:
Government buyers fall into two very different groups. That is why the range is wide.

GROUP 1: counties, cities and risk pools that insure themselves. They buy SaaS RMIS or claims systems. Typical spend is $40K to $250K a year.
- Charlotte County, FL (verified): Origami Risk, $43,000 a year, $129,000 over 3 years.
- Marion County, OR (verified): Origami Risk, $695,625 over 5 years. $221,025 in year one, then $118,650 a year.
- Search snippets also show Placer County at $248,230 over 3 years and San Mateo County at up to $923,863. These were not opened and are not used for the range.

GROUP 2: state workers' comp funds and public monopoly insurers. They either buy enterprise suites or run decades-old systems built in-house. Typical spend is about $1M to $6M a year on claims.
- icare NSW (verified): its Guidewire subscription contract rose from A$37.6M to A$87.2M through 2024. It covers policy, billing and claims for the Nominal Insurer, and more than A$83M of it is subscription through Aug 2023. A separate consultancy contract is worth A$36.96M, and on-premise licences cost A$23.5M from 2016 to 2020. icare puts the total at more than A$140M over eight years. That is about A$17.5M (about US$11M) a year for the whole suite plus consultants. Claims at one third to one half of that is about US$4M to $6M a year.
- Washington L&I (verified): runs about 100 legacy systems, some over 40 years old, handling 100,000 new claims and $2.6B in payments a year. Its replacement program is estimated at $292M and had spent $31M in 10 years. The state suspended it on 22 Aug 2025 and lifted the suspension on 12 Jan 2026. It is being reset as phased waves, with claims modernization as wave 2.
- FEMA (verified): awarded an $18M contract to an ERP International joint venture for DevSecOps development of NFIP PIVOT. PIVOT replaces more than 40 legacy applications, including claims administration. This is a custom build by an integrator, not a software licence, so it supports the build-in-house rating rather than the spend range.
- NYSIF (verified): open RFP 2026-36-INS for a Claims Management System. Proposals are due 8 Dec 2026. No value is published.

BUILD VS BUY: some. Large state funds often run systems built in-house or built by integrators (Washington L&I's legacy estate, FEMA PIVOT). Counties buy.

CORRECTIONS:
- The high end moved from $10M to $6M. The only hard data point, icare, is about US$11M a year for policy, billing, claims and consultancy together. No source supports $10M a year for claims alone.
- Reframed FEMA as a build contract, not a purchase.
- Added the source for the Washington L&I suspension dates. The Governing article cited originally predates them.
- Dropped 'with Deloitte' as the builder of L&I's system. Deloitte is a consultant on the program (about $15.8M from 2020 to 2030), and no build vendor has been chosen.

best_icp: Start with lower mid-market carriers, MGAs and TPAs, roughly $50M to $1B in premium: they rarely build in-house, many still run 20-year-old cores that their retiring staff can no longer maintain, they decide faster than enterprise carriers locked into five-year Guidewire terms, and they spend about $250K to $1.5M a year on claims, which is enough to fund an AI-native claims core; once there are references, add self-insured counties and risk pools ($40K to $250K a year, fast SaaS buys), then bid on state-fund replacements such as NYSIF's open claims RFP.

criticality_why:
VERDICT: critical. Confirmed on review, with one weak argument replaced.

TEST 1. Does the business stop without it? Yes.
The policy admin system (PAS) is the system of record for every policy. It holds product rules, rating, quote and bind, endorsements, renewals, premium billing and the policy data that regulators and reinsurers require. If it is down, the carrier cannot write new business, change or renew existing policies, or bill premium.

TEST 2. Is it where carriers compete? Yes, for product and pricing.
Carriers compete on which products they offer, how fast they launch them and how finely they price them. Those products and rating rules are configured in the PAS. Novarica's 2021 P&C policy admin report lists the top buying reasons as faster product development, entering new niches (for example excess and surplus lines, workers' comp) and new pricing methods such as micro-rating. It also reports that legacy cores eat about 60% of IT budgets on average, and over 75% at many carriers, just to keep running, which leaves little room for new products.
(Review note: the earlier draft used Guidewire pricing by direct written premium as proof of differentiation. That shows how the vendor charges, not where carriers compete, so it was removed.)

TEST 3. Do buyers behave as if it is critical? Yes.
- Long commitments. Guidewire's FY2025 10-K says initial subscriptions are generally 5 years, some 7 years or longer. Citizens Property Insurance of Florida signed a 10-year initial term with ten optional 1-year renewals, up to 20 years in total (Citizens board action item, July 2023).
- Long sales cycles. Sapiens' 2024 20-F says its sales cycle for new customers is typically 1-2 years.
- Rigorous selection. Citizens ran a formal Invitation to Negotiate between Guidewire and Duck Creek and took the award to its board.

enterprise.evidence:
WHO
Tier 1 and Tier 2 carriers, roughly $1B+ direct written premium (DWP). The common industry split is Tier 1 above $5B DWP and Tier 2 at $1B-5B. That definition comes from a search snippet and was not confirmed in a primary source.

BUILD VS BUY: some (confirmed)
- Some large carriers still run home-grown mainframe cores. Guidewire's FY2025 10-K lists 'customers' internally developed proprietary solutions' first among its competitors. Duck Creek's FY2022 10-K says a large part of the P&C market still relies on home-grown legacy systems that are costly to maintain and hard to upgrade.
- New in-house builds are now unusual. The current pattern is to buy Guidewire, Duck Creek, Sapiens or similar and keep the old core running only for closed books. Duck Creek's 10-K says 4 of the top 5 North American carriers use its products (Progressive, Liberty Mutual, AIG, The Hartford and GEICO are named customers).

SPEND: $3M-25M a year (confirmed, no change)
This is the vendor bill only: software subscription or licence, support, hosting and vendor services. It excludes internal staff and third-party integrators.

Step 1. The floor. Guidewire ended FY2026 with ARR of $1.242B and 105 customers whose fully ramped ARR exceeds $5M, up from 86 a year earlier (Q4 FY2026 earnings call). These are almost all Tier 1 and Tier 2 carriers, so $5M a year is a normal figure for a large carrier on a full suite. Tier 2 carriers on one line of business or a cheaper vendor sit lower, which sets the $3M floor. For scale, Guidewire's average across its 570+ customers is about $1.8M ($1.041B ARR / 570).

Step 2. The ceiling. Guidewire's 10 largest customers held 20% of its $1.041B ARR at July 31, 2025 (10-K and Q4 FY2025 release). That is about $21M each. Adding vendor services (Step 4) gives about $25M.

Step 3. A real contract. Citizens Property Insurance of Florida, one of the largest US property insurers, approved a 10-year Guidewire contract with a not-to-exceed value of $66,283,867: $58.2M subscription, $4.3M implementation, $2.4M post-go-live services and $1.3M contingency. That is about $6.6M a year, and it assumes Citizens' premium shrinks as it moves policies to private carriers. Its earlier Guidewire setup cost $115M from July 2011 to June 2023 (about $9.6M a year), including Guidewire and third-party services to maintain and expand it. Both fall inside the range.

Step 4. Services uplift. Guidewire's FY2025 revenue was $1,202.5M: subscription and support $731.3M (61%), licence $251.9M (21%), services $219.2M (18%). Vendor services therefore add roughly 20-30% to the software fee.

WHAT IS EXCLUDED
Third-party integrator fees (Accenture, Deloitte and others) during a replacement can add tens of millions of dollars. Vendorbenchmark.com puts full replacement programmes at $35M-68M a year for $2B-10B carriers and $72M-145M a year above $10B. Those figures cover the whole programme (licences, consulting, data migration, training, and running old and new systems in parallel) and cite no underlying data. They are used only as an outer bound. (Review note: the earlier draft said this benchmark counts internal staff. It counts programme costs, not staff, so the wording was corrected.)

CONFIDENCE: high. Based on two audited filings and one public contract.

smb.evidence:

Small carriers, county and farm mutuals, startup and small MGAs, and insurtechs, mostly under about $100M DWP. Ordinary small businesses outside insurance do not buy this system.

BUY VS BUILD: rare (confirmed)

Government-owned or statutory insurers only. Ordinary government agencies do not buy policy admin. Examples:

The largest state-owned insurers, such as LIC and ICBC, may spend more than $10M a year, but no opened source gave their annual figure.

best_icp: Sell first to mid-market carriers and large MGAs with about $100M-1B DWP. Why this tier: (1) Each spends $0.5M-3M a year on the system, enough to support a real contract. (2) Many still run ageing AS/400 or COBOL cores, and the staff who know them are retiring. (3) They almost never build in-house, so they will buy. (4) Each deal is far smaller than a Tier 1 programme, which lowers the buyer's risk. The 1-2 year sales cycle Sapiens reports is an all-tier figure, so do not assume mid-market deals close much faster. Two ways in avoid a risky full core replacement on day one: an AI layer over the legacy core, or one new product line or closed block on a new system. Small mutuals and new MGAs are a faster but smaller second target: published SaaS prices start at about $12K a year, and Novarica reports more small insurers now looking to replace.

criticality_why:
VERDICT: critical. That holds for independent and reference labs, the buyers this study targets. For hospitals it is closer to important. The check found the call justified, with the caveat in point 3.

1) The lab stops without it. The LIS takes each order, tracks the specimen, takes results from the analyzers, runs the QC and validation rules, and releases the signed report to the EHR or client portal. If it is down, a lab cannot release results at scale. CLIA, CAP and ISO 15189 require changes to it to be validated. The FDA regulates blood bank software as a medical device. So a failure stops the business and puts accreditation at risk.

2) Independent and reference labs compete through it. Turnaround time, client connectivity, test menu setup and billing capture all run through the LIS. The two largest US labs treat it as their own infrastructure. Labcorp's FY2015 10-K (checked) says it runs "standard platforms for its core business services including laboratory diagnostics". The same filing says its primary lab systems process tests that make up about 93.6% of domestic diagnostics revenue. Quest's FY2005 10-K (checked) says it began rolling out a standard LIS across all operations in 2002. Neither filing names an outside vendor.

3) Caveat: hospitals do not compete on their LIS. The hospital needs its lab, but the LIS is not where it competes. That is why hospitals increasingly take the lab module that comes with their EHR. KLAS's 2026 acute-care EHR market-share report (2025 data, via HealthSystemCIO, checked) puts Epic at 43.7% of US acute-care hospitals and 56.9% of beds. Beaker is sold only inside the Epic contract. For a hospital buyer, rate the LIS important, not critical. (The draft called this "KLAS 2025". Corrected to the 2026 report.)

4) Buyers rarely switch, and switching is risky. Roper's CEO cited Sunquest retention of over 98% a year (Dark Daily, 2012, checked). Queensland Health signed a 10-year AUD 68.5m Sunquest contract (later restated as AUD 64m). It spent about AUD 37.5m, cancelled, and extended its legacy Auslab system to 2029 (iTnews and Pulse+IT, checked).

WHO: national reference labs (Quest, Labcorp) plus large health systems and academic medical centres (10 or more hospitals, or 500 or more beds).

BUILD OR BUY: 'some', because the segment splits in two.
(a) National reference labs own and run one standard LIS across the company. Quest FY2005 10-K: began a standard LIS 'across all of our operations' in 2002. Both checked. Neither names an outside vendor.
(b) Large health systems buy, mostly the lab module that comes with their EHR: Epic Beaker or Oracle Health PathNet. Some run best-of-breed SCC or Sunquest. Epic holds 43.7% of US acute-care hospitals and 56.9% of beds (KLAS 2026 report, checked), and Beaker cannot be bought outside the Epic contract.

(1) Per-hospital cost from vendor revenue. Roper's 8-K (checked) says Sunquest software ran in more than 1,700 hospitals. Two cross-checks: analysts estimated about $225M (Seeking Alpha), and Roper paid $1.416B at about 6x revenue, which implies about $236M. Roper expected $140M or more of EBITDA in 2013. So Sunquest earned about $120k to $140k per hospital per year in 2012 dollars, or about $170k to $200k today. That covers licence, maintenance and services.
(2) Scale it up. A system with 10 to 30 hospital labs at $50k to $200k each comes to about $0.5M to $5M a year.
(3) Tender cross-check (weak). SUNY Downstate, one academic hospital, put out a tender of at least five years for Cerner lab maintenance, licences, hosting and services (PathNet, CoPath, Bridge). HigherGov puts it at $5M to $15M, about $1M to $3M a year. That figure is HigherGov's AI-generated estimate, not an award value. Even so, it suggests one large academic hospital can approach $1M a year.
