criticality_why:
Verdict: critical. The call holds. Two tests decide it.

Test 1. Does the business stop or lose its licence if the system fails? Yes. The register is the legal record of who owns land and what is charged against it. If it goes down, the office cannot record deeds, mortgages or liens, and sales and lending in that jurisdiction stop. Errors also cost money. HMLR's state-backed title guarantee paid out £1.6M on 948 claims in 2025-26 (HMLR Annual Report 2025-26). Data integrity sets the pace of change. HMLR moved the Local Land Charges register completion date to the end of the 2028-29 financial year so it could 'prioritise data quality and accuracy over speed' (same report).

Test 2. Is it where the firm differentiates? For a registry, the register is the product. No separate product sits on top of it. This is clearest for private operators, whose whole business is running the register: Teranet (Ontario, Manitoba), ISC (Saskatchewan) and the Australian concessionaires. Public registries are measured on the same system's turnaround times. Landgate's rebuilt register cut paper processing from 7-10 days to 1.5 days and e-lodgement to 23 seconds (Princeton ISS case study).

Corrections to the earlier draft: (a) Landgate and HMLR do not compete with each other. They are statutory monopolies, judged on service levels. (b) HMLR's £474.8M total operating cost is accurate, but it says nothing about criticality, so it has been dropped from this argument.

government.evidence:
Summary: government buys almost all of this category. Spend scales with the size of the jurisdiction, from about $15k a year for a small US county to about $90M a year for a national registry. US counties mostly buy from vendors. National and state registries mostly build or co-build. Four tiers follow, smallest first. Each figure was checked against its source unless marked otherwise.

TIER 1. Small US counties (under about 50k people): about $15k-$60k a year.
- Crow Wing County, MN: paid TriMin $16,490 in 2018 maintenance on its legacy system (Brainerd Dispatch, verified). This is old and was for a system being replaced, so treat $15k as the floor, not the norm.
- Fannin County, TX: pays Fidlar $54,156 a year gross. That is AVID at $51,456, which includes $900 a month for on-site servers, plus microfilm at $2,700 (2022 cost sheet, verified). The bundle also covers vital-records software and $9,816 a year of hardware maintenance, so it is not pure land records.
- Fannin offsets: the county receives about $24,300 a year in Fidlar remote-access credits (Monarch $14,700, AVA about $9,600). It also keeps $80 or $200 per Laredo subscriber per month. Net cost is about $30k a year.

TIER 2. Mid-sized and large US counties (about 60k to 1M people): about $70k-$260k a year.
- Crow Wing, MN: Tyler Eagle Recorder SaaS quoted at $69,775 a year, including auto-indexing, fraud guard and document management (verified).
- Fort Bend County, TX (about 900k people): pays Harris Recording Solutions $148,535.70 for FY2025 maintenance and support on Aumentum Recorder (verified). The land-records lines come to about $122k: recorder $47.4k, public access $25.4k, aiINDEX $24.9k, e-recording $24.3k. The rest is court-minutes software ($11.2k), marriage licences, vital records and service-level support. HRS supplies support and enhancements on a sole-source basis through a proprietary integration layer.
- Hillsborough County, NH: 5-year hosted Fidlar contract for $1.293M, about $259k a year (verified). Fidlar was the only respondent, and it serves 9 of New Hampshire's 10 counties.
- Utah, 2006: Tyler's seven-county deal was worth more than $3M (verified). It also covered assessor, treasurer and financial software, so it overstates spend on land records alone.
- One-off conversion and implementation fees come on top of all of these.

TIER 3. The very largest US counties: mixed. Some build, some buy.
- Cook County, IL: replaced a 20-year-old recording system with an employee-built system (EBESS) after years of failed vendor procurements. The county says this saved more than $7M (verified).
- Harris County, TX (the largest county in Texas): buys. It has run County Fusion since a 2019 four-year contract. That contract expired in December 2024 and was extended while a land records system is re-bid (RFP 24/0128, responses due March 2025) (FY2026 Records Archive Plan, verified).
- Maricopa County, AZ: building in-house is not confirmed. The page cited earlier returned 403, and a fresh search shows only in-house sub-capabilities such as ICR and redaction. The draft's claim that the largest counties 'often build' is therefore downgraded to 'sometimes'.

TIER 4. State and national registries: about $5M-$90M a year.
- Landgate, Western Australia: a 5-year, A$140M (US$105M at the time) IT services contract with its subsidiary Advara, with Ajilon as the delivery partner. That is about US$21M a year, and it covers all of Landgate's IT, not only titles (Princeton ISS case study, verified).
- HMLR (England and Wales), 2025-26 report (verified): 'IT and professional services', including equipment maintenance and licences, cost £36.6M (£29.5M in 2024-25). Purchases of intangible assets were £54.0M, but £22.1M of that was capitalised staff cost. Vendor-facing spend is therefore £36.6M opex plus about £31.9M of non-staff capex, about £68.5M or US$90M. Opex alone is about US$48M.
- Correction: the draft's US$110M ceiling included capitalised staff, which this field excludes. The ceiling is now US$90M.
- Philippines LRA: the build-own-operate (BOO) operator LARES had collected about P21.8B by end-2020 (Malaya Business Insight, via search). The BOO contract was signed in 2000. Spread over the roughly 10 years of live operation, that is about US$40M a year; spread over 20 years, about US$20M. These are fees paid by users to the operator, not a budget line.

BUILD VS BUY: 'some' overall.
- US counties: building is rare. There are 3,031 county governments (Census of Governments 2022, verified). Most buy from Tyler, Harris, Fidlar, Catalis, GovOS, Kofile and others. Cook County is the notable exception.
- National and state registries: building is common. HMLR runs bespoke, internally developed and mainframe software (its asset-life notes list both). Singapore built INLIS, Indonesia built KKP and India's NIC built Bhoomi. Telangana moved Dharani operations from TerraCIS to NIC from 1 December 2024 (Hans India, verified). Landgate co-built its New Land Registry with its outsourcer after finding nothing cloud-based to buy.
- Landgate's survey (itnews, verified) found about 37 Torrens jurisdictions running 35 different systems, all of them bespoke builds from around 2000.

enterprise.evidence:
Summary: the only private enterprises that run a land registry system of record are the companies that hold long licences or concessions over government registries. There are about 6 to 8 of them worldwide, not 'fewer than 5' as the draft said. They own and run their platforms, so building in-house is common. Spend is an inference from comparables; no operator discloses it.

WHO THEY ARE
- Teranet (Ontario, Canada). In 2010 it paid Ontario C$1B to extend its exclusive electronic land registration licence by 50 years, to 2067, with a commitment to keep the system modern and secure (Lexpert). It also runs Manitoba's Land Titles registry end to end. The draft missed both.
- ISC, Information Services Corporation (Saskatchewan, Canada). A listed company that runs the Saskatchewan Land Titles Registry. Its Registry Operations segment earned C$125.6M of revenue in 2024. The draft missed it.
- NSW Land Registry Services (Australia). Paid A$2.6B for a 35-year concession. The operator is responsible for upgrading the legacy IT. The NSW regulator called the upgrade critical in August 2020, and completion was expected no earlier than January 2025 (NSW Audit Office, verified).
- Victoria (Australia). A 40-year concession for A$2.86B (earlier research, not re-checked).
- South Australia. Its land services were also concessioned in 2017 (from general knowledge, not re-checked).
- LARES (Philippines). The private BOO operator of the national land titling computerisation system (see the government segment).

CORRECTION: Titles Queensland is not a private buyer. It is a company owned indirectly by Queensland government entities through the QIC-managed Queensland Future Fund (Titles Registry) Act 2021 structure. It maintains the 1994 Automated Titles System. It belongs with government, not here.

HOW THE SPEND WAS ESTIMATED
- No operator discloses what it spends on registry IT.
- The range rests on state-scale comparables: Landgate's IT contract is about US$21M a year, and HMLR's IT opex is about US$48M a year.
- A provincial or state-sized operator therefore plausibly spends about US$10-40M a year. That is roughly 10-30% of the revenue of an ISC-sized registry business.
- This is an inference, not an observed figure. Teranet, which runs Ontario's very large registry, could sit at or above the top of this range.

EXCLUDED: title insurers' private title plants. DataTrace alone gives access to more than 1,855 of them. They copy registry data rather than hold the legal record, so they are an adjacent category.

mid_market.evidence:
Summary: mid-market firms do not buy this system, so spend is null.

WHY
- Title agencies, conveyancers, lenders and mid-size law firms use registry data. None of them owns a register.
- They pay per use instead. One route is e-recording fees: Simplifile served 2,019 US counties, covering more than 80% of the population, as of December 2019 (ICE press release, verified).
- The other route is search subscriptions. In Fannin County, TX, the county sets Fidlar Laredo end-user prices at $100 a month on the Personal Plan and $250 per subscriber a month on the Business Plan. Fidlar charges the county $20 or $50 per subscriber licence and passes the remainder back as credits (2022 cost sheet, verified).
- In Vermilion County, IL, the reported price is $100-$325 a month. This was not re-checked.

These are usage fees paid to a county or vendor. They are not spend on a land registry system.

smb.evidence:
Summary: SMBs do not buy this system, so spend is null.

WHY
- Small abstractors, solo conveyancers and real estate agents never own or run a register.
- They use registry data through pay-per-search portals. On Fidlar Tapestry, Fidlar pays the county $2.75 per search plus $0.50 per printed image (Fannin contract, verified). The user pays more; the draft's figure of about $8.75 a search was not re-checked.
- The other option is a low-tier Laredo plan, about $1.2k-$3k a year at Fannin's $100-$250 monthly prices.

Note on small counties: small US county recorder offices are SMB-sized by headcount. They are still government buyers, and they are covered in the government segment at about $15k-$60k a year.

best_icp: Sell first to US county recorder and clerk offices serving about 50k-1M people. Five reasons. (1) They buy rather than build. (2) They already pay about $70k-$260k a year. (3) There are about 3,000 counties to sell to. (4) They already buy AI indexing as a separate line item: Fort Bend pays $24.9k a year for aiINDEX. (5) Contracts come up for renewal; Harris County, TX is re-bidding now. The draft's wedge needs two corrections. First, incumbents lock add-ons into their own platforms. Harris Recording Solutions supports and enhances Fort Bend's system only on a sole-source basis through a proprietary integration layer, so a newcomer's add-on may not be able to plug in. Second, larger procurements are competitive. Sedgwick County, KS drew seven bids, from Harris, Catalis, Fidlar, GovOS, Tyler, BIS and Questys. Hillsborough, NH's single bidder was the exception, not the rule. Wagoner County, OK moved to SaaS with its incumbent, Tyler, so it was not an open opportunity. The realistic path: win a full replacement of the recorder system at contract expiry in counties under about 1M people, where a hosted platform with AI indexing and fraud detection built in competes on price against the Tyler, Harris and Fidlar on-prem stack. Leave the national registries and the private concessionaires (Teranet, ISC, the Australian operators) for later. They build their own systems, run multi-year statutory programmes, or are locked into licences lasting 35 to 50 years.

criticality_why:
VERDICT: critical. The call holds up after checking. Four supporting facts needed fixing (listed at the end).

TEST 1. Does the business stop or break the law if the system fails? Yes. The servicing system is the ledger for the lender's main asset, the loan book. It posts payments, runs escrow, handles defaults and produces investor and regulator reports. If it is wrong, the lender is out of compliance. Example: in April 2017 the CFPB sued Ocwen, alleging that its in-house platform (REALServicing) produced errors from system failures and faulty programming even when the input data was correct. A broken system is a legal problem, not only an IT outage.

TEST 2. Is it where the firm competes? Yes, for mortgage lenders, servicers and specialty lenders. (a) Origination cost is the main cost lever: about $11,000 per mortgage ($12,200 retail), with technology about 4% of direct cost and rising (MBA Quarterly Performance Report data, analyzed in HousingWire). (b) Servicing cost per loan sets margin. PennyMac reports its own system (SSE) cut servicing cost per loan by about 30%. Rithm expects about $65M a year in savings from moving Newrez's 4M+ loans onto Valon by 2027. (c) Lock-in is high. MSP contracts typically run 5 to 7 years (EverBank 5; Fremont Bank, New American Funding, 360 Mortgage and myCUmortgage 7).

CAVEAT. For a diversified bank, the loan modules inside its core banking system are closer to 'important', because the bank competes on relationships and deposits more than on loan software. For mortgage lenders, servicers and specialty lenders, the system is the business.

CORRECTIONS. (1) The cost-to-originate source is MBA data analyzed by Roque and Deitch, not STRATMOR. (2) The FTC press release does not describe LOS switching as expensive or lengthy, and gives no Encompass share. It only calls Encompass 'the dominant LOS'. That claim is removed. (3) The 5-to-7-year contract length is now backed by Black Knight client press releases. (4) PennyMac's saving is 'about 30%', not 'more than 30%'.

criticality_why:
Verdict: critical. Both tests pass for the commercial buyers who make up most of this market. The differentiation test is weaker for government buyers.

Test 1. Does the business stop if it fails? Yes. These systems run core ledgers, payments, card authorisation, claims, benefits and tax. Evidence: (a) IBM's 2025 annual report says mainframes handle 70% of the world's transactional workflows. Note that this is IBM's own claim, citing IBM IBV, and the 2022 z16 release qualifies it as 70% "on a value basis" from an IBM-commissioned Celent study. (b) An SSA OIG audit from 2013 says the Social Security Administration runs its workloads on eight IBM mainframes, four in Baltimore and four in Raleigh. (c) Services Australia signed a AU$109.4M IBM contract in 2026 to keep the mainframes behind Medicare and Centrelink running to June 2031, with an option to 2033. It did this after abandoning, in 2023, a project to replace the Centrelink entitlements calculation engine. (Correction: the earlier draft said a 2023 mainframe upgrade failed. The project that failed was a replacement of the application, not of the mainframe.) (d) GAO-25-107795 names 11 critical federal legacy systems. Two of them are Treasury systems written in COBOL and Assembly, aged 59 and 51 years. An outage stops payments or benefits. That is a regulatory event, not an inconvenience.

Test 2. Is it where the firm differentiates? Mostly yes. This category covers custom COBOL, PL/I and Assembler code that firms wrote themselves. That code holds their own product, pricing, underwriting and eligibility rules, which is why they built it instead of buying a package. Two limits apply. First, the platform under the code (z/OS, CICS, IMS, Db2) is a commodity, so the differentiation sits only in the custom application logic. That logic is exactly what an AI-native entrant would rewrite. Second, much of this code is ledger posting and batch processing that packaged cores also do, and government agencies do not compete at all. For them it is mission-critical but not differentiating. The category-level call stays critical because banks and insurers, the bulk of buyers, carry proprietary rules in this code.

enterprise.evidence:
VERIFICATION SUMMARY. The range of $3M to $150M a year stands. Every source figure I checked matched the filing or article. No number was off by more than 2x. I added caveats where a figure is dated or broader than mainframe.

1. WHO BUILDS IN-HOUSE. Common, by definition. Large enterprises wrote their COBOL applications and still own them. They buy only the platform (hardware, z/OS, CICS, Db2, ISV tools) and some outsourcing. IBM's z16 launch release (2022) says IBM Z serves 45 of the top 50 banks, 8 of the top 10 insurers, 7 of the top 10 retailers and two thirds of the Fortune 100. Verified.

2. TOTAL VENDOR REVENUE POOL: about $20-25B a year. Each part was checked against its source.
(a) IBM Transaction Processing software: $8,603M in 2025, up from $8,408M (IBM 2025 annual report). Verified. Caveat: this line also includes storage, analytics and integration software, so not all of it is mainframe.
(b) IBM Z hardware: IBM does not report it in dollars. Hybrid Infrastructure rose from $8,913M to $10,618M, with IBM Z up 51.7% and Distributed down 1.8% (verified). Solving the two equations gives IBM Z of about $3.5B in 2024 and $5.3B in 2025, the z17 launch year. I re-ran the arithmetic and it holds. The average over a product cycle is about $4.4B a year.
(c) IBM Infrastructure Support: $5,100M (verified). The 40-50% mainframe share is my assumption, giving about $2-2.5B.
(d) Broadcom/CA Mainframe Solutions: $2,176M in FY2018, the last year disclosed (CA 10-K, verified).
(e) Unisys License & Support, mostly ClearPath: $428.1M in 2025 (Unisys 10-K, verified). ClearPath is not IBM Z, so this slightly inflates the per-IBM-Z-customer average below.
(f) BMC, Rocket, Precisely and the outsourcers (Kyndryl, Ensono) come on top. Not verified.
Subtotal of (a) to (e): about $18B, so $20-25B including (f) is reasonable.

3. AVERAGE PER BUYER: about $4-5M a year. Futurum's Steven Dickens (CIO.com, Oct 2024) says about 5,000 customers run IBM Z (verified). $20-25B divided by 5,000 gives $4-5M. Spend is heavily skewed to the largest buyers, so the median enterprise sits below that average.

4. LOW END: about $3M. IBM's 2007 TCO deck prices a 540-MIPS system at $69,562 to $78,810 a month in MLC for z/OS, Db2 and CICS alone (verified). That is about $0.9M a year at 2007 prices, before ISV tools, hardware and maintenance. A small enterprise shop therefore totals about $2-3M.

5. HIGH END: about $150M. The largest buyers are comparable to SSA. SSA paid about $56M a year for IBM software, made up of $26.1M MLC and $29.9M maintenance and support (SSA OIG audit A-04-13-13046, verified). Caveat: that is the 2012-2014 contract. SSA also awarded Broadcom $738.6M over 7 years on 28 Sept 2026, about $105M a year (verified). SSA is separately soliciting a 7.5-year IBM Z hardware contract, so its true total is above $160M. Top-tier banks and insurers likely run $100-150M+ in vendor spend alone. A vendor blog's '4,000 MIPS costs $12-20M a year' fits the middle of the range, but it likely includes staff, so I treat it as indicative only.

RANGE: about $3M (small enterprise shop) to $150M (top-tier bank or insurer), vendor spend only, excluding internal staff.

mid_market.evidence:

1. WHO BUILDS IN-HOUSE. Some. Mid-market firms that still run COBOL usually own the application code. They are more likely than enterprises to have done one of three things: (a) outsourced the mainframe to a hosting provider, (b) rehosted the COBOL onto Windows or Linux with Rocket (formerly Micro Focus) Enterprise Server, or (c) moved to a packaged system such as a bank core. Packaged systems are covered by other categories in this study. IBM's 2007 TCO deck describes a 'small mainframe customer' tier averaging 400-600 installed MIPS (verified). That is the realistic ceiling for mid-market buyers.

2. LOW END: rehosted COBOL, about $150-800K a year.
(a) AWS lists Rocket Runtime at $5.55 per CPU core per hour (verified). That is about $48.6K per core per year, so a 4-16 core production estate costs about $0.2-0.8M a year in runtime licence before AWS infrastructure.
(b) AWS's own worked example (dev tools, test and 2 production instances) totals $11,452.16 a month, about $137K a year (verified).
(c) Correction: Rocket's AWS Marketplace listing is $600,000 per 36 months per licensed vCPU. That is about $200K per vCPU per year, not a flat $200K for the whole entitlement as the earlier draft implied. 4. MIDDLE: outsourced mainframe. This usually lands between the two paths above, because hosting providers spread fixed software costs across clients. I found no public mid-market contract values. The IBM deck notes small shops pay a higher price per MIPS.

RANGE: $150K to $3M a year, vendor spend only.

2. TIER 1, SMALL STATES AND COUNTIES: about $0.3M to $16M a year. Vendor spend only, excluding agency staff.
(a) Wyoming ETS awarded IBM $300K for z/OS software maintenance and ISV support (verified). Caveat: the source does not state the term, so this may not be an annual figure.
(b) Kansas OITS fully outsources its mainframe to Unisys DCaaS, migrated in 2017. FY2025 contractual services were $15.97M (verified). Caveat: that line also covers data center hosting, space rental and software renewals, so it is an upper bound for mainframe.
(c) California's State Data Center bills mainframe CPU at $545 an hour, rising to $573, and forecasts about 14,400 CPU hours (verified). It raised mainframe processing rates about 10% in FY2023/24. Taken alone, those hours equal about $8M a year in billings across all client departments.
(d) Sacramento County awarded $150K for a z/OS upgrade alone (one-time).

3. TIER 2, NATIONAL AGENCIES: about $15M to $150M a year. AUD converted at about 0.65.
(a) Australian Taxation Office: AU$87.7M original contract, extended by AU$104.8M to a total of AU$192.5M through mid-2031, including z17 hardware and software (verified). That is about AU$24M, or US$16M, a year.
(b) Home Affairs: an 18-year IBM deal worth AU$924M ending June 2025 (verified), about AU$51M or US$33M a year. It was followed by a AU$165M, 4-year contract for licences, hardware, maintenance and storage (verified), about AU$41M or US$27M a year.
(c) Services Australia: CORRECTED. The 'AU$110M' headline and the 'AU$109.4M storage refresh' are the same contract: AU$109,381,053 over five years for a mainframe DASD upgrade, running to June 2031 with an option to 2033. That is about AU$22M, or US$14M, a year. It covers storage only, so total Services Australia mainframe spend is higher.
(d) US SSA: IBM software about $56M a year (OIG audit; 2012-2014 contract, dated, verified) plus Broadcom $738.6M over 7 years, about $105M a year (awarded 28 Sept 2026, verified). A separate 7.5-year IBM Z hardware solicitation adds more on top, so SSA's total is above $160M.
(e) US IRS: IBM ESIS IDIQ, one base year plus seven option years, $1B ceiling. That is about $125M a year at the ceiling, covering hardware, software and services. Caveat: a ceiling is a maximum, not actual spend.
(f) US DISA is sourcing IBM mainframe software (IPLA and MLC) for Oct 2026 to Sept 2031. No value disclosed.

RANGE: $0.3M a year for a small state software line to about $150M+ for the largest federal agencies.

best_icp: Sell first to the lower end of enterprise and the upper end of mid-market: regional insurers, regional banks with their own COBOL, and logistics or retail firms running about 400-2,000 MIPS and spending about $1-5M a year on mainframe vendors. Three reasons. They pay the highest price per MIPS (IBM's own TCO deck), so the savings case is strongest. They lack the large in-house teams and long IBM, Kyndryl or Accenture relationships that slow top-50 banks. And they can sign a fixed-price migration quickly, while the largest buyers ($50-150M a year) and national agencies run multi-year procurements dominated by incumbents. A likely fourth reason, that their codebases are small enough to migrate in quarters, is my assumption and not sourced. After landing referenceable wins, move to small and mid-size US state agencies (Wyoming and Kansas scale), then to large banks and federal agencies.

criticality_why: VERDICT: important, not critical. Checked and kept. A system is critical only if it passes two tests. Billing passes the first and fails the second. TEST 1: Does the business stop or lose its licence if billing fails? It nearly stops, but the licence is safe. Billing is how a provider gets paid, and an outage cuts off cash within days. Evidence: the Change Healthcare cyberattack (Feb 2024). An AHA survey of nearly 1,000 hospitals (9-12 March 2024) found 94% had a financial impact and 82-83% had cash flow affected (the PDF says 82%, the web page 83%). Nearly 60% of the hospitals affected put the revenue hit at $1M a day or more, and 74% reported a direct impact on patient care. No hospital lost its licence. They fell back on manual claims, other clearinghouses and CMS advance payments, although 67% said switching clearinghouses was difficult. TEST 2: Is billing where the provider competes? No. Hospitals and physician groups win patients and contracts on clinical quality, access and payer networks, not on how they bill. Billing is judged on cost per claim and speed of cash, and most providers buy or outsource it. R1's 2023 10-K says it serves over 3,700 hospitals and covers more than $1T of net patient revenue. RESULT: the business depends heavily on billing but does not compete on it, so it is important. WHAT THIS MEANS FOR AN ENTRANT: (a) buyers pay for more cash collected, faster; (b) buyers accept almost no go-live risk, because a bad cutover hits payroll within weeks.

enterprise.evidence: WHO: large health systems and academic medical centres, with about $2B or more in net patient revenue (usually 10+ hospitals). BUILD OR BUY: they buy. Checked and kept as rare. Almost none write their own billing system. They run the billing module of their EHR (Epic Resolute or Oracle Health Patient Accounting), because billing shares one database with scheduling and clinical records. LA County's June 2026 memo (checked) requires one integrated database across EHR, population health and revenue cycle, and says only Epic now meets that. Epic has 43.7% of US acute hospitals and 56.9% of beds (KLAS via HealthSystemCIO, checked). Enterprises do keep the work around the software in-house: revenue cycle departments, analytics and automation bots. R1's 10-K lists 'internal RCM departments of healthcare organizations' as a competitor (checked). So 'build' here means doing the operations in-house, not writing the system. SPEND ANCHORS (licence, maintenance, hosting, clearinghouse and vendor services; staff excluded). (1) Steady state. LA County DHS was quoted a 10-year total cost of ownership above $200M for Oracle's revenue cycle module alone, so more than $20M a year (memo checked). (2) Implementation year. NYC Health + Hospitals (2017): $289M over five years for Epic revenue cycle across 11 hospitals and 70+ clinics, about $58M a year (checked). CORRECTION: the article says the software was already bought in the earlier $764M Epic deal, and the $289M pays for staffing to customise the system and for training. So the $58M is one-off implementation labour, part of it possibly internal staff that this field excludes. It is not a recurring software bill. (3) Add-on layer. Waystar had 1,391 clients paying it more than $100K a year in FY2025 (checked). That is one tool bought on top of the EHR. HOW THE RANGE IS BUILT: about $5M a year at the low end, for a system with about $2B in net patient revenue (its share of EHR maintenance and hosting, plus clearinghouse, coding and denial tools). About $60M a year at the high end, reached only by the largest multi-state systems or by a 10+ hospital system in an implementation year. My estimate for a typical large system in steady state is $10M-$30M a year. LA County is the only firm point in that band. WHAT THIS CHECK CHANGED: the range stays. The low end was defined as a 5-10 hospital system, which falls outside this segment, so it is now defined by revenue. The NYC anchor is relabelled as implementation labour. FULL OUTSOURCING is a different and much larger purchase, because the fee mostly replaces the buyer's own staff. Ascension was 40% of R1's net services revenue in 2023 (checked), roughly $900M of about $2.25B.

mid_market.evidence: WHO: two groups. (a) Community hospitals of about 25-200 beds, which run MEDITECH (14.7% of US acute hospitals, checked), TruBridge or Altera Paragon. (b) Multi-site and specialty physician groups and MSOs with about 20-300 providers, which run athenahealth, NextGen, eClinicalWorks or AdvancedMD. BUILD OR BUY: they buy. Checked and kept as rare. Neither group can afford to build a billing system. Many outsource the billing work. Weston County Hospital (Wyoming) authorised talks with Inova RCM to take over billing, coding and credentialing (checked; no cost given). TruBridge's 10-K describes hospitals of 400 beds or fewer that run their revenue cycle in-house on another vendor's EHR. 'In-house' there means the staff, not the software. SPEND ANCHORS. (1) TruBridge FY2025 10-K (checked): $346.8M in revenue from more than 1,500 healthcare organisations, about $230K per client a year. This covers EHR plus billing software and services. About 98% of its acute-care hospital clients have under 100 beds, so this is the low end of the segment. (2) athenaOne is priced as a percentage of collections. Third-party guides put it at 4-8%, with groups of 10+ providers negotiating 3-4% (athena does not publish rates). CORRECTION: a 50-provider group collecting about $25M a year would pay about $0.75M-$1.5M, not $1M-$2M, because large groups get the lower rates. (3) Waystar averages about $37K per client ($1.1B revenue across about 30,000 clients, checked). That is the claims layer only, paid on top of the core system. (4) Greene County General Hospital (Indiana), a small rural hospital, puts its one-off Epic switch at about $6.3M (checked). That cost covers the whole EHR, not billing alone, and spread over a typical contract it comes to under $1M a year. HOW THE RANGE IS BUILT: about $200K a year for a small community hospital or a 20-provider group on software only. About $4M a year for a 300-provider group on percentage pricing (300 providers x about $400K collections each = about $120M, x about 3-3.5%), or for a 200-bed hospital that outsources part of its billing. WHAT THIS CHECK CHANGED: the high end rises from $2M to $4M. The original math was inconsistent: if 50 providers pay $1M-$2M, then 300 providers on the same model pay several times that, not $2M.

smb.evidence: WHO: independent practices with 1-10 providers, plus small clinics, therapists and dentists. BUILD OR BUY: they almost never build (kept as rare). They choose between a cloud billing subscription and an outsourced biller. Their pain is manual work on payer portals, phone and fax (CAQH Index), not an old core system. SPEND ANCHORS. (1) Tebra's pricing page (checked): $349-$799 per physician per month for its platform bundles, $199-$449 for non-physicians, $225-$299 for therapists, and $99-$199 for Billing Starter alone. That is about $1.2K-$9.6K per provider a year. (2) CORRECTION: AdvancedMD. The cited ITQlick page lists $169-$729 per provider per month, plus 4-8% of collections if AdvancedMD also does the billing work. It does not support the $429-$1,070 and $130-$399 figures in the original. (3) Outsourced billing usually costs 4-10% of net collections, and most small-practice quotes fall at 5-8% (cited cost guide, checked). CORRECTION: the guide cites MGMA's benchmark as about 5% of collections, not about 8%. HOW THE RANGE IS BUILT: about $5K a year for a solo provider on a subscription. About $250K a year for a 10-physician practice that outsources billing: 10 physicians x about $400K collections each = about $4M, x about 5-6%. WHAT THIS CHECK CHANGED: the high end rises from $100K to $250K. The original assumed a 10-provider practice collects $1M-$1.5M a year, which is about $100-150K per provider. That fits a therapy practice, not a medical one, and understates a medical practice's spend by more than 2x. A 10-provider practice on software only still lands near $100K (10 x $9.6K). Per-buyer spend is small, so this segment is a volume business.

government.evidence: WHO: publicly owned hospital systems. In the US: county and city systems (NYC H+H, LA County DHS, Alameda Health System, Harris, Parkland, Jackson) and the VA. Abroad: public hospital authorities such as Queensland Health, Singapore's public clusters and DACH public hospitals on SAP IS-H. BUILD OR BUY: some build, more often than in other segments. Kept as 'some', with one example corrected. Real in-house builds: the VA built VistA (including its billing module) and is now replacing it with Oracle Health. Singapore runs a separate national billing system next to its Epic-based NGEMR. Many Indonesian public hospitals develop or adapt their own SIMRS hospital systems (earlier research, not re-checked). CORRECTION: Queensland's HBCIS is an old system kept running on extended support, not an in-house build. iTnews (checked) says it is nearly 30 years old, runs in all of the state's public hospitals, and fell out of vendor support in 2015. It shows public buyers delaying replacement, not building their own. US county systems buy, through formal tenders or sole-source deals. SPEND ANCHORS. (1) LA County DHS memo, June 2026 (checked): Oracle's revenue cycle module was quoted at more than $200M over 10 years, more than $20M a year. The county is now opening sole-source talks with Epic for EHR, population health and revenue cycle. (2) NYC H+H: $289M over five years, about $58M a year, but as noted under enterprise this was implementation staffing and training, not recurring software. (3) CORRECTION: the Alameda figure is mislabelled. The document is from Alameda County Health (county clinics, behavioural health and the Sheriff's Santa Rita Jail), not from the Alameda Health System hospitals. It is also for the whole EHR, not billing. The figures: Epic licence about $27.5M plus Epic hosting about $9.07M, from 3/2026 to 6/2030. That is about $8.6M a year for a county health department's whole EHR. It is a useful comparison but not a hospital billing number. (4) Queensland's HBCIS replacement is estimated at more than $200M over about seven years (iTnews, checked; covers patient administration, not billing alone). HOW THE RANGE IS BUILT: about $1M a year for a single small county hospital. More than $20M a year for a large county system in steady state (LA). Up to about $60M a year for the largest municipal systems in an implementation year (NYC). Small public district and critical-access hospitals spend at mid-market levels. WHAT THIS CHECK CHANGED: the range stays. The Alameda and Queensland examples are corrected, and the NYC figure is relabelled.

best_icp: Sell first to mid-market multi-site and specialty physician groups and MSOs (about 20-300 providers). They spend about $200K-$4M a year on billing. They buy rather than build. They can change billing vendors without replacing a hospital EHR (though often with their practice management system). They decide faster than hospitals, which run board reviews and multi-year tenders. Enterprise and government budgets are 10-30x larger, but their billing sits inside Epic or Oracle, so an entrant there can sell only an add-on layer (the route AKASA and Adonis take), not a replacement.

criticality_why: VERDICT: critical. The call holds, with two factual fixes noted below. WHY IT IS CRITICAL. (1) The business stops if it fails. The servicing system is the book of record for every loan. It posts payments, runs escrow for tax and insurance, drives collections and loss mitigation, and sends remittances and reports to investors and to Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac and Ginnie Mae. If it goes down, cash stops reconciling, the servicer misses CFPB Regulation X timelines and investor servicing-guide deadlines, and its agency approvals and state licences come under threat. (2) It is where the firm competes. For nonbank servicers and subservicers, servicing is the business. Cost per loan is the main lever: MBA puts fully loaded cost for a performing loan at $127 to $132 a year for large servicers and about $100 more for mid-size servicers ($176 industry average in 2024). Customer experience and refinance recapture are the other levers. (3) It is deeply embedded. Black Knight's 10-K says switching providers can take 12 to 18 months or longer. When PennyMac left MSP, an arbitrator awarded Black Knight six years of avoided licence fees: $155.2M in the interim award, cut to $150.2M plus interest in the final award (January 2024). Mr. Cooper committed to a 7-year licence of Sagent's platform when it sold its own platform to Sagent in 2022. CAVEAT: for a bank whose mortgage book is a side business, servicing is closer to 'important'. Across the category it is critical. CORRECTIONS MADE: the PennyMac award is $150.2M final, not $155.2M. UWM's 2025 press release cites MSP's features, scalability, customer-service support and ICE's neutrality, not recapture or broker relationships, so that framing was removed.

enterprise.evidence: WHO: the largest US banks, nonbank servicers and subservicers, each with roughly 500K to 4M+ loans. UWM (in-house servicing on ICE MSP from 2025) sits at the low end of this tier given its retained book, so it belongs here rather than in mid-market. BUY OR BUILD: most buy, a meaningful minority build. Buying: ICE MSP runs about 36M active loans (Black Knight FY2022 10-K; this count includes first and second liens) and, per ICE's MSP product page, 7 of the top 10 servicers in the J.D. Power 2024 study. Sagent reports 16M+ active loans and 40+ clients, with Mr. Cooper (3M+ loans) as a top customer. Building: PennyMac built its own SSE platform and left MSP from 2019, and the arbitrator confirmed PennyMac owns SSE outright. Mr. Cooper built a servicing platform, then sold it to Sagent in March 2022 for $260M total consideration (a 19.9% Sagent stake plus $9.9M cash) and committed to license it back for 7 years. Valon built ValonOS and ran its own 810K-loan book on it before Carrington bought the servicing business. Three top-tier builders out of a few dozen enterprise servicers is 'some', not 'rare'. (Removed: the claim that Lloyds and JPMorgan service mortgages on Thought Machine. No source supported it, and JPMorgan's Thought Machine use is for UK retail deposits. Also removed: 'tiered per-active-loan pricing' for the Mr. Cooper licence, which the cited filings do not state.) HOW MUCH, three ways. (1) Average unit price: Black Knight servicing software revenue was $838.9M in 2021 (Q4 2021 earnings exhibit) and about $880M in 2022, on about 36M loans. That is roughly $23 to $25 per loan a year across all clients, including add-on modules and services. (2) A top-10 servicer's actual bill: the PennyMac award of six years of avoided licence fees ($150.2M final) implies about $25M a year. PennyMac services millions of loans, so its effective rate was well under the $24 average. Large books get volume discounts, so the straight per-loan math overstates the top end. (3) Client concentration: Wells Fargo was about 10% of Black Knight's 2019 consolidated revenue (about $118M across all Black Knight products, 12% of the software segment). The five largest clients were 31% of revenue in 2019 and 23% in 2022, which works out to roughly $70M each on average across all products. RANGE: about $10M a year for a servicer with roughly 500K loans, up to about $120M for the single largest bank buying the full suite. Most top-10 servicers likely fall in the $25M to $70M band. Confidence: medium. No list price is public, and contracts combine base minimums with per-loan fees.

mid_market.evidence: WHO: regional banks, independent mortgage banks newly bringing servicing in-house, large credit unions and nonprofit lenders, each with roughly 25K to 500K loans. BUY OR BUILD: they license a vendor platform and almost never build. A custom build means recreating escrow, investor accounting and Reg X logic, which only top-tier scale has justified (PennyMac, Mr. Cooper, Valon). Public examples of buying: Ruoff Mortgage, Union Home Mortgage, Pulte Mortgage, Fahe and Mortgage Clearing Corp chose MSP, Evergreen Home Loans chose Sagent's Dara platform (2026), and FICS sells to mid-size banks and credit unions. The usual alternative to buying software is outsourcing the whole job to a subservicer (Cenlar, Dovenmuehle, LoanCare). That is a services spend, not a software spend. (Moved: UWM was listed here, but its book puts it at the enterprise tier.) HOW MUCH: apply the roughly $20 to $25 per loan a year implied by Black Knight's servicing revenue divided by active loans. 25K loans gives about $0.5M to $0.6M, 50K loans about $1M to $1.25M, and 400K loans about $8M to $10M. Smaller books often pay a higher effective rate because of contract minimums. RANGE: about $0.5M to $10M a year. CORRECTION: the low end was $1M, but the tier starts at 25K loans and the stated unit price gives $0.5M there, so the low end is lowered to match its own math. Confidence: low to medium. This is derived from the unit price; no mid-market contract value was found in public sources.

smb.evidence: WHO: community banks and credit unions holding about 1K to 25K mortgages. The pool is large: 4,238 FDIC-insured institutions (FDIC, Q2 2026) and 4,214 federally insured credit unions, of which only 748 have assets over $500M (NCUA, Q2 2026; both verified). Many qualify for the CFPB small-servicer exemption (5,000 loans or fewer, all self-originated or owned). BUY OR BUILD: they almost never build. They do one of three things: (a) sell loans servicing-released or hire a subservicer, (b) use the loan module of their core banking system, or (c) license a low-cost in-house package such as FICS Mortgage Servicer. FICS's site promises a low initial investment and a nominal monthly support and maintenance fee, but publishes no prices. Fully loaded cost to service a performing loan averaged $176 in 2024 (MBA), and software is only a slice of that. HOW MUCH: no public price exists. The estimate applies $15 to $25 per loan a year for software plus hosting to books of 2K to 15K loans, which gives about $25K to $300K a year. Institutions using a core-banking module may pay little or nothing extra, so the true floor is lower. RANGE: about $25K to $300K a year. Confidence: low. There is no contract or pricing page with numbers, and nothing found contradicts the estimate by more than 2x.

government.evidence: WHO: US state housing finance agencies that service their own loans, and federal direct lenders. BUY OR BUILD: both buy. Pennsylvania HFA (about 63K loans, $4.9B) moved from LSAMS, which it had used for in-house servicing since 1999, to Black Knight MSP in Q2 2019 (National Mortgage News). Virginia Housing renewed MSP after 25 years. USDA Rural Development licenses LoanServ (Fiserv, now Sagent) for its Single Family Housing Direct portfolio. Many smaller HFAs avoid owning a system by using a subservicer. HOW MUCH, from public contracts (all verified in the USAspending API): USDA's annual LoanServ support, upgrade and licence task orders were $3.47M (FY2015, Fiserv), $3.0M (April 2021 to March 2022, Sagent, which includes licences), $2.2M (FY2024, Sagent), plus a 2025 to 2030 order with $4.6M obligated so far. The FY13 and FY14 figures ($2.27M, $2.34M) were not rechecked. So one federal agency pays about $2M to $3.5M a year for servicing software alone. Adding its separate UniFi origination-system orders, USDA's total Sagent spend runs about $4M to $5M a year. For an HFA with 20K to 100K loans, the $20 to $25 per-loan rate implies about $0.5M to $2.5M a year. No HFA contract value was found. RANGE: about $0.5M to $5M a year. Confidence: medium at the federal end (real contract data), low for HFAs (derived). Outside the US, state housing lenders such as Thailand's Government Housing Bank are buyers, but no contract values were found.

best_icp: Sell first to US mid-market servicers with 25K to 500K loans that are about to choose a platform anyway (independent mortgage banks moving servicing in-house from a subservicer, large credit unions and regional banks outgrowing FICS or a core-banking module, and state housing finance agencies at renewal), because they spend about $0.5M to $10M a year, rarely build, and leaving a subservicer is a cleaner cutover than a top-10 MSP deconversion, which takes 12 to 18 months and can draw a PennyMac-style licence claim, while SMB budgets of $25K to $300K are too small to fund agency-grade compliance; note that Valon took the other route, proving its platform on its own 810K-loan book before selling that book to Carrington.

criticality_why:
VERDICT: IMPORTANT. The business cannot run without payroll, but no firm competes on it. Checked and kept.

WHY NOT "SUPPORTING": the dependency is severe and legally enforced. If payroll fails, staff go unpaid, tax and social-security filings are missed, and the employer faces statutory penalties and labour disputes. Payroll runs on a fixed date and connects to the general ledger, banks, benefits and pensions, so errors spread fast. The best-known failure is Queensland Health's 2010 SAP payroll go-live. It mispaid a workforce of about 78,000 and the total cost was put at about AUD 1.2bn. This figure is widely reported (2013 Commission of Inquiry) and was carried from the earlier research file, not re-opened here. Failures like this are why buyers are risk-averse and replace payroll slowly.

WHY NOT "CRITICAL": "critical" needs both conditions: the business stops if it fails, AND it is where the firm competes. Payroll meets only the first. No firm wins customers through its payroll engine. The market shows buyers treat it as a commodity. ADP has over 1.1 million clients and pays over 42 million workers in 140+ countries (ADP FY2025 10-K, verified). Even the US federal government pools civilian payroll into four shared providers (DFAS, USDA National Finance Center, Treasury, GSA per OPM) instead of treating it as core.

CHANGES FROM THE DRAFT: none to the rating. One wording fix: the Queensland figure is "staff affected / workforce size", not "staff underpaid or missed".

enterprise.evidence:
WHO: firms with about 5,000 to 100,000+ employees, often in several countries.

BUILD OR OWN: SOME (checked, kept). Enterprises almost never write a payroll engine from scratch. Many do own and operate a licensed one: SAP ERP HCM, PeopleSoft or Oracle EBS, run on-premise and heavily customized.
- EPI-USE Labs (SAP HCM consultancy) says the majority of SAP HCM customers globally are still on-premise, often with SAP Payroll. Verified.
- SAP mainstream maintenance runs to 2027. Optional extended maintenance runs 2028 to end-2030 at a 2% premium over existing maintenance. Verified.
- The migrated group buys SaaS. Workday has 11,500+ customers and reaches 65%+ of the Fortune 500 (FY2026 results). Verified.

ANNUAL SPEND: USD 1M to 15M per buyer (checked, kept). Covers licence or subscription, hosting, payroll processing fees and vendor or AMS services. Excludes internal staff. Three cross-checks:
(a) Vendor average. Workday FY2026 subscription revenue was $8.833B across 11,500+ customers, about $770k each. Only about 7,000 of those are core HCM or Financials customers. Spread over that core group it is about $1.26M each. That supports a $1M floor for an enterprise HCM-plus-payroll account.
(b) Per-employee pricing. VendorBenchmark (Apr 2026) gives effective negotiated core-HCM rates of $10 to $35 per employee per month (Workday $14-32, SAP and Oracle $10-26, ADP $14-35, UKG $12-30). Payroll per-run fees add $5 to $15 PEPM at ADP, Dayforce and UKG. Implementation runs 1.0 to 2.5x first-year licence. Worked examples:
  - 5,000 employees at about $17 PEPM all-in: about $1.0M a year.
  - 10,000 employees at $12 to $25 PEPM: $1.4M to $3.0M.
  - 50,000 employees at $10 to $20 PEPM (volume discount): $6M to $12M.
  - 100,000 employees at about $12 PEPM: about $14M to $15M.
  This is a third-party benchmark, so treat the rates as indicative.
(c) Real contract. San Mateo County, CA pays about $2.1M a year on a 10-year, $21M Workday agreement (Sept 2025, 2% annual uplift). Caveat: the source describes the deal as expanding HR scope (learning, engagement, AI help tool), so not all of it is payroll.

CORRECTIONS FROM THE DRAFT: the draft's all-in rate of $10 to $20 PEPM for a 10,000-employee firm sat below the benchmark's own floor once payroll fees are added. Restated as $12 to $25. The range itself did not move. Added the Workday core-customer cross-check.

CAVEAT: many Workday, SAP and Oracle HCM customers still run payroll on ADP or a local provider, so HCM spend and payroll spend are not always with the same vendor.

CONFIDENCE: medium. Vendors do not disclose spend per customer by size band.

mid_market.evidence:
WHO: firms with about 50 to 1,000 employees. In the US this is the core market for Paylocity, Paycom and ADP Workforce Now.

BUILD OR OWN: RARE (checked, kept). Mid-market firms buy payroll as SaaS or as a bureau service.
- Paylocity targets firms with 10 to 5,000 employees (FY2025 10-K, verified).
- Paycom targets 50 to 10,000+ employees (2025 10-K, verified).
- ADP Workforce Now serves over 90,000 mid-sized and large businesses (ADP FY2025 10-K, verified).
The remaining legacy footprint is software they bought and run on-prem or hosted, not software they wrote: older Sage and regional packages, IBM i (AS/400) payroll applications, and Kronos Workforce Central for time and attendance. The AS/400 point is from the earlier research and was not re-sourced here. No evidence was found of firms this size writing their own payroll.

ANNUAL SPEND: USD 25k to 150k per buyer (checked, kept). Derived from revenue per client at public vendors:
(a) Paylocity. FY2025 revenue $1,595.2M over about 41,650 clients = about $38k per client. Average client has over 150 employees, so at most about $255 per employee per year. Verified.
(b) Paycom. 2025 revenue $2,051.7M ($1,938.7M recurring) over about 39,200 clients by tax ID = about $52k each. By parent company (about 20,300) = about $101k each. Verified. Paycom's base skews larger, since it is moving toward 1,000+ employee clients.
(c) Public buyers of similar size. Paris, TX: $88k for UKG launch fee plus first year (Jul 2025). Vernon County, WI: $118k a year for a Tyler ERP+HRIS subscription (Apr 2025). Both verified.

HOW THE ENDS ARE SET: low end ($25k) is a ~100-employee firm buying payroll and core HR at about $250 per employee per year. High end ($150k) is a ~1,000-employee firm on a discounted rate of about $150 per employee per year. criticality_why: VERDICT: critical. The rating holds on both tests, and the 2025 HESTA case makes the licence test concrete instead of an inference. TEST 1, THE FUND STOPS WITHOUT IT. The pension admin system is the legal record of what each member is owed. It also calculates benefits and pays retirees. Haringey Council's 2022 contract award report (23,000-member LGPS fund) says that without the system it could not carry out core statutory functions, such as issuing annual benefit statements and paying new retirees correctly. TEST 2, THE LICENCE IS AT RISK WHEN IT FAILS. In April 2025 HESTA (1.1m+ members) moved its administration from MUFG/Link to Grow Inc. Members could not make withdrawals, switches or claims for about seven weeks. In December 2025 APRA put extra conditions on HESTA's licence and cited a severe, prolonged disruption (ABC News). So a failed system change has already led to regulatory action against a fund's licence. TEST 3, IT IS WHERE THE BUYER COMPETES. Most platform buyers are recordkeepers, TPAs and outsourced administrators, and for them the platform is the product. They win and keep clients on cost per member, accuracy and digital service. Fidelity keeps its own recordkeeping platform, with about $1.6tn of DC assets on it (InvestmentNews). Link RSS sells administration at about A$48 per member. Bravura's FY25 report says its products are typically key to clients' operations, so switching is hard and slow. CAVEAT: public funds such as LGPS funds, US state systems and EPFO do not compete for members. For them, the system is critical on Test 1 and Test 2 only. If those buyers were scored alone, 'important' would be the stricter call. The overall rating stays critical because the commercial buyers meet all three tests.

criticality_why:
VERDICT: critical. The call holds after checking. The system meets both tests: the terminal stops when it fails, and large operators compete on it.

WHAT THE SYSTEM DOES. A terminal operating system (TOS) runs the terminal in real time: vessel and yard planning, equipment dispatch, gate transactions and billing.

TEST 1: FAILURE STOPS THE BUSINESS. Each case below was checked against its source.
(1) Port Houston, June 2024 commission minutes (opened). Staff called the Navis TOS and the gate system 'critical to the daily core functions of the Container Terminals'. The minutes also show the TOS handles billing at all three container terminals.
(2) DP World Australia, November 2023 (The Conversation, opened). After a cyber intrusion, DP World shut down its port systems. Ships could still unload, but trucks could not enter or leave the Brisbane, Sydney, Melbourne or Fremantle terminals for several days. DP World handles about 40% of Australia's container trade.
(3) Felixstowe, June 2018 (WorldCargo News, opened). The port moved from Navis SPARCS plus in-house applications to Hutchison's nGen, and the article reports major delays that month. The rest of the article is paywalled. These details come from search snippets only and are NOT verified: truck queues of up to 16 hours, lost boxes, more than two months of disruption, and shipping lines moving services elsewhere.
Weaker case, from a headline only: Kenya's KWATOS (about $7M, Total Soft Bank's CATOS) reportedly 'paralysed' Mombasa when it went live in 2008. The article returned 403.

TEST 2: IT IS WHERE LARGE OPERATORS COMPETE. The biggest operators build their own TOS for a productivity edge.
- Hutchison built nGen from Feb 2001 to Aug 2005 on a US$10M original budget, finished 10% under budget, and planned it for all HPH ports (PMI case study, opened).
- DP World runs CARGOES TOS+ at 70+ sites in 20 countries (DP World page, opened). The page does NOT state the earlier '18+ years in-house' figure, so that figure is dropped.
- PSA built CITOS in 1988. This is widely reported, but no source was opened for it.
- The buyers of vendor systems also call it core. COSCO's vice chairman called N4 'the brain' of its terminal business (FreightWaves, opened). The new owner of Tideworks called it a 'mission-critical product' (Oct 2026 deal reports).

enterprise.evidence:
VERDICT: range kept at $3M to $30M a year, with one caveat added. It is an estimate built from per-terminal costs. No group-level contract value was found.

WHO BUYS. Global and regional multi-terminal operators running about 10 to 60 terminals each: PSA, Hutchison, DP World, APM Terminals, COSCO Shipping Ports, TIL/MSC, ICTSI, SSA/Carrix.

BUILD OR BUY: building is common. The operators split into two camps.
- Builders: Hutchison (nGen, US$10M budget 2001-2005, verified), DP World (CARGOES TOS+, 70+ sites, verified), PSA (CITOS, 1988, not opened). SSA/Carrix owned the vendor Tideworks from its founding in 1999 until Diversis Capital bought a majority stake, announced 1 Oct 2026 (verified). Tideworks serves 130+ facilities.
- Buyers who standardise on one vendor: COSCO Shipping Ports signed a global Navis N4 subscription in March 2018 (verified). COSCO then ran 38 ports, but the article does not say N4 went live at all 38. APM Terminals calls N4 the 'world standard' across its network (verified).

CAVEAT. The range applies to the buyer camp. For builders, vendor spend is mostly hosting and hardware, and their real cost is internal staff, which this measure excludes. Their vendor spend could fall below $3M. No source puts a number on it.

HOW THE RANGE IS BUILT.
Step 1, cost per terminal per year. Three anchors, all checked:
(a) Navis had 2020 sales of EUR 107M, about $122M to $126M (Cargotec release, opened). Kaleris marketing cites 490+ terminals and 350+ N4 customers. That gives about $250k per terminal, or $350k per customer. This is an upper bound for TOS spend, because Navis revenue also includes carrier and vessel software.
(b) Port Houston pays Navis up to $864,549 a year in maintenance alone for 3 terminals, about $290k per terminal (verified). The fee scales with the port's annual TEU volume, so hub terminals of several million TEU pay more.
(c) APM Terminals put $5M into N4 at Valencia, which went live on 4 Feb 2022 after more than 2 years of setup (verified). Spread over 7 to 10 years and added to maintenance, that is about $0.6M to $1M a year for a large terminal.
Step 2, multiply by fleet size. About $0.3M per terminal across 10 terminals gives the low end, about $3M. About $0.5M per terminal across 60 terminals gives the high end, about $30M.

VERDICT: range kept at $150k to $1M a year. All four anchors check out, with small arithmetic fixes below.

BUILD OR BUY: building is rare. These buyers license Navis, Tideworks, CATOS, RBS TOPS, Octopi or similar. Homegrown systems survive mainly as legacy, such as Patrick's long-running in-house TOS (search snippets only).

HOW THE RANGE IS BUILT. Four anchors:
(a) Navis: about $122M to $126M of 2020 sales over 490+ terminals is about $250k per terminal per year (verified). This is an upper bound, since revenue includes non-TOS products.
(b) Total Soft Bank, maker of CATOS (KOSDAQ 045340): FY2025 revenue of KRW 27.5B (verified), about $19M to $20M. (c) INTECH 5-year cost model (consultancy illustration, opened, internal staff excluded). On-premise: hardware $1.2M, licence $900k, upgrades $600k, disaster recovery $400k, integration $500k.
