best_icp: Sell first to independent mid-market container and multipurpose terminals of about 100k to 1M TEU, especially new terminals or ones replacing an end-of-life SPARCS or homegrown system: they pay about $150k to $1M a year, rarely build their own, and have one operational decision-maker, unlike port authorities (slow public tenders) or global operators (who build in-house like Hutchison and DP World or standardise on N4 like COSCO and APMT), and because a full cutover is risky (Felixstowe 2018), the safest way in is a planning or optimisation layer on top of the current TOS before attempting full replacement.

criticality_why:
Verdict: important. The call holds on review. One wording fix was needed: the Birmingham figures describe a whole-ERP failure, not a P2P-only one.

What the system does. Procure-to-pay (P2P) runs from purchase request through purchase order, invoice and 3-way match to supplier payment.

Why it is above "supporting". The business depends on it. If it fails, suppliers go unpaid, supply and month-end close are disrupted, and the controls over cash leaving the business break (segregation of duties, fraud checks, the vendor master). The payment run cannot be done by hand for long at volume. Birmingham City Council's SAP R/3 to Oracle Fusion replacement shows the cost of a failed finance and procurement core. Its forecast grew from GBP 19M to GBP 144.4M through 2027/28, and it spent more than GBP 5M on manual workaround labour, mostly for broken bank reconciliation (The Register, Jan 2026). Those numbers cover the whole ERP programme, not P2P alone.

Why it is not "critical". Under the rubric, "critical" needs both: the business stops or loses its licence, and the system is where the firm competes. P2P fails the second test. Almost no firm wins customers on how it pays invoices. It is a standard back-office control function, so it is bought as an ERP module (SAP MM/FI-AP, Oracle Payables) or a SaaS overlay (Coupa, BILL, AvidXchange), not built. A P2P failure also does not cost a licence the way a core banking or clinical system failure can.

Context. Manual work already carries much of the load. Ardent Partners' 2025 survey (204 AP professionals) finds 48.6% of invoices still arrive by non-electronic means, only 35.4% are processed straight-through, and the exception rate is 18.4%.

enterprise.evidence:
Verdict: the range of $200K to $2M a year stands. Two supporting inputs were wrong and are fixed below. The top of the range rests on indicative vendor tiers, not observed deals.

Build vs buy: rare. Enterprises buy. The core is a licensed ERP module (SAP ECC/S4 MM + FI-AP, Oracle EBS/Fusion Payables), often heavily customised in ABAP or Oracle Forms. A source-to-pay suite (Coupa, SAP Ariba, Ivalua) or an AP-capture overlay usually sits on top. Building from scratch is rare. Heavy customisation means they own a lot of bespoke logic inside a bought system.

What the number covers: the P2P/AP layer only (suite subscription or AP overlay, plus vendor services). It excludes the share of the ERP licence and maintenance (for example SAP's 22% maintenance on the whole ECC estate), because that cannot be separated out.

How the range was built.
1. Coupa filings (checked). Subscription revenue for the quarter ended 31 July 2022 was $192.7M, about $770M annualised. 1,519 customers had annualised subscription revenue above $100K (10-Q). The filing does not say what share of revenue that cohort pays, so this is an assumption: if it pays 70% to 100% of subscription revenue, the average large customer pays about $355K to $510K a year.
2. Vendr Coupa page (checked). Average contract value is $94,519 across 85 deals (not 126 as first stated), with observed deals from $20,717 to $331,806. Vendr's indicative tiers: $200K to $800K a year for 500 to 5,000 employees, and $800K to $2M+ for 5,000+ employees, plus implementation of $100K to $1.5M+.
3. Removed: SAP Ariba ranges ($80K-$300K core procurement, $400K-$1.5M+ full suite). They do not appear on the cited Redress Compliance page, which gives no buyer price list. Its 0.155% Ariba Network fee (capped per relationship) is charged to suppliers, so it is not buyer spend.

Result. A typical enterprise P2P/AP spend is about $200K to $2M a year. The Coupa large-customer average (about $355K-$510K) sits inside the range. The $2M top comes from Vendr's large-enterprise tier, not from an observed contract. Global multi-ERP groups can exceed it.

mid_market.evidence:
Verdict: the range of $15K to $200K a year stands. Every figure below was checked against its source.

Build vs buy: rare. Mid-market firms buy. Purchasing and AP live in a packaged ERP (NetSuite, Sage Intacct, Dynamics, JD Edwards World/E1 on IBM i, Epicor), with an AP-automation or intake overlay on top. They rarely have the developers to build. Older IBM i shops keep customised RPG code inside a bought package.

How the range was built.
1. Low end, AP automation only. AvidXchange's FY2024 10-K reports $438.9M total revenue: $121.2M software, $313.5M payment, $4.3M services. It serves 8,500+ mid-market buyers. Software revenue is billed to buyers, which works out to about $14K per buyer a year. Most payment revenue comes from interchange and interest on customer funds, not buyer fees, so it is excluded.
2. High end, full P2P suite. Vendr puts Coupa for small and mid-market firms (100 to 500 employees) at $50K to $200K a year, plus $25K to $100K implementation. The observed Coupa average is $94.5K.
3. Price-list checks. Tipalti AP starts at $99 a month platform fee, plus per-invoice and per-payment charges and add-on modules (procurement, expenses). Real mid-market contracts are custom-quoted. BILL Corporate is $89 per user per month (about $10.7K a year for 10 users), plus $0.59 per ACH payment.

Result. Mid-market P2P/AP spend is about $15K a year at the low end (AP automation only) to $200K (a full procure-to-pay suite).

smb.evidence:
Verdict: the range of $500 to $6,000 a year stands. Every figure below was checked against its source.

Build vs buy: rare. SMBs do not build this, and most do not buy a separate procurement system either. Purchasing and payables run inside desktop or cloud accounting software, with spreadsheets and email for approvals. Examples: QuickBooks, Xero, Tally (2.5M+ businesses, India), Accurate (110K+ companies, Indonesia), MISA (Vietnam), MYOB (Australia). Some add a lightweight AP or spend tool.

How the range was built.
1. BILL FY2025 results. $272.1M subscription revenue across 493,800 businesses is about $550 per business a year. Core revenue (subscription plus transaction fees) of $1,300.8M is about $2,600 per business. Part of the transaction revenue is card interchange the SMB does not pay directly, so $2,600 overstates SMB spend.
2. BILL price list. Plans run $49 to $89 per user per month. For 1 to 5 users that is about $600 to $5,300 a year, plus $0.59 per ACH payment and $1.99 per check.
3. Ramp price list. The Free plan is $0. Plus is $15 per user per month plus a platform fee. Procurement is an add-on with no listed price. Free tiers push the floor toward zero.

Result. SMB spend on AP and purchasing is about $500 to $6,000 a year. The low end overlaps with the accounting-suite licence the SMB already pays.

government.evidence:
Verdict: the low end is corrected from $90K to $10K. The original floor was a large city buying a sourcing tool, not a small government buying P2P. The $4M high end stands.

Build vs buy: some. Most states and local governments buy, often through cooperative contracts such as NASPO ValuePoint eProcurement (Ivalua, Jaggaer, Periscope). Periscope says Arkansas is its 8th state and that it has 1,000+ public-sector customers (checked). Some large national bodies own their systems. The US DoD's PIEE/WAWF procure-to-pay suite is run and sustained by the Defense Logistics Agency. WAWF was fielded in FY98-FY02, is required by DFARS 232.70 for DoD invoicing, and handled about $521B of invoices in FY21 (checked). Virginia's eVA runs on Ivalua, delivered by CGI. It is funded mainly by a supplier fee of 1% of each order, capped at $1,500 per order (DGS fee schedule; the Ivalua release does not mention the fee).

What the number covers. Government 'buyers' range from small cities to whole states. Small cities run purchasing and AP inside their finance ERP and buy add-ons for bidding and contracts.

How the range was built.
1. Low end, corrected. La Palma, CA (2023): OpenGov Procurement at $13,529 a year plus $11,470 implementation (checked). Sweet Home, OR: about $9K a year (search snippet only). Fresno, CA (2024): the same product at $94,415 a year plus $28,811 implementation (checked). Fresno is a city of about 545,000 people, so it is a mid-to-large city, not the 'small-city floor' first claimed. Note that OpenGov Procurement covers bidding and contract management, not invoice-to-pay. Lincolnshire County Council's Panacea contract (GBP 488,600 over a 48-month initial term, about $150K a year) is also a tendering and contract-management system.
2. High end. Maryland's statewide eMMA (March 2019 Board agenda, checked): Nitor Partners on Ivalua, $38,166,071 for a 10-year base term, about $3.8M a year. It covers implementation, licensing, maintenance, help desk, training and work-order labour, plus modules for invoicing, expenses and FMIS integration. On the evaluated-price basis, Jaggaer bid $37,985,410 against Nitor's $42,998,741. The first draft compared Jaggaer's evaluated price to Nitor's award amount; that is fixed here.
3. Above the range. Federal departments and whole-ERP replacements cost far more. Birmingham City Council's SAP to Oracle programme reached GBP 144.4M, but that covers the whole ERP.

Result. A government P2P/procurement buyer spends about $10K a year (a small city adding e-procurement) to $4M (a statewide P2P platform).

best_icp: Sell first to mid-market firms of about 200 to 2,000 employees in the US and APAC that run legacy JD Edwards/IBM i, older Dynamics or Sage, or have outgrown QuickBooks/Tally: they buy rather than build, spend about $15K to $200K a year, buy faster than enterprises running multi-year SAP/Ariba replacements or governments running public tenders, and still receive about half of invoices on paper, so an AI-native AP and intake layer on top of their existing ERP can prove ROI before moving up to enterprise.

criticality_why: VERDICT: Critical. The call holds after review, with one refinement: the two halves of this category pass different tests, and together they pass both. TEST 1, the business stops if it fails: this is the POS half. If checkout goes down, the store cannot take money and revenue stops at once. Retailers buy offline-capable lanes (for example Toshiba SurePOS ACE) and schedule replacements around peak-season change freezes for this reason. TEST 2, it is where the firm competes: this is the merchandising half (assortment, pricing, promotions, inventory valuation). Lidl is the clearest evidence. It spent about 7 years and about EUR 500M trying to move its homegrown merchandising system onto SAP for Retail (eLWIS), then abandoned the project and returned to the old system. A core reason was that its stock system valued inventory at purchase price while the SAP software used retail price (RetailDetail). The largest retailers also treat checkout as proprietary. Walmart Global Tech built Cloud Powered Checkout, which runs in all US Walmart stores, all Sam's Club locations and most international markets. Target's engineers build its Electron/Node.js POS apps in-house and open-sourced the peripheral layer, POSSUM. CAVEAT BY SEGMENT: Transaction capture on its own is a commodity. For a single-store SMB this category is closer to 'important', bought off the shelf for $0 to $149 a month per location. The 'critical' rating applies mainly from mid-market upward, where pricing and promotion logic sit in the same system.

enterprise.evidence: REVIEW RESULT: Range kept. Build call kept. Two vendor-share claims corrected. 1) WHO BUILDS. Only the very largest chains build. Walmart (Cloud Powered Checkout, built by Walmart Global Tech, in all US Walmart and Sam's Club stores) and Target (in-house Electron/Node.js POS apps plus the open-source POSSUM peripheral layer) build their own POS. Lidl runs a homegrown merchandising system after its SAP project failed. Kroger took a hybrid path: it agreed with OneView Commerce to develop a next-generation POS, and OneView's platform now runs digital order pickup at 1,000+ Kroger stores. Most of tier 1 still buys. Toshiba says it holds the #1 worldwide share of EPOS installations, with 2.6M+ POS and self-checkout units installed. CORRECTION: the earlier claims of '7 of the top 10 US and 4 of the top 10 European retailers' and '~17% global share' could not be found in the cited Toshiba Tec integrated report. They are replaced with Toshiba's own current statistics, which are vendor claims. GK Software says more than a quarter of the world's top 50 retailers use it (verified on GK's site). NCR Voyix signed long-term POS deals with Colruyt Group (850+ stores) and 7-Eleven Philippines (4,500+ stores, six-year term), both reported with its FY2025 results in February 2026. Conclusion: 'some' build, and most buy. 2) SPEND, HOW DERIVED. Includes licence or subscription, maintenance, hosting and vendor services. Excludes hardware capex and staff. (a) POS software: VendorBenchmark's 2026 index puts modern cloud POS at $200K to $1.2M a year per 100 stores (verified), which is about $2K to $12K per store per year. A 500-store chain pays about $1M to $6M a year. A 3,000-store chain pays about $6M to $36M. (b) Merchandising and planning: the same index puts tier-2 deployments of Blue Yonder, Symphony RetailAI or Relex at $1.4M to $6.8M a year (verified). (c) Sum: a 300-to-500-store tier-2 chain pays about $2M to $13M a year (POS plus merchandising). A multi-thousand-store tier-1 chain on a full Oracle-class stack pays up to about $40M. 3) CROSS-CHECKS FROM VENDOR FILINGS. NCR Voyix's FY2025 10-K shows Retail segment revenue of $1,842M (down 6%, hardware included). Hardware and software licence revenue fell while hardware and software maintenance rose, and Retail recurring revenue grew 4%. That shows spend moving to recurring fees. Its 80,000 platform sites are company-wide (retail plus restaurants), not retail only. GK Software reported EUR 194.4M revenue in FY2024 across 685k+ installations in 70+ countries. Aptos claims 135,000+ stores. Third-party revenue estimates of about $82M to $280M (Latka, unverified) imply about $0.6K to $2K per store per year, which is consistent with the low end of the VendorBenchmark rate. 4) ONE-TIME COSTS (excluded from the range). A 500-store POS replacement runs $14M to $48M over 18 to 30 months, including hardware and integration (VendorBenchmark, verified). A full Oracle merchandising stack can run $15M to $50M+ over 24 to 48 months (StayModern, not re-verified). 5) CONFIDENCE: medium. VendorBenchmark and StayModern are secondary aggregators, so treat per-store rates as directional, not audited. The vendor filings agree with them on order of magnitude.

mid_market.evidence: REVIEW RESULT: Range kept. Build call kept. One pricing detail corrected (Shopify Plus). 1) WHO BUILDS. Mid-market chains (about 10 to 200 stores) almost never build. They run packaged or partner-implemented suites: LS Central on Dynamics 365 Business Central (successor to LS Nav), Lightspeed, Shopify Plus with POS Pro, or Aptos. Some still run legacy systems such as Microsoft Dynamics RMS (extended support ended July 2021) or JDA MMS on IBM i. Their IT teams are too small to own payment certification (EMV, PCI) and peripheral integration. 2) SPEND, HOW DERIVED. (a) Low end, from published list prices. A Riyadh partner's worked LS Central example for a 5-store chain (10 POS lanes at SAR 470 a month, 8 back-office users at SAR 350 a month, plus BC Essentials, loyalty, a ZATCA e-invoicing add-on and about SAR 105K a year of partner support) comes to about SAR 220K a year from year 2. That is about $59K a year at SAR 3.75 per USD (verified on the Novasoft blog). Shopify Plus starts at $2,300 a month on a 3-year term, about $27.6K a year. CORRECTION: POS Pro is included for the first 20 locations, or the first 200 if the merchant uses Shopify Payments. It is not included at every location, as the draft said. Lightspeed Retail's top plan lists at $289 a month per location with one register (verified), so 10 to 100 stores cost about $35K to $350K a year before extra registers. (b) High end. Applying VendorBenchmark's modern-POS rate of $2K to $12K per store per year gives about $100K to $600K for a 50-store chain and $400K to $2.4M for a 200-store chain. That rate comes from enterprise contracts, so the top of it overstates mid-market prices. Merchandising and planning tools (for example Toolio, Nextail or Increff) add to the total. (c) Result: about $40K to $1.5M a year, most commonly $100K to $500K. 3) ONE-TIME COSTS (excluded). The LS Central example quotes SAR 380K to 540K of implementation, about SAR 76K to 108K (about $20K to $29K) per store for a 5-store rollout. CORRECTION: the draft's 'from about $4,500 per store' figure does not appear in the source. 4) CONFIDENCE: medium. The LS Central figures come from one Saudi partner's blog, and LS Retail does not publish list prices. Shopify and Lightspeed prices are first-party list prices.

smb.evidence: REVIEW RESULT: Build call kept. High end CORRECTED from $7,000 to $15,000. The draft set the high end with Lightspeed's blended ARPU, which includes payments revenue. Payments are excluded by this field's definition, and the field is spend per buyer, not per location. 1) WHO BUILDS. SMBs (1 to about 5 stores) do not build. They buy cloud POS off the shelf. In Southeast Asia, many go straight from cash registers or paper to KiotViet or StoreHub. 2) SPEND, HOW DERIVED (published list prices per location, card fees excluded). Square: $0 (Free), $49 a month (Plus, $588 a year) or $149 a month (Premium, $1,788 a year). Shopify: a plan from $39 a month (Basic) or $105 a month (Grow), plus POS Pro at $89 a month per location billed yearly ($1,068 a year). Lightspeed Retail: $89, $149 or $289 a month ($1,068 to $3,468 a year) with one register and one location (verified). So one location costs $0 to about $3,500 a year, and typically $600 to $3,500. A 5-store SMB on Lightspeed's top plan pays about $17K a year before extra registers. On Square Plus it pays about $3K. The high end of $15K reflects a 4-to-5-store buyer on a premium tier. 3) FILING CROSS-CHECK. Lightspeed's FY2025 MD&A (year to 31 March 2025) reports subscription revenue of $344.8M across about 144,000 customer locations. That is about $2,400 of subscription revenue per location per year, which sits in the middle of the list-price range. Its monthly ARPU of about $545 (about $6,540 a year) includes payments revenue, so it is not used for the range. 4) WHAT IS EXCLUDED, AND WHY IT MATTERS. Card processing (for example Square at 2.4% to 2.6% plus 15 cents per in-person transaction) is excluded. It often exceeds the software fee, and it is how Square and Lightspeed earn most of their SMB revenue. 5) CONFIDENCE: high for list prices, which are first-party.

government.evidence: REVIEW RESULT: Range kept. Build call CORRECTED from 'some' to 'rare'. Two claims removed as unsupported. 1) WHO BUYS. Only governments that run retail operations: state and provincial liquor monopolies (Virginia ABC, Pennsylvania LCB, New Hampshire Liquor Commission, Ontario's LCBO) and military commissaries and exchanges (DeCA, AAFES). General government agencies do not buy retail POS or merchandising systems. 2) BUILD VS BUY. Every buyer checked runs commercial POS. Virginia ABC (about 400 state-run stores) runs GK OmniPOS and estimates its tech stack saves over $300K a year. LCBO is retiring its legacy ERP, order management and POS for commercial software from GK, Blue Yonder, Manhattan, SAP, Microsoft and others. Pennsylvania LCB moved its POS onto Oracle around 2011 (state audit). AAFES installed 6,000 NCR POS terminals, maintained by NCR Services. CORRECTION: the draft cited New Hampshire as a custom-built POS. NHLC's FY2025 annual report shows it has run Microsoft Dynamics 365 for ERP, supply chain and POS across 64 outlets since March 2024 (NextGen program, implemented by Accenture). The older 'design, development and deployment' contract is superseded. The only partial exception is DeCA, whose agency-specific systems (DeCA Enterprise Business Solution, CARTS RM) are maintained by a contractor. Hence 'rare'. 3) SPEND, HOW DERIVED. (a) High end: DeCA's DEBOSS contract with NCR's federal unit is worth up to $335M over one base year plus four option years, about $67M a year. It covers maintenance and operations of POS, catalog, ordering, receiving and pricing systems at about 240 commissaries, including hardware sustainment (Washington Technology, NCR Voyix; verified). It is a ceiling, so actual annual spend may be lower. (b) Low end: about $0.5M a year for a small state liquor monopoly. Basis: NH's legacy POS support contract (about $4.1M over Feb 2020 to July 2027, about $0.55M a year), taken from a Governor and Council agenda via search, because the PDF returned 403. NH's Accenture D365 contract reportedly carries a total price limitation of about $16.9M through June 2033, implementation included. That figure is also from search snippets and was not opened. Virginia ABC's $300K a year in savings implies recurring spend of at least several hundred thousand dollars. Typical ranges: about $0.5M to $5M a year for a state liquor monopoly, and up to about $67M for a military commissary system. 4) REMOVED: 'Pennsylvania LCB budgeted $8.0M for a POS upgrade'. The cited state audit does not contain this figure. 'Virginia ABC POS hardware replacement of about $12.7M': no source was cited, and it was hardware capex in any case. 5) CONFIDENCE: medium for the high end (contract award verified), low-to-medium for the low end (agenda PDFs were blocked).

best_icp: Sell first to mid-market multi-store retailers (about 10 to 200 stores, about $40K to $1.5M a year), especially those on end-of-life Microsoft Dynamics RMS, LS Nav or JDA MMS on IBM i: they cannot build in-house, they pay real money, and they are not locked in the way enterprises are (Walmart and Target build, and other tier-1 chains sign multi-year Toshiba, NCR, GK or Oracle deals). SMB cloud POS is already sold at $0 to $289 a month per location by Square, Shopify and Lightspeed, who earn mainly from payments.

criticality_why:
VERDICT: Important, not critical. The call holds after checking the sources.

THE TEST. Critical needs two things: (1) the institution stops or loses its licence if the system fails, and (2) the system is where the institution competes. The SIS passes (1) and fails (2).

(1) PASSES: THE INSTITUTION DEPENDS ON IT.
- The SIS is the system of record for admissions, enrolment, timetables, grades, transcripts, tuition billing and financial-aid eligibility.
- It feeds regulatory returns: IPEDS and Title IV in the US, HESA/OfS in the UK, the DfE school census, and Indonesia's PDDikti Feeder.
- If it fails at registration or census time, the institution cannot enrol, bill or report. Bad records can put Title IV aid or UK visa-sponsor status at risk.
- Buyer behaviour confirms this. Lehigh has set a 5-year Banner SaaS programme, started fall 2024 (Lehigh ITS, opened). Barton CC's 2009 board paper estimated $300,000 to run two systems in parallel for 18 months during any switch, and Banner offered renewals with 4-8% annual increases (board paper, opened). Barton's board weighed those costs rather than switching casually.

(2) FAILS: IT IS NOT WHERE THEY COMPETE.
- Universities and schools compete on programmes, faculty, brand, price and outcomes. Registrar software is not one of them.
- Most run one of a handful of products (Banner, Colleague, PeopleSoft Campus Solutions, SITS, PowerSchool, Workday Student) with similar setups.
- The parts of the student experience that do set institutions apart (advising, CRM, the LMS) increasingly sit on top of the SIS, not inside it.

enterprise.evidence:
WHO THIS IS: large public and research universities and university systems, roughly 15,000+ students, running Banner, PeopleSoft Campus Solutions, SITS or Workday Student.

SUMMARY: $1M-$6M a year. Build in-house: some, and falling. Both numbers hold after checking. The $6M top is set by one institution (WashU) whose figure also covers HR and finance, so a student-only top is probably nearer $3.5M-$4M. That is within 2x, so the range stands with this caveat.

BUILD VS BUY: some
- WashU (opened, Student Life): replaced 'nearly 80' student systems with Workday Student, live 2024-25. Separate WashU and Student Life pages describe these as homegrown 1990s apps (WebSTAC, WebFAC, SIS Admin). CONFIRMED.
- University of Washington (opened, UW admin page): the page confirms SDB is the university-wide student records system. CORRECTED: the page does not say SDB is a mainframe system or that it is being replaced. The earlier claim that it is being replaced by vendor SaaS has no source and is removed.
- Callista, Australia (opened, Tribal and ITBrief): a group of 10 universities (Monash, Deakin, UWA, ECU and others) funds and directs the Callista student system under a 5-year A$55M support and development agreement with Tribal (CSA 4, 2022). CORRECTED wording: this is a consortium-directed system with a vendor doing the work. It is not a pure in-house build.
- Read-across: homegrown systems survive at this size, but new builds are rare and the WashU case shows them being retired.

SPEND: $1M-$6M a year. This counts licence or subscription, hosting and vendor managed services. It excludes internal staff and one-time implementation.

HOW DERIVED (each line marks how it was checked)
1. Workday Student list price, E&I cooperative price sheet (opened, dated Sept 2019). Ranges from $33.42 (community college, over 20,000 FTE) to $107.96 per FTE per year, with a $300,000 minimum annual subscription. A non-community-college institution with a budget over $500M and over 20,000 FTE pays $66.83 per FTE. So 30,000 FTE is about $2.0M a year and 50,000 FTE is about $3.3M. CONFIRMED. CORRECTED wording: the earlier text gave a $66.83-$78.22 band for 30-50k FTE; only the $66.83 tier applies above 20,000 FTE. The totals are unchanged.
2. WashU (opened, Student Life, Dec 2025): $5.7M annual licensing fee. Total programme $265M over at least 7 years: HCM $81M, Student Sunrise $98.9M, planning and data $56.5M, FY2026 support $23.8M. CONFIRMED. The $5.7M covers HCM and Student together. The article does not split them and does not give enrolment; about 16,000 students is outside knowledge.
3. Jackson State, Banner SaaS (opened, Mississippi IHL minutes, June 19 2025): $6,968,198 subscription plus $3,633,716 managed services, both July 2025-June 2030. That is about $2.1M a year. There is also a one-year hosting bridge of $496,644. CONFIRMED. Caveats: JSU has about 7,000 students, so it is below this segment's size. The contract covers the whole Banner ERP (finance and HR too), so the student-only share is lower.
4. Callista (opened): A$55M over 5 years across 10 universities. That is about A$1.1M (about $0.7M) per university per year for support and development, before hosting. CONFIRMED.
5. Tribal SITS (opened, Tribal FY2025 results). CORRECTED: the roughly £1.0M ARR is for two deals combined, London South Bank's full SITS and Durham's SITS Admissions. LSBU's own value is not disclosed and is below £1.0M (about $1.3M). It shows a full UK SITS deal lands around or under $1M a year.
6. Implementation is separate and much larger. WashU's student portion alone was $98.9M (confirmed). Treat $50M-$100M+ one-time as the range for large research universities.

mid_market.evidence:
WHO THIS IS: community colleges, regional publics and mid-size private colleges (about 2,000-15,000 students), UK FE colleges and smaller UK universities. Typical systems are Ellucian Colleague, PowerCampus, Banner, Jenzabar, Tribal SITS or ebs, and Anthology.

- These institutions have small IT teams. They cannot carry the regulatory-reporting and financial-aid logic in-house.
- Many go the other way and outsource IT operations to the vendor. Washtenaw CC pays $32.8M over 5 years for Ellucian managed services, up 26% on the prior deal (Higher Ed Intel, opened). That covers IT services broadly, not only the SIS licence, so it is evidence on build vs buy, not a spend point.

HOW DERIVED (low to high)
1. Barton CC, KS, 2009 (opened, board paper). Banner annual fee about $143,000, covering student, financial aid, HR, finance and alumni. The rival Jenzabar bid was $66,730 a year (rising 5% a year) plus $685,000 to convert, $300,000 for 18 months of parallel running, $100,000 of hardware and $150,000 of extra staff. CONFIRMED. 6. UDC, about 4,000 students (opened, Higher Ed Intel): Banner, $3.18M over 3 years (Oct 2024-Sep 2027), about $1.06M a year, split roughly evenly between licence and managed hosting. CONFIRMED.

smb.evidence:
WHO THIS IS: small private colleges, seminaries and bible colleges (under about 2,000 students), single schools including private K-12, and Southeast Asia's long tail of small private campuses (Indonesia alone has 2,813 private HEIs; this count was not re-checked).

SUMMARY: $3k-$100k a year. Build in-house: some, split by region. CORRECTED the low end from $5k to $3k, because the source cited for single schools (Arbor) prices a typical primary school at about $3.7k.

criticality_why: VERDICT: critical. The call holds, but one of the original supporting facts was wrong and has been replaced. TEST 1, DOES THE BUSINESS STOP IF IT FAILS? Yes. Billing and charging is where an operator's revenue is rated, invoiced and collected. If online charging fails, prepaid customers lose service. If rating or billing fails, postpaid invoices are wrong or late and cash stops. Billing accuracy is also regulated (for example, Ofcom's General Conditions include billing rules), so a failure is a regulatory event as well as a revenue one. TEST 2, HOW DEPENDENT ARE BUYERS? Very. CSG gets 19% of its 2025 revenue from Charter ($236M) and 17% from Comcast ($210M), and says many of its main customer relationships span decades (CSG 10-K). Nepal Telecom officials say a billing cutover needs at least 24 months of migration preparation (Kathmandu Post). At Cerillion, 93% of revenue comes from existing customers and about 83% from customers of more than 5 years (Cerillion FY2025 results deck). TEST 3, IS IT WHERE OPERATORS COMPETE? Partly, and enough to pass. Operators compete on network, price and bundles. The BSS sets how fast a new tariff, bundle, 5G or enterprise offer can launch and how clean the bill is. The clearest proof is Jio, which moved off SAP to a BSS stack it built itself and now sells to other operators (Light Reading 2019; Jio Platforms). CORRECTION: the original said Rakuten built its own BSS and quoted it on vendors that assumed they knew how telecom should work. That is wrong. The source (a Rakuten Symphony newsletter) describes METAVSHN, which was built inside Ticinocom, a small Swiss ISP. The quote is from that ISP's founder. It is now used only as SMB build evidence.

enterprise.evidence: WHO: Tier 1 national mobile, fixed and cable operators. Ofcom's threshold is a useful definition: more than GBP 1bn in relevant turnover. The UK has 7 of them (Ofcom security report, period to Oct 2025, verified). BUILD VS BUY: 'some' (unchanged). Most Tier 1s buy a vendor core, customise it heavily and own the integration around it. A minority build or own the core. (a) Jio first chose SAP for charging, billing and CRM (Light Reading, Sept 2019, verified). It later built its own cloud-native BSS stack, which Jio Platforms now sells to other operators (jio.com and the TM Forum case study). The original cited Light Reading for the in-house build, but that 2019 article only covers open-source trials. The citation is now fixed. (b) Comcast's CSG contract kept the right to take some billing components in-house with written notice (Light Reading on the 2008 to 2012 extension). (c) The Rakuten example was removed. That build was a small Swiss ISP, not Rakuten (see criticality). SPEND ANCHORS, STRONGEST FIRST: (1) CSG 2025 10-K, verified: Charter $236M (19%) and Comcast $210M (17%) a year. This is mostly billing and customer care, plus statement print and mail. (2) Cerillion FY2025, verified: its largest customer, a European Tier 1 mobile base, paid GBP 13.1M (about $17M) in the year. (3) Omantel signed Cerillion for about GBP 42.5M over a 5-year term, including hosting and managed services. That is about GBP 8.5M (about $11M) a year (Cerillion RNS, Jan 2026, verified). Omantel clears the GBP 1bn Tier 1 bar. (4) Verizon's 2003 Amdocs billing and directory-assistance deal: more than $700M, possibly $1B, over 5 years. That is $140-200M a year (Telecompaper, June 2003, verified, dated). (5) Ceiling check: Amdocs FY2025 revenue was $4.53B. AT&T was 25.9% (about $1.17B) and T-Mobile 19.9% (about $0.9B) (Amdocs 20-F, verified). These are total vendor relationships covering managed services, testing, cloud and media work, and the 20-F gives no BSS-only split. They are extreme outliers, not typical spend. CORRECTIONS: the high end was cut from $1.2B to $300M. The $1.2B was AT&T's whole Amdocs bill, not BSS spend, and the original text itself put most Tier 1s at $30-250M. The billing-specific anchors (Verizon $140-200M, Comcast $210M, Charter $236M) cluster below $250M, so $300M covers the largest typical buyer. The low end was cut from $20M to $10M. The original's own Omantel evidence shows a GBP 1bn-plus incumbent spending about $11M a year all-in, which contradicts a $20M floor. RANGE: about $10M to $300M a year. Smaller national incumbents sit at $10-30M, large national operators at $50-250M, and the US mega-carriers' total vendor relationships can reach about $1B.

mid_market.evidence: WHO: Tier 2 and Tier 3 operators, regional cable and fibre operators, altnets and larger MVNOs. In Ofcom's terms these have GBP 50M to 1bn turnover, and the UK has 31 of them (Ofcom, verified). BUILD VS BUY: 'rare' (unchanged). Most lack the engineering depth to build. They buy suites from Cerillion, Tecnotree, Qvantel/Optiva, Oracle BRM, Netcracker and others. No source directly measures how often they build, so this is a judgement, but nothing found contradicts it. SPEND ANCHORS: (1) Cerillion FY2025 (year to 30 Sept 2025), verified: revenue GBP 45.4M across about 70 installations, an average of about GBP 0.65M (about $0.85M). One customer was GBP 13.1M (30% of revenue). Without it, the average is about GBP 0.47M (about $0.6M) per installation per year, including implementation services. (2) Cerillion's Ucom (Armenia) deal is $11.4M over 5 years, about $2.3M a year, for a national provider with more than 1M customers (Cerillion RNS, Jan 2025, verified). (3) Amdocs' tail: the top ten customers are about 70% of $4.53B, which leaves about $1.36B across about 390 of its roughly 400 customers, an average of about $3.5M (Amdocs 20-F, verified). That tail also includes Tier 1s ranked below the top ten, plus media and financial-services customers, so $3.5M overstates the mid-market average. It is a ceiling check, not a midpoint. CORRECTION: the original said about 89% of Cerillion installations are more than 5 years old, so the base is ageing. The results deck does not say that. It says about 83% of revenue comes from customers of more than 5 years and 93% from existing customers. That measures how long customers stay (sticky relationships), not how old the software is. RANGE: about $0.5M to $5M a year (unchanged; the anchors support it).

smb.evidence: WHO: small ISPs, WISPs, rural telcos and cooperatives, small fibre builders and small MVNOs. They buy per-subscriber SaaS billing, not legacy Tier 1 BSS. BUILD VS BUY: 'some' (unchanged). A share run homegrown tools, spreadsheets or accounting software. METAVSHN started as the in-house system of Ticinocom, a small Swiss family ISP, replacing an early-2000s ColdFusion monolith (Rakuten Symphony newsletter, verified). It is the correct example for this segment, not for Tier 1. Most buyers here use cheap SaaS. SPEND, FROM PUBLIC PRICE LISTS (verified): Sonar charges $1.25 per active subscriber per month for 1-5,000 subscribers, $1.00 for 5,001-10,000 and $0.75 for 10,001-50,000, with a $500 monthly minimum on an annual contract. That works out to $6k a year at the minimum, $75k at 5,000 subscribers and about $135k at 10,000 if tiers apply in steps (about $120k if not). Splynx licenses in blocks of 100 from a 400-subscriber minimum and does not publish its per-subscriber rate. Its ACS add-on costs $100-1,000 a month. CORRECTION, MINOR: the original said 'about $150k with add-ons'. Sonar's premium add-ons are quote-only, so that figure is an estimate, not a list price. $150k stays as a reasonable top for an ISP of about 10-12k subscribers. RANGE: about $6k to $150k a year (unchanged). The segment is crowded with low-priced vendors.

government.evidence: WHO: state-owned or state-controlled operators, such as BSNL and MTNL (India), Nepal Telecom, Omantel, and VNPT, Viettel and MobiFone (Vietnam). A smaller group is municipal fibre utilities, such as Palo Alto's OSS/BSS RFP, which spend at SMB to mid-market levels. Governments do not otherwise buy telecom BSS for themselves. BUILD VS BUY: 'some' (unchanged). They mostly buy through public tenders, often with domestic integrators. Some push for local development. Nepal's ministry and PMO advisers proposed splitting the online charging system and hardware from the BSS so that domestic companies could build part of the software (Kathmandu Post, Aug 2026, verified). SPEND ANCHORS: (1) Nepal Telecom's replacement tender is about NPR 5bn, about $37-38M. It replaces an AsiaInfo system installed in 2011, and the current contract ends in 2027 (Kathmandu Post, verified). The new contract's term is not published. Spread over 5-7 years, and including hardware, that is about $5-7.5M a year. (2) Omantel, majority state-owned, pays about $11M a year over a 5-year term, including hosting and managed services (Cerillion RNS, verified). (3) BSNL awarded INR 12bn (about $300M at 2007 exchange rates) to TCS, HCL and Wipro in Sept 2007 for its CDR convergent-billing project, due for completion by Dec 2008. It served about 65M subscribers (Telecompaper, verified; this replaces the ktpl.com link, which returned 403). That price included building data centres and a countrywide network, so billing-only spend was lower. Over a 5-year life it is at most about $60M a year, which sets the top of the range. OUTLIER NOTE: China's state-owned big three are far above this range. AsiaInfo's 2024 revenue was about RMB 6.6bn (about $0.9bn), mostly from Chinese carriers. They are excluded as untypical and largely closed to foreign vendors. RANGE: about $3M to $60M a year for state operators (unchanged; the anchors support it).

best_icp: Sell first to mid-market operators (Tier 2 and Tier 3 mobile, fixed and cable operators, altnets and larger MVNOs). Each spends about $0.5M to $5M a year (a Ucom-sized national provider is about $2.3M), they rarely build in-house, and they award contracts in competitive tenders that a challenger like Cerillion wins. That beats Tier 1s, which spend $10M to $300M but are locked into decades-long Amdocs or CSG relationships, sometimes build their own (Jio), and need 24-month migrations; it also beats SMB ISPs, which pay 10 to 30 times less through cheap per-subscriber SaaS. Expect long sales cycles and loyal customers once won: about 83% of Cerillion's revenue comes from customers of more than 5 years.

criticality_why:
VERDICT: important (unchanged after review). The test for "critical" has two parts: the business stops or loses its licence if the system fails, AND the system is where the firm competes. Trade finance passes the first part only in a narrow sense and fails the second.

1) How much the bank depends on it. The trade finance engine books letters of credit (LCs), guarantees and collections, sends the SWIFT messages and applies the ICC rules (UCP 600, URDG). If it goes down, the trade desk cannot issue or pay, and live instruments that run for months or years go unserviced. That is real dependence. But it is one product line. Core banking, payments and lending keep running, and the bank keeps its licence. So it does not meet "the business stops".

2) Whether banks compete on it. For most banks, no. The Fed (May 2026) reports that about 90% of US banks report zero commercial LCs, and the five largest providers hold over 75% of trade loans (Y-14) and over 87% of trade claims (FFIEC 009). The big trade banks compete on balance sheet, network and client channels. Per IFC (2017), Citi, HSBC, ICICI, Deutsche Bank, Santander and JPMorgan run their own proprietary supply chain finance platforms, which is where they differentiate. The back-office LC and guarantee engine they mostly buy: HSBC chose CGI Trade360 (April 2019), SBI runs Finastra.

3) The exception. For trade-specialist banks (the Fed notes some banks under $25B in assets where trade is a material share of the business) and for export-credit banks, the system is close to critical. They are a small part of the buyer base, so "important" is the right rating overall.

Review note: the criticality reasoning matched its sources. No change.

enterprise.evidence:
RANGE: $1M to $8M a year per bank (unchanged after review). Low end is anchored to a public tender. High end is an inference, not a cited figure.

WHO: global and tier-1 trade banks running trade across many countries. Verified examples: HSBC (CGI Trade360) and SBI (Finastra). They hold most of the volume: the five largest US providers account for 75-87% of US trade finance (Fed, May 2026).

BUILD OR BUY: some.
- Client-facing layers are often built. IFC (2017) names Citi, HSBC, ICICI, Deutsche Bank, Santander and JPMorgan as running proprietary supply chain finance platforms, and says the build option is expensive.
- The back-office LC and guarantee engine is usually bought, then heavily customised. HSBC chose CGI Trade360 on 30 April 2019 and went live in the UK and Hong Kong on 7 October 2022 (about 3.5 years). CGI says the platform supports about $800bn of trade a year.
- SBI consolidated trade processing for 25 countries onto Finastra in 14 months (Finastra case study, 2018). Corrected: the draft said 25-29 countries and cited the wrong source.

SPEND, step by step:
(a) Market average. Aite (Feb 2023) forecast global trade finance software spend of $925M by end-2025. Disclosed vendor footprints: Finastra 200+ banks, Surecomp 300+ clients (banks and corporates), BankTrade 100+ banks, CGI Trade360 322 bank locations (locations, not separate banks, so this overstates the count), plus Oracle, Intellect and others. That suggests roughly 1,000 to 1,500 buyers at most, so an average of about $0.6-0.9M per buyer. Because buyers overlap and CGI counts locations, the true average is probably at or above the top of that band.
(b) Floor from a public tender. Bank of Baroda's 2026 tender (GeM bid GEM/2026/B/7384384, opened and checked) covers supply, implementation and maintenance of a trade finance solution over 5 years. It sets an earnest-money deposit (EMD) of Rs 2 crore (Rs 20,000,000) and a bidder turnover floor of Rs 50 crore. Under India's General Financial Rules, Rule 170, EMD is "ordinarily" 2-5% of estimated value. That implies Rs 40-100 crore over 5 years, about $0.9-2.3M a year at roughly Rs 88 per dollar. Bank of Baroda is a large bank with an overseas network, and Indian prices run low, so $1M is a fair floor for a global bank.
(c) Ceiling. No HSBC/CGI or Intellect deal value is public. Cross-check: if the top 100 or so trade banks take about half of the $925M, the average is about $4.6M each, and the largest multi-country platforms would sit above that. $8M is consistent with that, but treat it as an estimate.

WHAT CHANGED IN REVIEW: numbers kept. SBI country count and source corrected. CGI figure relabelled as locations.

mid_market.evidence:
RANGE: $150K to $800K a year per bank (unchanged after review). Triangulated from a vendor list price, a vendor revenue estimate and the market average. No mid-market contract value is published.

WHO: tier-2 regional banks, trade-specialist banks and single-country banks that run a dedicated trade engine. Examples named in vendor material: Bank of the West and First Hawaiian (Finastra), Bank of Ireland, I&M Bank, Banco Pichincha and Crown Agents Bank (Surecomp), Bank BTPN Indonesia (Surecomp IMEX), Raiffeisenlandesbanks (Intellect). These client names were not individually re-checked in review. The Fed notes some banks under $25B where trade is a material share of the business.

BUILD OR BUY: rare. These banks lack the budget and trade-IT staff to build an engine that must handle SWIFT MT and ISO 20022 messaging and the ICC rules. They buy from Finastra, Surecomp, China Systems or BankTrade ("over 100" trade banks), or use the trade module of their core banking system.

SPEND, step by step:
(a) Floor. Surecomp's press release of 22 Sep 2021 (opened and checked) prices its SaaS back office for "smaller and mid-sized banks" from $50K a year, covering LC and guarantee processing, live within 10 weeks. A mid-market bank adding a customer portal, supply chain finance and more users pays a multiple of that.
(b) Vendor average. Third-party estimates put Surecomp revenue at about $57-63M (Owler and similar, not audited). Corrected: the draft said $50-100M and cited a page that gives no revenue. Spread over 300+ clients, that is about $190-210K per client a year, and the mix leans to mid-market banks.
(c) Ceiling. The market average from Aite's $925M is about $0.6-0.9M per buyer, and tier-1 banks pull it up. Mid-market spend should sit under it, so $800K is a sensible top.

WHAT CHANGED IN REVIEW: range kept. Surecomp revenue figure narrowed and re-sourced.

smb.evidence:
RANGE: $50K to $150K a year, but only for the few small banks that buy at all (unchanged after review).

WHO: community banks, small banks, and small UK and EU subsidiaries of foreign banks.

MOST DO NOT BUY. The Fed (May 2026) reports that about 90% of US banks report zero commercial LCs. When a community bank's customer needs an LC, the bank usually passes it to a correspondent. Example: INTRUST Bank's correspondent unit (page checked) offers import and export LCs, banker's acceptances and documentary collections to other banks. For the typical small bank, spend on a dedicated system is zero.

BUILD OR BUY: rare. No small bank builds one.

SPEND for those that buy:
- Floor: Surecomp's SaaS price "from $50K" a year for smaller banks (Sep 2021 press release, checked).
- Top: $150K allows for portal or add-on modules. This is an estimate, not a cited figure.
- Named small adopters (vendor material, not re-checked): Sonali Bank UK, Crown Agents Bank.

OUT OF SCOPE: small importers and exporters are a separate buyer group. They use corporate front-ends such as Surecomp allNETT/RIVO and multi-bank platforms. Not sized here.

government.evidence:
RANGE: $150K to $2.5M a year per bank. CORRECTED: the low end was $50K and is raised to $150K (3x). The high end is unchanged.

WHO: state-owned commercial banks and export-credit or development banks. Examples: Indian public sector banks (Central Bank of India, Bank of Baroda), J&K Bank (state-controlled), BNI Indonesia (Finastra), National Bank of Pakistan, EXIM Bank India. Governments do not run LC engines directly. Their state banks do.

BUILD OR BUY: rare. Public tenders buy a vendor product through a systems integrator. Central Bank of India (2022 RFP, opened and checked) wants a licence that includes ATS and all upgrades, and bidders with 3+ years of trade finance implementation experience. Its existing system, FX24, was supplied by Intellect. Bank of Baroda (2026) sets a minimum bidder turnover of Rs 50 crore.

SPEND, step by step:
(a) High end. Bank of Baroda, GeM bid GEM/2026/B/7384384 (checked): EMD Rs 2 crore, 5-year contract, supply, implementation and maintenance. At 2-5% EMD under GFR Rule 170, that implies Rs 40-100 crore, about $0.9-2.3M a year at Rs 88 per dollar. Rounded up to $2.5M.
(b) Middle. J&K Bank's 2026 trade finance RFP sets an EMD of Rs 50 lakh (from search results; the PDF would not load, so not opened). At 2-5%, that implies Rs 10-25 crore, roughly $0.2-0.6M a year if the term is 5 years.
(c) Low end, and why it was corrected. The draft used Central Bank of India's EMD of Rs 10 lakh to imply a contract of only Rs 2-5 crore ($50-120K a year). The RFP itself does not support that. Its scope covers about 4,600 branches, end-to-end trade, a customer portal and supply chain finance, the bidder's hardware at both data centre and DR site, and onsite facility management for 5 years. It also demands a bidder turnover of Rs 100 crore. A Rs 10 lakh EMD is a flat token amount here, not 2-5% of value (GFR Rule 170 binds ministries and departments, says "ordinarily", and allows a bid-securing declaration instead). J&K Bank, a much smaller bank, set an EMD five times higher. So $50K understated what a state bank pays. $150K reflects the smallest state-owned or development banks buying at mid-market prices.

CAVEAT: EMD only bounds the estimated value. No award prices were published.

best_icp: Sell first to mid-market, trade-active banks (tier-2 regional banks, trade-specialist banks under about $25B in assets, and mid-size Asian and emerging-market banks), because they buy rather than build, already pay about $150K-$800K a year, and can go live on vendor SaaS in about 10 weeks by Surecomp's own claim, while tier-1 banks take years (HSBC took about 3.5 years from choosing CGI to first go-live) and most community banks have no LC book at all.

criticality_why:
VERDICT: changed from 'critical' to 'important'. The rubric gives 'critical' only when two things are both true: (a) the business stops or loses its licence if the system fails, and (b) the system is where the firm competes. Test (a) clearly passes. Test (b) fails for most buyers.

TEST (a), THE BUSINESS STOPS: PASS. All revenue runs through the billing system (CIS), and failures are public and regulated. Ontario, CA bills about $125M a year through CIS Infinity (40,000 bills a month; checked in the council report). LADWP's CIS went from an $87M budget to $187M spent, and the utility then had $681M in past-due bills (checked, NBC LA, citing the state auditor). Con Edison's Oracle project cost $509M against a $421M cap. The New York PSC disallowed the $88M overrun, which caused a $37M net loss in Q2 2024 (checked). Duke Energy's 2022 SAP 'Customer Connect' cutover produced 106,453 billing errors in Ohio within a year and drew a PUCO settlement (checked, WCPO/Journal-News). Disconnection rules, tariff compliance and rate-case cost recovery all run through the system.

TEST (b), WHERE THE FIRM COMPETES: FAILS FOR MOST BUYERS. Most buyers by count are regulated monopolies: US municipal utilities, co-ops, investor-owned utilities, and Asian state utilities. Their customers cannot leave, so billing is not how they win. The original research admitted this ('closer to important for those buyers') but kept 'critical' anyway. Our recommended first customers (US municipal and co-op utilities) are all in this monopoly group. The one exception is competitive energy retailers (UK, Australia, Texas, Singapore), where billing is a real edge. Octopus built Kraken in-house for this reason, and Origin expected A$100-150M a year in savings from moving 3.8M accounts onto it (checked, ESD News). For those buyers the label 'critical' holds.

NET: 'important' across the market. Treat billing as 'critical' only when selling to competitive retailers.

enterprise.evidence:
WHO: investor-owned utilities and large energy retailers with about 1M or more accounts (Con Edison, Duke, PG&E, Origin, EDF, E.ON).

BUILD VS BUY: 'some' (unchanged). Most buy a packaged core, either SAP IS-U/S4 Utilities or Oracle CC&B/C2M, and then own a heavily customised copy built by system integrators. Con Ed spent $86M on outside labour (checked). LADWP paid PwC about $60M (widely reported, not re-checked). A few build their own. Octopus built Kraken in 2017 and now licenses it. Some older home-grown and Customer/1 mainframe systems are still running.

criticality_why:
VERDICT: Critical. The call holds for the core buyers (3PLs, retailers, e-commerce sellers, distributors). It does not hold for every buyer. See the caveat at the end.

HOW THE TWO TESTS WERE APPLIED
Test 1. Does the business stop if the system fails? Yes. The WMS directs every receipt, putaway, pick, pack and ship. If it is down, nothing leaves the dock and orders miss their ship dates. Two signs that operators treat it this way: (a) companies freeze WMS changes and block cutovers during peak season, and (b) migrations go one site at a time. The US Defense Logistics Agency (DLA) took about eight years to move its distribution network to SAP, from a pilot at Corpus Christi in June 2018 to the last site (Hill, Utah) in August 2026 (DLA news, Federal News Network).

Test 2. Is it where the firm competes? Yes, for the core buyers.
- 3PLs: warehousing is the product they sell. Client billing, client portals and service levels all run on the WMS.
- Retailers and e-commerce sellers: delivery speed and order accuracy are competitive weapons, and both depend on the WMS.
- The strongest proof is what the biggest players do. Amazon runs a proprietary WMS it built in-house and does not sell (SupplyKick). Firms only build in-house what they believe sets them apart.

CORRECTIONS MADE IN REVIEW
- The earlier draft cited Walmart as building its own WMS. The cited Walmart Global Tech post covers an AI inventory forecasting engine with a patent-pending anomaly filter. It does not show Walmart building warehouse execution software, so it is no longer used as proof.
- The earlier draft said DLA's migration ran "2020 into 2026" across 34 warehouses. The program started in 2018 and DLA's own 2026 release counts 24 distribution locations (Nextgov's 2023 article said 34 regional distribution centers). Both figures are now stated.

CAVEAT: For a manufacturer whose warehouse only stores parts and finished goods, the system is important but not where it competes. These buyers often stay on their ERP's built-in module (for example SAP LE-WM) rather than buy a standalone WMS. If the target market were mainly manufacturers, the rating would be "important".

criticality_why:
Verdict: important, not critical. The call holds after review.

Why the business depends on it. Portfolio accounting is the book of record for positions, cost basis, performance and fees. If it fails, client statements, fee billing, NAV strikes and regulatory reports stop. Goldman Sachs Asset Management calls its InvestOne platform "a mission critical application", and every downstream system there (order management, regulatory, compliance, client reporting) is built around its data. A fund administrator that misses a NAV, or a trust bank that cannot reconcile, is in regulatory breach.

Why it is not where buyers compete. Wealth managers, private banks and pension funds win on advice, returns and the client relationship. The accounting engine is a commodity they license or outsource. SEI, Avaloq, SimCorp, FIS and SS&C all sell it as shared infrastructure. SEI's Private Banks segment alone books $381M a year in Investment Technology and Operations revenue running this for banks (SEI 10-K 2024). Client-facing reporting (Addepar's pitch to UHNW firms) is the part closest to a differentiator.

Exception. Firms whose product is the accounting itself (fund administrators, custodians running InvestOne or Eagle for others) would rate it critical. For the typical buyer it is important.

Review correction: the earlier draft labelled SEI's $381M as "information processing and software fees". The 10-K line is "Investment Technology & Operations". The number is correct.
